binding: overview: Bound in brown calfskin over pasteboards with blind stamped and rolled decoration, by WisemanWiseman, 1862. Evidence preserved in MSS Ff.1.25(1) and MS Ff.1.25(5) (recycled endleaf bearing four friction-holes and rust stains, suggesting the presence formerly of four corner-bosses and a chain staple) indicates that all five volumes were previously bound together in similar style to that of the binding on other manuscripts donated to the University Library by Matthew Parker (for an example, see: MS Ii.2.4). See Provenance and Acquisition for further details. Thomas James's catalogue, Ecloga Oxonio-Cantabrigiensis (1600) allocates two numbers to MS Ff.1.25: 244: 1. Gu. Malmesbury de pontificum gestis, lib. 59, vltimus liber scriptus est a neoterico ... 2. Nouella historia Anglorum ... 245: 1. Liber cum hac inscriptione. Itinerarium peregrinantium in terram sanctam ... 2. Galfridu Monumetensis ... This implies that the manuscript was bound in two volumes at this time. However, in the list of manuscripts donated by Parker to the University Library in 1574, the manuscript is described as containing 460 pages. Such statements of extent were given for each of Parker's donations and were also written onto one of the opening leaves of the manuscripts themselves (see MS Ff.1.25(1), f. 3r). None of the other manuscripts within the Ff.1.25 classmark contain such an inscription, and the total number of pages amounts to 460, by the Parkerian pagination (see Foliation for further details). Furthermore, as described above, Parker's donations were (with the odd exception) bound in a consistent format, and where the manuscripts have been rebound since that time this evidence is often preserved within the new binding. In MS Ff.1.25(1), only the recycled endleaves at the front of the volume have been preserved. Only Ff.1.25(5) contains similar endleaves, and only at the rear; they are found in none of the other volumes. The material evidence thus points to the manuscripts that are now Ff.1.25(1)-(5) having arrived bound as a single volume. Furthermore, each of these volumes bear evidence of having had the author(s) and title(s) of their contents inked onto the fore-edges of their leaves, presumably by Wheelocke, Abraham, 1593-1653 Abraham Wheelocke , who treated other manuscripts in a similar manner (see, for example, MS Ff.1.28. This indicates moreover that the manuscript remained as a single volume in the mid-17th century. In his History of the University Library, David McKitterick recounts that the part of this manuscript containing the Historia regum Britanniae (now MS Ff.1.25(5)) was discovered to be missing when the manuscripts in the Old Library were inspected in 1732 and again in 1748: the number '245' assigned by James in 1600 is in both lists, in the first with the partial title 'Galfrid: monumethensis etc' (see Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 4451, ff. 18r and 19r). The implication is that by this stage Ff.1.25 had been rebound into two volumes. However, a more probable explanation is that James's assigning of two numbers to the manuscript misled the compilers of these lists of missing books, who were searching fruitlessly for Geoffrey of Monmouth and other texts bound into a discrete volume, when in fact they remained in place in the same volume as what James has designated '244'. Indeed, that no mention is made in the Catalogue of manuscripts preserved in the Library of the University of Cambridge, vol. 2 (1857) means that it is almost certain that it was not divided into separate volumes until 1862.

provenance: overview: Probably owned by Alice de Reydon Reydon, Alice de, née Reymes, wife of Robert de Reydon. Her obituary is added to the Calendar in a contemporary hand, on the 5th July (fol. 16r): 'Obitus Alicie de Reidon anno domini Mo ccco x...'. The year is uncertain, but must be after 1310 (the first limb of 'x' is visible; if any number followed, it has been cropped) but before 1323: the Inquisitions Post Mortem held in that year on Alice's husband gives the name of his widow as Margaret. The manuscript may have been produced for her prior to her marriage, since her family's coat of arms features on f. 19r. The female figures on ff. 1v and 19r may have been intended to represent her: the mantle of the former figure has had the Reymes family coat of arms painted over it (the cross or has been divided in two vertically and painted along each edge). Calendar of Inquisitions Post Mortem, vol. 6, Edward II (1910), no. 419 Raimes (1939) ; Two early fourteenth century hands have inserted additional feast days that confirm an East Anglian provenance: St Winwaloe ('Sancti Winewaloei') on 3rd March (f. 14r) and St Ethelbert on 21st May (usually 20th; f. 15r). Winwaloe is more commonly patron saint of foundations in the south-west, his reputed homeland, however a Benedictine priory dedicated to him was founded at Wereham in 1199; it was later dissolved in 1321 and given to nearby abbey of West Dereham. ; Stranle family: the birth dates of John Stranle (17th February) (f. 13v) and Matilda Stranle (9th April) (f. 14v) were inserted in the calendar, by perhaps the same hand. Another, later hand glossed the entry for John Stranle with the year of his birth: 'anno Regis Ricardi secundi quarto' (1380/81).

codicology: collation: The manuscript comprises two parts, both written on paper but of different stocks. The first part comprises two quires, originally of 18 leaves each. The first leaf of Quire 1 was perhaps a former pastedown, which has been excised when the manuscript was rebound. A stub before the beginning of Quire 2, and the absence of any interruption to the text, suggests that the 1st leaf was cancelled. The 2nd leaf, now f. 18, has no conjoint leaf. The 17th and 18th leaves of Quire 2, to which the 1st and 2nd leaves would have originally been attached, are no longer present. It is possible, however, that these are in fact ff. 2:37-38, which appear to be from the same paper stock and bear notes by the same hand that was responsible for copying the text in the first part of the manuscript. (This hand is nowhere to be found in the second part of the manuscript, which points to the two parts - their shared subject-matter notwithstanding - having been produced entirely separately and only bound together at a later juncture). The damage that these leaves have suffered, however, is of the same pattern as those towards the end of the second part of the manuscript, suggesting that they have been bound in this location for a lengthy period of time. The status of f. 39 is less clear, however. It too is of the same paper stock, so originally belonged with the leaves of the first part of the manuscript, but is more likely a remnant of an endleaf, pastedown or wrapper than part of either Quires 1 or 2. The second part of the manuscript comprises two quires of 16 leaves, plus a third quire of 4 leaves: these may be two bifolia, however the tightness of the binding means that the sewing is not visible and so the structure remains uncertain. codicology: foliation: 20th-century foliation [i] + 1-32 | 1-36 | 37-39 + [ii] Numbered in pencil, in the upper right-hand corner of the rectos, by a hand of the 20th century. The hand has numbered the parts of the manuscript separately rather than in one continuous sequence. For the purposes of cataloguing, digitisation and display, an additional prefatory number is added to each of these sequences, in order to signify the relevant part of the manuscript. So: [i] + 1:1-32 | 2:1-36 | 2:37-39 + [ii].
binding: overview: Quarter-bound binding in modern leather with marbled paper, vellum tips, by Douglas Cockerell and SonDouglas Cockerell and Son (Firm), 1974. In an unpublished description of the manuscript by M.R. James (see Source), the manuscript is described as being bound in 'paper boards'. MS Ii.6.33 was bound with MS Ii.6.34 in this form since at least the publication of the relevant volume of the Catalogue of manuscripts preserved in the Library of the University of Cambridge (vol. 3, 1858), where this is noted. In the first listing of the contents of John Moore's library in 1697 (see Provenance), these two manuscripts were described separately: Ii.6.33 as no. 253 and Ii.6.34 as no. 200. This indicates that they were at that stage physically separate items. It may be that they were bound together only after the arrival of Moore's library at Cambridge University Library in 1715, only to be separated again in 1974.

binding: overview: Bound in brown calfskin over pasteboards with blind stamped and rolled decoration, by WisemanWiseman, 1862. Evidence preserved in MSS Ff.1.25(1) and MS Ff.1.25(5) (recycled endleaf bearing four friction-holes and rust stains, suggesting the presence formerly of four corner-bosses and a chain staple) indicates that all five volumes were previously bound together in similar style to that of the binding on other manuscripts donated to the University Library by Matthew Parker (for an example, see: MS Ii.2.4). See Provenance and Acquisition for further details. Thomas James's catalogue, Ecloga Oxonio-Cantabrigiensis (1600) allocates two numbers to MS Ff.1.25: 244: 1. Gu. Malmesbury de pontificum gestis, lib. 59, vltimus liber scriptus est a neoterico ... 2. Nouella historia Anglorum ... 245: 1. Liber cum hac inscriptione. Itinerarium peregrinantium in terram sanctam ... 2. Galfridu Monumetensis ... This implies that the manuscript was bound in two volumes at this time. However, in the list of manuscripts donated by Parker to the University Library in 1574, the manuscript is described as containing 460 pages. Such statements of extent were given for each of Parker's donations and were also written onto one of the opening leaves of the manuscripts themselves (see MS Ff.1.25(1), f. 3r). None of the other manuscripts within the Ff.1.25 classmark contain such an inscription, and the total number of pages amounts to 460, by the Parkerian pagination (see Foliation for further details). Furthermore, as described above, Parker's donations were (with the odd exception) bound in a consistent format, and where the manuscripts have been rebound since that time this evidence is often preserved within the new binding. In MS Ff.1.25(1), only the recycled endleaves at the front of the volume have been preserved. Only Ff.1.25(5) contains similar endleaves, and only at the rear; they are found in none of the other volumes. The material evidence thus points to the manuscripts that are now Ff.1.25(1)-(5) having arrived bound as a single volume. Furthermore, each of these volumes bear evidence of having had the author(s) and title(s) of their contents inked onto the fore-edges of their leaves, presumably by Wheelocke, Abraham, 1593-1653 Abraham Wheelocke , who treated other manuscripts in a similar manner (see, for example, MS Ff.1.28. This indicates moreover that the manuscript remained as a single volume in the mid-17th century. In his History of the University Library, David McKitterick recounts that the part of this manuscript containing the Historia regum Britanniae (now MS Ff.1.25(5)) was discovered to be missing when the manuscripts in the Old Library were inspected in 1732 and again in 1748: the number '245' assigned by James in 1600 is in both lists, in the first with the partial title 'Galfrid: monumethensis etc' (see Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 4451, ff. 18r and 19r). The implication is that by this stage Ff.1.25 had been rebound into two volumes. However, a more probable explanation is that James's assigning of two numbers to the manuscript misled the compilers of these lists of missing books, who were searching fruitlessly for Geoffrey of Monmouth and other texts bound into a discrete volume, when in fact they remained in place in the same volume as what James has designated '244'. Indeed, that no mention is made in the Catalogue of manuscripts preserved in the Library of the University of Cambridge, vol. 2 (1857) means that it is almost certain that it was not divided into separate volumes until 1862.

codicology: foliation: Preliminary note: Unfortunately, the manuscript has been subjected to a series of attempts at foliation. With one, later exception, none of these attempts covered the manuscript as a whole: 9th-century core as well as the extraneous, later medieval leaves that enclose it. The first sequence to be added appears to be by the hand of Henry BradshawBradshaw, Henry, 1831-1886, University Librarian 1867-1886, who numbered the 9th-century leaves '2-98' (in pencil, in the top right-hand corner of the rectos). He assigned '1' to a leaf at the beginning that he judged to be missing (as per the foliation practice he established at Cambridge University Library). A later foliator numbered the extraneous leaves in two continuous sequences of Roman numerals: i-xxvi at the front and i-xxviii at the back. Subsequently, these were subdivided with letters A-F, apparently in order to demarcate codicological divisions between the added leaves. However, not every such division was captured by this intervention: compare the first and second leaves of 'C' with the third and forth. The likelihood is that whoever added these letters was following the quire numbers added in ink to the centre of the bottom margin by an 18th- or 19th-century hand. Furthermore, a haphazard change was then made to the Roman numeral foliation, restarting the sequence at each lettered division by overwriting the superceded numerals. This was done tentatively, however, with the cancellation being not always obvious. The only consistent and correct sequence are the Arabic numerals written in pencil, in the bottom right-hand corner of the recto side, probably during the 20th century. These are written continuously for the extraneous leaves, but only at intervals for the 9th-century core, which regrettably obstructs straightforward reference. It is recognised that most scholarship has referred and will refer to foliation in the place where it is most commonly found in medieval manuscripts: that is, in the top right-hand corner of the recto side of each leaf. In order to minimise the disruption to citations past and future, the decision has been made to follow the approach used in A.N. Doane, Anglo-Saxon Bibles and 'The Book of Cerne', Anglo-Saxon Manuscripts in Microfiche Facsimile, vol. 7 (Tempe, 2002). There, the manuscript is divided into three broad parts, as follows: Part 1: a collection of bifolia and quires containing memoranda of documents relating to Cerne of various origins and dates Part 2: the 9th-century prayer book Part 3: the sequentiary Recognising the separate origins of the component sections of Parts 1 and 3, Doane subdivided these using letters, which will be followed here and prefixed to the foliation. This permits the continuous sequence of Roman numerals to be followed, while ensuring that the duplicated sequences at the front and rear are unique - necessary for the preparation of a digital catalogue description. Bradshaw's foliation will be retained for Part 2. The sequence as a whole will thus be: [a] + 1a:i-1a:ii | 1b:iii-1b:iv | 1c:v-1c:vi | 1d:vii-1d:viii | 1e:ix-1e:xviii | 1f:xix-1f:xxvi | 2:2-2:99 | 3a:i-3a:xxiv | 3b:xxv-3b:xxviii + [b]
binding: overview: The manuscript has undergone several successive rebindings, encompassing the 9th-century core alone as well as with the later additions, and traces of their structure may be seen in the sewing patterns left on the leaves. For a diagrammatic illustration of these, see Brown (1996), p. 234. Full goatskin binding by Sandy Cockerell Cockerell, Sydney Morris, 1962. A typescript summary of Cockerell's work in attached to the rear pastedown. Bowtell-style quarter sheepskin binding with marbled paper-covered sides, late 18th-century. For a description of the make-up and condition of this binding upon its arrival at Grantchester for rebinding in 1962, see Brown (1996), p. 33. A spine label from this binding - reading 'MAGNA CARTA ETC. M.S.' - has been retained on the front pastedown. Although the microfiche that accompanies the description in Doane (2002) antedates the 1962 rebinding, neither the exterior nor interior of the covers was captured.

binding: overview: Bound in brown calfskin over pasteboards with blind stamped and rolled decoration, by WisemanWiseman, 1862. Evidence preserved in MSS Ff.1.25(1) and MS Ff.1.25(5) (recycled endleaf bearing four friction-holes and rust stains, suggesting the presence formerly of four corner-bosses and a chain staple) indicates that all five volumes were previously bound together in similar style to that of the binding on other manuscripts donated to the University Library by Matthew Parker (for an example, see: MS Ii.2.4). See Provenance and Acquisition for further details. Thomas James's catalogue, Ecloga Oxonio-Cantabrigiensis (1600) allocates two numbers to MS Ff.1.25: 244: 1. Gu. Malmesbury de pontificum gestis, lib. 59, vltimus liber scriptus est a neoterico ... 2. Nouella historia Anglorum ... 245: 1. Liber cum hac inscriptione. Itinerarium peregrinantium in terram sanctam ... 2. Galfridu Monumetensis ... This implies that the manuscript was bound in two volumes at this time. However, in the list of manuscripts donated by Parker to the University Library in 1574, the manuscript is described as containing 460 pages. Such statements of extent were given for each of Parker's donations and were also written onto one of the opening leaves of the manuscripts themselves (see MS Ff.1.25(1), f. 3r). None of the other manuscripts within the Ff.1.25 classmark contain such an inscription, and the total number of pages amounts to 460, by the Parkerian pagination (see Foliation for further details). Furthermore, as described above, Parker's donations were (with the odd exception) bound in a consistent format, and where the manuscripts have been rebound since that time this evidence is often preserved within the new binding. In MS Ff.1.25(1), only the recycled endleaves at the front of the volume have been preserved. Only Ff.1.25(5) contains similar endleaves, and only at the rear; they are found in none of the other volumes. The material evidence thus points to the manuscripts that are now Ff.1.25(1)-(5) having arrived bound as a single volume. Furthermore, each of these volumes bear evidence of having had the author(s) and title(s) of their contents inked onto the fore-edges of their leaves, presumably by Wheelocke, Abraham, 1593-1653 Abraham Wheelocke , who treated other manuscripts in a similar manner (see, for example, MS Ff.1.28. This indicates moreover that the manuscript remained as a single volume in the mid-17th century. In his History of the University Library, David McKitterick recounts that the part of this manuscript containing the Historia regum Britanniae (now MS Ff.1.25(5)) was discovered to be missing when the manuscripts in the Old Library were inspected in 1732 and again in 1748: the number '245' assigned by James in 1600 is in both lists, in the first with the partial title 'Galfrid: monumethensis etc' (see Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 4451, ff. 18r and 19r). The implication is that by this stage Ff.1.25 had been rebound into two volumes. However, a more probable explanation is that James's assigning of two numbers to the manuscript misled the compilers of these lists of missing books, who were searching fruitlessly for Geoffrey of Monmouth and other texts bound into a discrete volume, when in fact they remained in place in the same volume as what James has designated '244'. Indeed, that no mention is made in the Catalogue of manuscripts preserved in the Library of the University of Cambridge, vol. 2 (1857) means that it is almost certain that it was not divided into separate volumes until 1862.

codicology: condition: The manuscript is generally of a good condition. The leaf height and width offered above is, however, an average measurement. codicology: collation: 18 (wants 1), 214, 312, 48 There are no conventional catchwords or quire signatures visible in MS Ll.5.18. Having said this, there is equally no explicit evidence to suggest that trimming to remove such inclusions has occurred. Certainly, the retention of the marginalia on f. 36r, in which the final letters are obfuscated by wear rather than trimming, shows that the size of the manuscript cannot have been significantly altered in size since this commentary was added. Although a compilation manuscript, texts regularly run unbroken between quires. There is a single example of a ‘catchword’ functioning between the recto and verso of a leaf as opposed to between quires on f. 28r. Here, at the centre of the bottom of the page the word ‘Scribe’ appears, distinct from the body of the text. This is the word with which the verso continues. This feature is found elsewhere in homiletic prose and to this end, particularly given the quarto structure of MS Ll.5.18, raises questions regarding the sequence in which pages of a quarto were filled and at which stage the pages were folded and ordered during the writing process. Similarly, it could potentially indicate the scribe offering himself an aide-memoire during the copying process, noting where to commence upon return to the manuscript. There is no evidence of pricking or ruling in MS Ll.5.18 and lines are written in free-hand throughout.

provenance: overview: Probably produced at Durham Cathedral Priory (Meehan, 1994; Norton, 1998); at an early point bound with Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 66 (Imago mundi; History of England etc.) which has colophon of 1188 and ex libris of c. 1200 from Cistercian Abbey of Sawley, Yorks. This part of Ff.1.27 is therefore also likely to have been at Sawley. However, Dumville, 1974, argues for later dating (s. xiii) and Sawley origin. For the original order of the Sawley manuscript, see Dumville, 1980. The part of the manuscript previously bound with the Bury portion of Corpus MS 66 (now MS 66a) is likely to be of the same provenance, although written in a different hand.
codicology: condition: The condition of the manuscript is generally good, with fresh, clean-coloured parchment that is not generally darkened or worn. There are, however, some small holes on certain leaves, and evidence of stitching to repair more serious tears, as on page 116. The script, which is largely clear and legible, has occasionally deteriorated in the rubrics, which, as in the bottom right corner of page 120 are now barely legible. Particular damage has occurred at the bottom of page 236, which was previously covered by a strip of parchment added a later date (now removed and inserted at the beginning of the volume).

provenance: overview: Produced at Bury St. Edmunds Abbey. Split into two parts in the sixteenth century, of which Ff.1.27 (Part II) is the second half of the original manuscript, the first half preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 66A. Owned by Matthew Parker in the sixteenth century, as suggested by an addition to the top of page 1, reading 'Matthaus Cantuar, 1574'.
codicology: condition: The condition of the manuscript is broadly good. Compared to Ff.1.27 (Part I) in the same volume, the vellum is relatively intact, bearing few of the holes that are so pervasive in the earlier part of the codex. Where damage has occurred, as on page 527, this has evidently taken place prior to the manuscript's inscription, as text has been written around the holes. On the whole, however, the script is regular and clear, and the manuscript's illuminations, including those containing gold leaf, have not become worn or tarnished. On some pages heavy ruling marks can be seen, as on page 611. The manuscript has also been cut down, as shown by the way in which some of the decoration has missing edges, as on page 610.

codicology: collation: The manuscript comprises 28 quires, typically of eight leaves; in some, two singletons are used in place of a bifolium (see Quires 10, 12 and 21). The two inserted leaves in Quire 20 are, by contrast, conjoined: a folded bifolium that has been stab sewn behind ff. 151|157. Two parchment stubs are found after Quire 1. The first of these connects with f. 1, a leaf probably added in the 16th century to accommodate a table of contents (rather than an originally blank leaf that was used for this purpose). The second connects only with a stub preceding f. 1: since it bears no evidence of having contained text or having been prepared for ruling, the likelihood is that this is the remnant of a single leaf that had previously formed the pastedown or a blank endleaf at the beginning of the manuscript. The manuscript comprises perhaps five codicological units. Quire signatures on Quires 8-13 ('i'-'vi') and 15 ('viii') indicate that these formed the core of the manuscript (with Quire 16), to which further quires were then added, both before and after. These divisions are indicated below by semi-colons. Owing to the way in which the manuscript developed, these do not always coincide with textual divisions. For instance, the first two leaves of Quire 16 provided the space for the completion of Ælfric's sermon on the remembrance of saints; a new hand takes over at this point, filling the remainder of the quire with his homilies, which then continue on subsequent quires. The quire numbers do not continue, but are supplanted by catchwords. Similarly, the quires inserted at the beginning of the manuscript contain Ælfric's preface to and part-translation of Genesis, which ends on f. 24v, the penultimate leaf of Quire 3. Another hand continued with homilies to the end of that quire, with three leaves (Quire 4) being added to provide the necessary space to accommodate it. The rest of f. 28v was left blank, perhaps because the text on Quires 5 and Quires 6-7 (each themselves a codicological unit) had already been copied. However, the current order of quires is not necessarily the original arrangement: a note by a 13th-century hand on f. 29r suggests that Quire 5 might once have been placed at the beginning of the volume. provenance: overview: The Augustinian Priory of Holy Trinity, Ipswich: although there is no explicit medieval evidence of provenance, it is highly likely that the roll was made by and subsequently was held at the priory. The list of tenants begins with property in the parish of St Margaret's and 'Thingstead', locations closest to the site of the priory. ; The roll likely remained among the muniments of the Christchurch manor, formed from the estate of the priory at its dissolution in 1536. The first membrane bears an inscription, perhaps of the 18th or 19th century: 'Rent Roll Christ Church Estate St Margaret Ipswich'. W.P. Hunt, in his 1847 transcript of the roll's contents, claimed to have accidentally found this and another roll (now Ipswich, Suffolk Record Office, HD1/9/1/4/1) among the muniments at Christ Church the previous year. ; Unidentified owner: included in the sale of 'Western and Oriental Manuscripts and Miniatures', Dreweatts and Bloomsbury, 6 July 2017, lot 69.

provenance: overview: Written in Wales; McKee tentatively suggests that the presence of the cryptogram on fol. 36r suggests that the manuscript may have been written in a monastery close to the court at Gwynedd where the code, devised by an Irishman, Dubthach, was known in the early ninth century or in the region of the lower Usk and lower Wye valleys where the bishop Cymelliauc was active (McKee 2000:28). By the early eleventh century, the manuscript was in England, possibly at Worcester, where fols 2-5 were glossed in an Anglo-Caroline hand (McKee 2000:38). There is no evidence of later medieval ownership; the earliest modern owner who can be discerned is Richard Amadas, rector of Hallingbury Magna, Essex 1585-1629 Amadas, Richard, rector of Hallingbury Magna, Essex, 1585-1629 who annotated the manuscript in several places. Directly or indirectly, Ff.4.42 passed into the possession of Richard Holdsworth (1590-1649) Holdsworth, Richard, 1590-1649 who acquired several other Amadas books. provenance: overview: Addition of St Etheldreda, patron saint of Ely, to the Calendar (f. 8v) and of a prayer to her (f. 102v) point to early ownership in East Anglia.; Addition of obituaries to the calendar indicate that the manuscript was in Suffolk by the first half of the fifteenth century: f. 5r: 'Obitus domine Margerie Carbonell uxoris domini I[ohannis] C[arbonell] m[ilitis], Anno domini Millesimo CCCCmo vicesimo vito, littera dominicalis e' / 'The death of Margerie Carbonell Carbonell, Margerie , wife of Sir John Carbonell Carbonell, Sir John [of Badingham in Hoxne Hundred], in the year of Our Lord 1426, dominical letter e': i.e. 2 March 1426 (not 4 March, the line on which the inscription begins). f. 8r: 'Obitus Margarete Heuenyngham, Anno domini Millesimo CCCCxxxii, littera dominicalis G' / 'The death of Margaret Heveningham Heveningham, Margaret , in the year of Our Lord 1432, dominical letter G': i.e. 2 September 1432 (not 1 September, the line on which the inscription begins). The individuals named may have been former owners, though no explicit evidence of their possession of the manuscript exists, and it is equally possible that the book was in the hands of unnamed relatives.; Addition of impaled coat of arms of the Tilney and Thorpe familiesTilney and Thorpe families (f. 2v) indicates that the manuscript was later in Norfolk, later in the 15th and/or in the early 16th centuries. ; Additions and notes relating to members of the Roberts family indicate the manuscript was in Middlesex, certainly during the second half of the 16th century and perhaps for longer: f. 33r: 'The tyme of Byrth of Thomas Robertz Children', with dates of birth ranging from 1508 to 1531. f. 109v: further dates of birth for Roberts family children, with dates ranging from 1550 to 1574. The individuals named may have possessed or accessed the manuscript, individually or jointly, and at varying times, however the only evidence that points more firmly towards ownership are the recurrent additions and inscriptions by Thomas Roberts (1470-1542)Roberts, Thomas, 1470-1542 and Edmund Roberts (1521-1585)Roberts, Edmund, 1520-1585 of Willesden. codicology: collation: At their core, most of the quires of this manuscript comprise eight leaves, however their structure is obscured by the addition in numerous places of single leaves bearing full-page miniatures. The picture is especially confused after the calendar, where there are several short suffrage texts interspersed with miniatures of the saints to which these prayers are directed. In an unpublished description of the manuscript, M.R. James described these simply as 'loose leaves'. Numerous of them have been repaired along the spinefold and it is possible that leaves that were originally singletons have been joined together to form artificial bifolia, since these may be more securely sewn into the binding; unfortunately, the tightness of the binding precludes a deeper examination of their structure. The leaf signatures in this section (written in red-orange ink, now much-faded) cannot necessarily be taken as an accurate guide to the quires' structure: although medieval, they are later additions. The collation of the manuscript by H.L. Pink, perhaps around the time the manuscript was rebound in 1960, and his addition of leaf signatures to indicate the sequence of leaves in each quire, only adds to the confusion. Pink often took the stubs of these decorative leaves - which had only ever been singletons - as evidence of a leaf having been cancelled in that location: hence the frequent occurrence in his formula (written on the rear pastedown) of quires of ten leaves, a structure atypical for manuscripts of this kind and of this date and place of origin. In this situation, it seems unwise to superimpose yet another interpretation of the structure of the suffrage / miniature quires (Quires 2-4 in Pink's formula) and risk further compounding the confusion. Instead, they are noted below as being of uncertain structure. In order to minimise the disjuncture between this formula and that which preceded it, but yet permit corrections to be made, the numbering of the quires that follow the suffrages and miniatures will include the letters assigned by H.L. Pink. What is provided here broadly follows the collation as given by M.R. James in an unpublished description (see Source for further details). 3 medieval parchment endleaves Quire 1/a6 (ff. 4-9) Quires Two-Four/b-d??uncertain (ff. 10-31) Quire 5/e8+2 (ff. 33-42: ff. 33 and 37 are single leaves inserted before the 1st and after the 3rd leaves of the quire) Quire 6/f8+6 (ff. 43-56: ff. 44, 47, 49, 51, 53 and 55 are single leaves inserted after the 1st, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th leaves of the quire) Quire 7/g8+1 (ff. 57-65: f. 59 is a single leaf inserted after the 2nd leaf of the quire) Quire 8/h8+1-1 (ff. 66-73: f. 68 is a single leaf inserted after the 2nd leaf of the quire; the final leaf of the quire is missing, but may have originally been blank) Quire 9/i8+1 (ff. 75-83: f. 75 is a single leaf inserted before the 1st leaf of the quire) Quire 10/k8+1 (ff. 84-92: f. 84 is a single leaf inserted before the 1st leaf of the quire) Quire 11/l8 (ff. 93-100) Quire 12/mthree/8-5 (ff. 101-103: three leaves, but probably originally a quire of 8, of which the 4th-8th are now missing, but may have originally been blank) Leaf signatures, medieval but added after the insertion of the single leaves that bear miniatures. codicology: collation: '[A]n unknown quantity of material has been lost from both the beginning and the end of the book as it now stands. What we have are the remains of fifteen gatherings (now bound as sixteen), of widely varying lengths. They fall into distinct groups of the kind commonly designated as booklets, five in number, each of which is largely devoted to a particular type of subject matter. Though the process of copying within these larger units seems to have been mostly continuous, differences in appearance from one booklet to the next suggest that the manuscript as a whole was accumulated over a period of time, as material came to hand. As is commonly the case in 'home-made' compilations of this kind, there are few signs that the copyist was much concerned with the more formal procedures involved in book production, such as pricking and ruling, or the provision of quire and leaf signatures, and he had no qualms about inserting new booklets within existing ones.' Summary of booklets: Booklet 1 = Quires 1-2 (ff. ['1']-['18']) Booklet 2 = Quires 3-4, with Quires 5 and 6 inserted after the 13th leaf in Quire 4, and Quire 7 (ff. 19-['73']) Booklet 3 = Quire 8 (ff. 74-81) Booklet 4 = Quires 9-13 (ff. 82-['137']) Booklet 5 = now misbound as Quires 15-16, but originally a single quire (ff. 138-['151']) Beadle (2017), pp. 100-03 Collation formula: Quire 112-3 (ff. 3-12: 1st, 2nd and 5th leaves, ff. The presence of scribal leaf signatures shows that Quires 15-16 were originally a single quire of 16 leaves (4th and 12th-16th leaves missing). The current Quire 16 was originally bound after the 4th leaf of Quire 15, i.e. after the first stub following f. 140. Leaf signatures in Roman numerals in Quires 15 and 16 only (see Collation). No quire signatures. 'Catchwords seem to have been added at a late stage, when the manuscript had come to be regarded as in some sense finished and ready for binding, since they supply links not only within the booklets, but, on occasion, between one booklet and the next (e.g. those on ff. 17v and 81v). The positioning of some catchwords suggests that some leaves had already gone missing by this stage, for example those at the quire divisions at ff. 17v and 109v, where the lost folios '18' and '110' are represented merely by stubs.' provenance: overview: Ian Harwood identified Mathew Holmes as the copyist of CUL MS Dd.5.78.3 and three other lute books in 1963. It has been possible to place Holmes' books in chronological order and Dd.5.78.3 is the second. It may have been started at Oxford where Holmes was precentor and singingman at Christ Church between 1588 and 1597 but was probably largely compiled after 1597 when Holmes moved to become 'chanter' and singingman at Westminster Abbey. It is not known when or where the manuscript was handled by John Dowland who added a title to his piece, Farwelland his name on fol. 44r. It seems likely that all Holmes' manuscripts were together in Westminster at the time of his death in 1621. It is not known when or by what means they entered the University Library. The first reference to Dd.5.78.3 is in CUL MS Oo.7.53, a manuscript catalogue of the library compiled in 1753.

provenance: overview: Ian Harwood identified Mathew Holmes as the copyist of CUL MS Dd.2.11 and several other lute books in 1963. It has been possible to place Holmes' books in chronological order and Dd.2.11 is the first. It was probably substantially copied at Oxford where Holmes was precentor and singingman at Christ Church between 1588 and 1597. On fol. 22r, John Dowland is described as Bacheler of Musicke; he received his degree at Oxford in 1588 suggesting that this piece was not copied before this date. On fol. 56v, Edward Pierce is described as >Regie Capellae, suggesting that this piece was written in or before 1600 when Pierce left the Chapel Royal to go to St Paul's. Harwood (2010) suggests that Holmes took his books to Westminster Abbey in 1597 when he became 'chanter' and singingman. Some of his later manuscripts were certainly copied there and it seems likely that all the manuscripts were together in Westminster at the time of Holmes' death in 1621. It is not known when or by what means they entered the University Library. The first reference to Dd.2.11 is in CUL MS Oo.7.53, a manuscript catalogue of the library compiled in 1753.

provenance: overview: The three men mentioned in the note on fol. 1r (John Reynolds, William Holman and Henry Rogers) can all be identified in Dorset records c. 1600. The volume was owned by William Trumbull (-1635) Trumbull, William, -1635 and was probably copied by him. Trumbull was an English diplomat at the Brussels court of Archduke Albert of Austria. His correspondence demonstrates a keen lifelong interest in music. On his return from Brussels, Trumbull was granted the estate of Easthampstead Park in Berkshire. The manuscript remained among the family papers at Easthampstead Park until it was deposited on loan at Berkshire County Record Office in 1954 by Trumbull's descendant, Lord Downshire (1894-1989) Downshire, Arthur Wills Percy Wellington Blundell Trumbull Sandys Hill, Marquess of, 1894-1989 . The manuscript was purchased by Cambridge University Library at the Sotheby's sale of 22 November 1989.

The pages were cut up by a bookbinder in the seventeenth century and incorporated into the bindings of printed books. Holdsworth was Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge between 1637 and 1649 and Spencer suggests that the books were possibly bound in Cambridge during this period. Holdsworth's collection was donated to the University Library in 1664.

The manuscript comprises probably 13 quires, mostly originally of 16 leaves each, made from three paper stocks, as follows: Quires 1, 3-11, 13: tête humaine, Briquet no. 15632 Quire 2: bouc, no match in Briquet Quire 12: couronne (with fleur-de-lys in the centre), no match in Briquet The original structure of Quires 11 and 13 remains uncertain. The watermarks found within their folio ranges do not exhibit a symmetrical pattern and – even taking into account lost or added leaves – cannot be used to indicate the centre of the quire. In Quire 11, one leaf is missing/excised before f. 138 and one leaf, without a watermark, from an unidentified paper stock different to those used elsewhere in the volume, has been added before f. 143. One or more other leaves may be singletons. In Quire 13, two leaves are missing/excised before f. 151. Bradshaw marked f. 156r with a ‘+’ symbol to denote the beginning of the second half of the quire, but the pattern of watermarks does not support this. An alternative structure might be that Quire 13 is in fact two quires each originally comprising eight leaves. The collation does not include leaves added in the 19th century by Joseph Romilly and others at the beginning, at the end and at various junctures within the manuscript. In CUL MS Dd.9.33 this same hand completes a piece started by Mathew Holmes and writes finis at the end. provenance: overview: This document was used as the binding for CUL MS Nn.6.36, a lute book. By examining this indenture, Ian Harwood was able to identify Mathew Holmes, the grantee of the lease, as the scribe and owner of MS Nn.6.36 and several other music manuscripts. Holmes moved from Oxford to become singingman and chanter at Westminster Abbey in 1597. MS Nn.6.36 was compiled and probably bound at Westminster between 1605 and 1615. It is likely that all Holmes' manuscripts were together in Westminster at the time of his death in 1621. It is not known when or by what means they entered the University Library. The wrapper was removed from MS Nn.6.36 in 1913 and given its current shelfmark.

provenance: overview: Ian Harwood identified Mathew Holmes as the copyist of CUL MS Dd.9.33 and three other lute books in 1963. It has been possible to place Holmes' books in chronological order and Dd.9.33 is the third. It was copied at Westminster where Holmes was chanter and singingman from 1597 until his death in 1621. Harwood (1963:46-47) suggests that the two requests for prayers for the sick men Davie Were [Wier] and William Hoper [Hooper] which Holmes wrote on the back flyleaf of the manuscript may have been rough drafts for memoranda collected by Holmes as part of his duties within the Abbey. Thieving Lane, where Davie lived, was in the parish of St Margaret's, Westminster and most of its houses belonged to the Abbey. The parish register records the burial of Davie Wier on 18 March 1600. The Westminster parish register records the burial of William Hooper on 15 April 1601. It seems likely that all the manuscripts copied by Holmes were together in Westminster at the time of his death in 1621, although some were copied in Oxford before his move to Westminster. It is not known when or by what means they entered the University Library. The first reference to Dd.9.33 is in CUL MS Oo.7.53, a manuscript catalogue of the library compiled in 1753.

provenance: overview: Given to the Library by Thomas Wriothesley, earl of Southampton Wriothesley, Thomas in 1635, from the library of William Crashaw Crashaw, William . On folio 1v is a sixteenth-century inscription of R. Benet, who appears to have been Mayor of Romney. Benet’s name occurs in other manuscripts collected by Crashaw. A partially erased inscription in the bottom margin of folio 5r reads ‘’Jhon Hurter [Hurtwell?] pbr’. According to John Whytefelde’s catalogue of 1389, this manuscript bore the shelf-mark A:V: in the collection of St Martin’s Priory, Dover; this shelf-mark appears both on the reverse of the original front flyleaf and in the bottom margin of folio 3r. Twelfth-century corrections in an English hand lead O’Neill to suggest that the manuscript may have arrived in Dover from Canterbury.

provenance: overview: German, made for, or at, the Benedictine nunnery of Holzen, Allmannshofen, founded in 1153. The MS. was acquired by Archbishop William Laud (d. 1645) in Germany between 1636 and 1638. Laud was a major collector of manuscripts. At the foot of f.1 “Liber Collegii S. Petri in academia Cantabrigiensi ex dono Iohannis Rothwell ciuis et stationarii Londinensis. Ita testor, Lazarus Seaman Magister”. Lazarus Seaman (d. 1675), was admitted Master of Peterhouse, Cambridge, by Edward Montagu, 2nd Earl of Manchester, in place of John Cosin, on 11 April 1644 and remained so until 1660. With this note, he testified that the MS. had been donated by the London bookseller John Rothwell - probably the elder John Rothwell, who was active at the Sun in St Paul’s churchyard from 1628 to 1649, rather than his son, also John, who inherited the business.

codicology: collation: The loss of many folios, the dismantling of quires among those that remain and the out-of-order binding of the early folios have destroyed the original quire structure, which cannot be reconstructed in the absence of quire signatures or catchwords. From f. 24 onwards, the visible stitching enables the current structure to be identified. This is made up of quires of variable lengths sometimes containing non-consecutive folios where others in between have been lost. Only towards the end of the manuscript does a continuous run of quaternia composed of consecutive folios suggest that the original quire structure has survived. In the early part of the manuscript, made up largely of isolated single leaves and many attached in an erroneous order on paper stubs, it has not been possible to group folios into a current quire structure, and they have been treated as autonomous entities, except where a brief consecutive run exists (ff. 20-23), which has been treated conjecturally as a portion of a single original quire, though these folios may in fact span two adjacent quires. binding: overview: Early modern binding of eastern Mediterranean origin. Textblock cut flush to the size of the boards. The sewing is an unsupported loop stitch. There are four sewing stations prepared with shallow v-shaped recesses. Remnants of laid paper pastedowns remain on the inner face of the right and left boards. Projecting compound endbands are present at the head and tail. The primary sewing is a single core woven endband sewn in natural coloured thread and sewn through the centre fold of each gathering. To facilitate the weaving, warp threads have been created by winding thread around the primary endband. The weaving is in a chevron pattern made with alternate red and yellow silk threads. The endbands extend approximately one quarter of the way onto each board. Where they extend onto the boards the endband is tied down to the head-most sewing stations and the tailband is tied down to the tail-most sewing stations. Evidence of an overall spine lining can be seen at the inner joints and through damage in the covering, extending at least a third of the board width. The board attachment is a zig zag pattern consistent with the Eastern Mediterranean tradition. There are four attachment stations, each consisting of a pair of holes perpendicular to the spine, with a recess cut between each hole. The sewing thread is wound between each pair of holes (the sewing path on the outside of the board is obscured by the covering). The start/end of the sewing thread can be seen at the head-most station of the left board and the tail-most section of the right board, tied off to the sewing thread as it passes to the next attachment station. The boards are made from wood. The head-, tail- and fore-edges of the boards are square cut, measuring 10mm thick. The outer spine edge of the boards are shaped to a gentle round to meet the spine of the textblock. Full covering in a dark red-brown tanned skin. The turn-ins suggest the skin was originally a red colour. The turn-ins are rough-trimmed and the corners are sewn-mitres. Through the thickness of the left board is a hole, in the centre towards the foredge, which likely held a metal fastening. There are two corresponding holes through the right board, in the centre toward the foredge, which would have held a strap. The cover is decorated with blind tooling. The tooling is of a varied design using only two tools - a wide double lines and a rectangular tool with a central dash. The tooling on the left board consists of two concentric frames created with double lines. Additional double diagonal lines start at the corners of the board, intersecting the corners of the frames and terminating at the innermost frame. Where the diagonals intersect the frames the rectangular tool is used. To fill the space between the outside of the board and the outer frame the rectangular tool is used to form a ‘zig-zag’ pattern, with each impression made perpendicular to the previous, running along the border. Between the frames the rectangular tool has been used to spell out the name of the four evangelists. Within the second (and central) frame is a cross formed of the same rectangular tool. There is evidence in the form of pin holes that there was once a metal furniture cross in this position. Surrounding the cross is the inscription Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς νίκα, made with the same rectangular tool. The tooling on the right board consists of two concentric frames created with double lines. Additional double lines diagonals start at the corners of the board, intersecting the corners of the frames, each pair from the head corners and tail corners terminate as they meet, approximately 80mm from the head and tail, respectively. The rectangular tool is used where the diagonals intersect the frames. Additional diagonal double lines are used, intersecting at the centre, passing out perpendicular to one another and terminating at the innermost frame. To fill the spaces between the outside of the board and each of the frames the rectangular tool is used to form a zig-zag pattern. The same zig-zag pattern runs along the head-, tail- and fore-edges of both boards. The former classmark G.3.9 appears on a patch on the spine. 222 174 71

codicology: collation: The manuscript consists of 31 quires, most comprising 8 leaves, but with minor variations in form in several places. The fourth leaf was cancelled from Quire 13, and the sixth leaf from Quire 31, with no interruption to the main text. Two quires are not solely comprised of nested bifolia; the fourth and fifth leaves in Quire 9, and the third and sixth leaves in Quire 16 are singletons arranged into two sets of paired half-sheets that take the place of a bifolium in each quire. The manuscript was completed in two possibly simultaneous copying stints, the first from pp. 1-206 (Quires 1-13), and the second from pp. 488 onwards (Quires 14-31); evidence for the stints can be seen in the two sequences of quire designations used in this volume, the first of which encompasses Quires 1-13 and the second of which encompasses Quires 14-30 (Quire 31 lacks its final leaf). In addition, the mise-en-page of p. 206 reflects scribal awareness of an approaching link with another portion of the text; the text on p. 206 is much more widely spaced than earlier in the volume, and the text ends abruptly, mid-sentence, not at the end of a line, and leaving a much larger lower margin than is typical even by the expansive marginal standards common to this volume. The manuscript has been rebound since it was examined by M.R. James for his 1912 Catalogue, and so his description of the binding and the endleaves is no longer an accurate reflection of the physical characteristics of the volume. The endleaves in the current binding are arranged as follows: two paper leaves coterminous with the current a binding (ff. [a]-[b], a c. 16th century parchment endleaf (f. i), the core 11th century leaves (pp. 1-488), a c. 16th century parchment endleaf (pp. 489-490), and two paper endleaves (ff. [c]-[d]. binding: overview: Rebound on 15 April 1953. A note recording the rebinding is present on f. a recto: 'MS. 41 Rebound by John P. Gray of 10, Green St. (Pilgrim Trust grant) 15.iv.53. . J. P. T. B.' (i.e. John Patrick Tuer Bury (1908-1987), historian and fellow of Corpus Christi College). Fully bound in light brown leather over mill-board. The leather covering the boards is undecorated except for decoration applied to the raised bands on the spine which extends across the joints and onto the front and back covers. Five raised bands on spine, each decorated with a blind single-fillet along the upper and lower perimeters of the band; the fillets extend in pairs across the joints and onto the front and back covers and taper into a decorative point. The upper and lower openings of the spine are each decorated with a blind single-fillet across the width of the spine and inset from the opening by c. 10 mm. Three compartments on the spine bear text tooled in gold, 'M S .' '41' and 'CCCC' respectively. The spine is capped at head and tail and no bands are visible. Paper pastedowns pasted over the turn ins, both blank. The present leaves f. i and pp. 489-490 are both former pastedowns and contain text in a hand of the 16th century; both leaves are coated in an adhesive residue on their outermost sides, and have wear in a pattern indicating their proximity to the former binding's turn ins. Neil Ker states that the binding replaced by J.P. Gray in April 1953 was 'of s. xviii'; this is the binding that M.R. James would have seen when he examined CCCC MS 41 for his Catalogue. The endleaves were probably added to the volume in a 16th-century binding, given the re-use of similar such documents in other manuscripts once in the possession of Matthew Parker. N. Ker, Catalogue of Manuscripts Containing Anglo-Saxon (Oxford, 2nd edn., 1990), no. 32

provenance: overview: Donation inscription on p. 488: 'Hunc librum dat leofricus episcopus ecclesie sancti petri apostoli in exonia ubi sedes episcopalis est ad utilitatem successorum suorum. Si quis illum abstulerit inde, subiaceat maledictioni. FIAT. FIAT. FIAT. Ðas boc gef Leofric. b. into sce petres mynstre on exancestre þaer se bisceopstol is for (his) saƿle alisednysse 7 gif hig hƿa ut æt brede god hine fordo on þære e...' (This book was given by Leofric, bishop of the church of Saint Peter the Apostle in Exeter where his episcopal seat is for the use of his successors. If anyone steals it, may they be put under a curse. Let it be so. Let it be so. Let it be so) . Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 41 was one of the manuscripts given to Exeter Cathedral by Leofric, bishop of Exeter (d. 1072) Leofric, Bishop of Exeter, -1072 , who was bishop there from 1050 to 1072, and it still contains a bilingual donation inscription cursing anyone who might try to remove the book from the Cathedral. Before being appointed Bishop of Exeter in c. 1050, Leofric was appointed Bishop of Cornwall and Bishop of Crediton by King Edward the Confessor. Leofric requested and received papal permission to move the episcopal seat to Exeter in 1050, and donated several manuscripts to Exeter upon his appointment there, so it is possible that this book and others in that donation might originate from Crediton, but this is far from certain.
acquisition: overview: Pages 1-488 given to Corpus Christi College in 1574 by Matthew Parker (1504-1575) Parker, Matthew, 1504-1575, archbishop of Canterbury. It is possible that f. i and pp. 489-490 were already bound with pp. 1-488 at the time of Parker's gift to Corpus Christi College.

provenance: overview: Edward Franton [? Frampton] (fl. 15th century) Franton [? Frampton], Edward, fl. 15th century: owned or accessed the manuscript. His name is written in reverse (Notnarf drawde) on a decorative banderol on f. i verso, on f. 147r and f. 151r. ; John Shirley (1366?-1456) Shirley, John, 1366?-1456, author, translator, and scribe: owned or accessed the manuscript. He added a Middle English verse prayer to f. 1r. ; Anne Neville (fl. 15th century) Neville, Anne, fl. 15th century: owned or accessed the manuscript. Her name is inscribed in the outer margin of f. 101v: Neuer foryeteth Anne Neuyll. Unidentified, but scholars have proposed various identities: one is Anne Beauchamp (1426–1492), 16th Countess of Warwick, and wife of Richard Neville, 16th Earl of Warwick, on the basis that the manuscript was once also accessed by the scribe John Shirley (1366-1456) [see above], whose main patron was Anne's father, Richard Beauchamp, 13th Earl of Warwick [for this identifciation, see Parkes (1978), p. 12; Connolly (1998), 41, 109-110; Driver (2007), pp. 181-182; on Ann Beauchamp, see Scott (1976), pp. 61-63]. Another candidate is Anne Neville (c. 1410-1480), daughter of Joan Beaufort and Ralph Neville, Duke of Westmorland, and wife to Humphrey Stafford, 1st Duke of Buckingham [see Vines (2011), pp. 22-25]. This identification is suggested by the name inscription Knyvett on f. 108r (see below). The latter may be William Knyvett (1440-1515), Sheriff of Norfolk and Suffolk, whose third wife was Joanna Stafford, one of Anne Neville's daughters. If this second identification is accepted, then it is possible that the manuscript passed down to Joan Stafford and William Knyvett. ; Knyvett (fl. 15th century) Knyvett, fl. 15th century: a member of the Knyvett family owned or accessed the manuscript. Their family name written upside down in the outer margin of f. 108r. Unidentified, but perhaps William Knyvett (1440-1515), Sheriff of Norfolk and Suffolk, if the identification of the Anne Neuyll whose name is inscribed in the outer margin of f. 101v as Anne Neville-Stafford (c. 1410-1480) [see above] is accepted: her daughter, Joan Stafford, married William Knyvett in 1477. provenance: overview: William Worcestre [Worcester] [Botoner] (1415–1480x85) Worcestre [Worcester] [Botoner], William, 1415–1480x85, secretary to Sir John Fastolf (1380-1459), antiquary, topographer, and chronicler: copied and owned the manuscript. A colophon in his own hand on p. 5: Willelmus worcetor [sic] est author huius libri .vi. post .fo. 4.. His name inscribed on p. 106 (lower margin): Botiner qui est Wurcester. His name inscribed on p. 118: Nomen patris [...] qui hunc librum scripsit W. Wurcester. Four other manuscripts with Worcestre's hand survive, including an account book concerning his surveyorship of the Manor of Castle combe, Wiltshire, for John Fastolf (London, British Library, Add MS 28208); his commonplace book (London, British Library, Cotton MS Julius F VII); a compilation of historical texts copied by different hands, including Worcestre's (London, British Library, Royal MS 13 C I) and a medical manuscript (London, British Library, Sloane MS 4). Worcestre's hand also occurs in Geoffrey Chaucer's Middle English translation of Boethius's De consolatione philosophiae in Cambridge, Pembroke College, MS 215. As Daniel Wakelin points out (see his Introduction to Pembroke College, MS 215), Worcestre appears to have used Chaucer's translation to read the original Latin passages from Boethius (book IV, metre 3 and prose 3) that he copied on p. 194 of Corpus Christi College MS 210. This is suggested by the fact that he has highlighted the same passage in the Middle English version on ff. 66r-66v of Cambridge, Pembroke College, MS 215. ; T.M. la Rosarius (fl. 16th century) Rosarius, T.M. la, 16th century: owned or accessed the manuscript. Their name inscribed on p. 219: T.M. LA. ROSARIVS . brugensis - I.R. Rosarius la - I.R.. ; Robert Talbot (c. 1505-1558) Talbot, Robert c. 1505-1558, prebendary of Norwich Cathedral (from 1547) and treasurer there until his death: copied information from the Registrum Primum of Norwich Cathedral on p. 226. ; Francis Rugge (1536-1607) Rugge, Francis, 1536-1607, Freeman of Norwich in 1563, alderman from c. 1570 onwards, Sheriff of Norwich in 1572-3, and Mayor of Norwich in 1587-9: his name (ffrauncis Rugge) inscribed on p. 286. While Harvey suggests that his name is written in the hand of that of Henry Aldrich (whose name occurs twice on the same page together with scribles), it is also possible that it was added by Rugge himself, either as an owner or user of the manuscript. Although Harvey does not identify Thomas Rugge, he almost certainly is the freeman, alderman, sheriff, and mayor of Norwhich who married Anne Aldrich (d. 1611). The latter was a daughter of John Aldrich (1520-1582), alderman and mercer of Norwich, and mayor of that city in 1570-71, and Elizabeth, daughter of Nicholas Sotherton (d.1540), alderman and Mayor of Norwich (1539-40), and sister of Henry Aldrich [see below] whose name is twice inscribed above that of Francis Rugge on p. 286. ; Henry Aldrich (d. 1593) Aldrich, Henry, d. 1593, Fellow of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, in 1569-1579; who was licensed to teach grammar in Norwich in 1583: his name inscribed on p. 286: Henricus Aldrichius and Henry Aldryche. His name inscriptions are accompanied by many pen trials, including initials and names (Mr Master Bristlye) that appear to have been written by the same hand. Henry may have inscribed the name of Thomas Rugge [probably his brother-in-law; see above] and a list of first names: Thomas / Henry / John / Michael / Thomas / John / Henry [This list may refer to the sons of John Aldrich and Elizabeth Sotherton: aside from a son named Henry, there were sons named John, Michael, and Thomas]. The name of Christian Aldrich (Christian Aldrichus) - who remains unidentified but almost certainly was a relative of Henry - is inscribed (upside down) in light brown ink on p. 278. According to Harvey (1969), the manuscript probably passed from Aldrich to Corpus Christi College but the presence of pagination in the hand of Matthew Parker (see below) and the existence of a partial transcription in a manuscript (now Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 101) that was copied for Matther Parker from books in his collection and elsewhere suggest otherwise. Venn ALDC563H ; Matthew Parker (1504-1575) Parker, Matthew, 1504-1575, archbishop of Canterbury: not recorded in his register of books donated Corpus Christi College, now Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 575, but his ownership is suggested by the presence of his pagination in red crayon throughout. As Rand (2009) notes, Parker owned two other notebooks that belonged to Robert Talbot. These are now Cambridge, Corpus Christi MS 111 and Cambridge, Corpus Christi MS 379.

codicology: extent: Codex: iv + 2 | 160 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 + iv leaves. 195-300 75-110 NB: These dimensions correspond to the range of leaves found in the manuscript's core part (Part 2) to give a sense of the manuscript's tall and narrow shape. The dimensions of the other parts are ignored here because they concern inserted leaves that typically have been bound in vertically and their original height and width have been cropped to match the dimensions of the manuscript's core part. As Rundle (2024) points out, the format of this mansucript is that of a so-called 'holster book'. Two other extant notebooks from Worcestre (London, British Library, Cotton MS Julius F VII and London, British Library, Sloane MS 4) and his account book (London, British Library, Add MS 28208) are in the same format.
codicology: collation: The collation of the manuscript's current structure - which does not reflect its original division into quires - has not been established, but it contains many short booklets of 2 and 4 leaves. It also features inserted single documents that have been folded into bifolia and to which William Worcestre has added notes from his Itineraria. Because these documents were produced separately from this manuscript, they are treated as separate parts in this catalogue record.

The leaves that contain pages 30a-30b, 294a-294b, and 304a-304b are fragmentary and have been restored to their original sizes with blank paper in modern times. The leaf that contains pages 330a-330b is a stub with a few scribles or notes written on it. The leaves were not paginated by Matthew Parker: a modern hand has written numbers with 'a' and 'b' supplements in pencil in the upper outer corners of both sides of these leaves. There is also one fragmentary leaf restored with blank paper that may have been paginated by Parker. This concerns the manuscript's final leaf to which a modern hand has added the numbers '333' and '334' in pencil to the upper outer corners of both sides of the leaf. The square brackets that contain two numbers (i.e. [2-3], [42-39], [78-79], [236-257], [244-249], [300-311]) refer to images that show texts that run across two pages. These typically involve pre-existing documents that Worcestre inserted into this manuscript, except for pp. [78 and 79] which contains a text by Worcestre that is part of the Itineraria and runs across two pages. These numbers have been added to the foliation statement for reference purposes in this eletronic catalogue record. Folios [i]-[iv] and [v]-[viii] are unfoliated/unpaginated modern paper flyleaves at the beginning and end of the manuscript [not photographed] that have been allocated Roman numerals for reference purposes in this catalogue record. These numbers have been placed between square brackets to indicate that they have been supplied. When the manuscript was rebound in 1953, it was decided to re-organise inserted leaves that originally were folded around the outsides of quires, and this new organisation was maintained when the manuscript was given its current binding in 2012. Consequently, Parker's pagination sequence is out of order. For a reconstruction of the manuscript's original order, see Harvey (1969), pp. 407-416 ('Conspectus of Pages').
binding: overview: The manuscript has a limp parchment binding [not photographed] that dates to 2012. It consists of veiny parchment that has been folded over thin paper covers laced onto an alum-tawed goatskin spine-covering featuring green headbands with six thongs of alum-tawed skin. Current binding height: 310mm; width: 120mm; depth: 40mm. The current binding (2012) replaces a binding that was made by the bookbinder John P. Gray of Cambridge in 1952. The latter has been preserved but is kept separately from the manuscript [not photographed]. It concerns a binding of brown leather over wooden boards with blind-tooled vertical 'teeth' on the covers that correspond with the positions of five raised bands on the spine. The latter features the gold-stamped classmark: MS. 210 and C.C.C.C.. The old binding is accompanied by two old paper flyleaves at the beginning, numerous rigid paper stubs, and two old paper flyleaves at the end. The classmark MS 210 is inscribed in ink on the first flyleaf at the beginning with a note about Gray. Old binding height: 315mm; width: 150mm. When the manuscript was re-bound in 1952, single documents that William Worcestre had folded around the outsides of quires were relocated so that they could be read across the fold without interuption. This modern organisation was maintained when the manuscript was bound again in 2012.

For the interim period, the manuscript's quires are kept in white paper folders marked with their shelfmark, and respective quire and folio numbers. Together, these thirteen folders are kept in a grey conservation folder with their shelfmark (MS 354) printed and written on it. The manuscript's former binding - removed in 2007 - is now kept separately from the manuscript. It consists of brown quarter leather over (?) wooden boards with the shelfmark (MS 354 C.C.C.C.) gold-stamped on the spine. This binding, as noted on the recto of its first former flyleaf (f. i recto), was made when the manuscript was rebound by J.S. Wilson and Son at 12 King's Parade, Cambridge, in December 1948. provenance: overview: 'TW' (fl. 16th century) 'TW', fl. 16th century: initials inscribed in red crayon by the manuscript's subsequent owner Matthew Parker (1504-1575) (see below) in the upper margin of f. 1r. As Mildred Budny (1997, p. 248) notes (building on James (1912), p. xxii), these initials can also be found in Cambridge, Corpus Christi, MSS 260, 326, 425, and 441; Cambridge, Trinity College, MS R.3.15; and London, Lambeth Palace Library, MS 430. James suggests that they either were John Twyne (?1501-1581), schoolmaster of the grammar school at Canterbury, or Thomas Wotton (b. in or before 1521, d. 1587), sheriff of Kent, who both had dealings with Parker. M.R. James later noted the initials' presence in Cambridge, University Library, MS Ii.3.1 (see Data Source(s)). Of these six manuscripts, four have Canterbury provenances: three were at Christ Church (Corpus MSS 260, 326, 441 and CUL MS Ii.3.1) and one at St Augustine's (Lambeth MS 430). The rubric 'Distingcione 7 . T primo' on f. 70v in MS 374 is not a St Augustine's pressmark, however (it seems instead to refer to textual divisions within the Manipulus cronicarum), and such a provenance was rejected by Neil Ker. Also, as Budny commented: '[T]he whole group of TW entries belong to a larger group of entries which Parker made in many books, consisting solely of names in a short form at the front, usually in red crayon. Usually these entries have been regarded as recording his sources for the books, but they probably register his intentions for distributing them instead.' N.R. provenance: overview: The manuscript seems to come from Christ Church Cathedral Priory, Canterbury, and it was counted among the books believed to have belonged to Theodore of Tarsus (d. 690), archbishop of Canterbury Theodore, of Tarsus, Saint, Archbishop of Canterbury, 602-690 , as a 16th-century hand stated on f. 1r: Liber quondam Theodori Archie(pisco)pi Cantuariensis . This note was propably added by William Sellyng Guilelmus Tillaeus ca. ca. 14301494 , known as Tilley or Tillaeus (d. 1494). Sellyng is among the first English men known to have studied Greek in Italy, and the monastery of Christ Church in Canterbury, of which he was prior from 1472 to 1494, was one of the earliest English centres in which Greek texts were studied; the manuscripts he collected passed into the Parker's collection.

It is listed in William Stanley's catalogue of 1722 at the classmark Q.7, which remains on f. 1r.

provenance: overview: Folios i-iv written and owned by Edmund Popley Popley, Edmund of the Diocese of York and Principal of Beef Hall in Oxford, c. 1496-1497. Popley may also have owned ff. 1r-77v, which would explain how his notes came to be bound with the rest of the volume, but there is no strong evidence to rule for or against Popley's ownership of ff. 1r-77v. The first four medieval endleaves in the volume (ff. i-iv) are in Popley's hand and contain a copy of the Articuli Cleri enacted in 1316 (ff. ii recto - iv verso), followed by some brief legal notes (f. iv verso). Popley signed the notes on f. iv verso as 'Edmundus Poplay' and mentioned a connection to an unspecified university ('studia quindecim annorum que habuit in hac uniuersitate in facultate arcium') and recorded the date of a legal action as 12 June 1489 ('Hec gracia concessa et confirmata est anno domini millesimo cccco lxxxxix mensia Jun. xiimo'). The name, the date, and the long connection to a university allows for the Poplay of ff. i-iv to be identified as the Edmund Poplay (Popley) of the Diocese of York, who was ordained as a deacon in 1484 and was Principal of Beef Hall in Oxford c. 1496-1497. There is no codicological evidence for or against the union of Parts 1 (ff. i-iv) and 2 (ff. 1r-77v) in 1489 , so it is not possible to determine if Poplay was the owner of ff. 1r-77v, or if their composite arrangement occured later, but Poplay's ownership of ff. 1r-77v offers the simplest explanation for how his notes came to be with the main section of MS 412. Full transcription of Poplay's note on f. iv verso: 'Litera domini regis iusticiariis directa supra ponitur infra constituciones prouinciales de foro competenti C circumspecte agatis in quo C continentur omnes casus in quibus iudex ecclesiasticus cognoscere potest regia prohibitione non obstante . Melius tamen est quod non faciat nisi regiam consultacionem optineat etc. Edmundus poplay. Supplicat venerabili etc. Edmundus poplay in jure canonico Baccallarius quatenus studia quindecim annorum que habuit in hac uniuersitate in facultate arcium et in juribus Ciuili et canonico sibi sufficiant ad hunc effectum ut admittatur ad incipiendum in jure canonico ita quod soluat markam . Hec gracia concessa et confirmata est anno domini millesimo cccco lxxxxix mensia Jun. xiimo condicio talis est quod soluat uniuersitati xls'. ; William Porter Porter, William : name written in large gothic letters on f. i verso, probably in the 16th century, and presumably indicating his possession of the manuscript. No William Porter with plausible biographical information has been identified. M.R. James noted in his Catalogue that a William Porter also signed his name in Cambridge, Trinity College, MS B.16.3, front flyleaf 3r , but as both the script and the spelling ('Willyam Porter') are different, it is not necessarily the case that these are the same William Porter. M. R. James, A Descriptive Catalogue of the Manuscripts in Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, 2 vols (1912), Vol. II, no. 412

provenance: overview: Given (?to Ely Cathedral Priory) by a William de Stradesete William de Stradesete : donation inscription (with unnamed beneficiary) in a ?13th-century hand on folio i recto, 'Hunc librum dedit Willelmus sacerdos de stradesete cuius memoriam cum oratione faciat qui in eo legerit' ('The priest William de Stradesete gave this book, he who reads [this book] should remember [him] with prayer'). There is a village called Stradsett in Norfolk, England, approximately 19 miles (30 kilometres) from Ely and it is possible that William may have originated from that village. No biographical details of William are known (a William Ockley William Ockley was vicar of Stradsett from 1402-?1408 but his lifespan postdates the date at which the donation inscription was written). ; Partial names visible on f. 153v under handheld ultraviolet light, now badly rubbed and damaged. The names appear to be in 14th or 15th century hands. What little can be read of the names is as follows: Johannes Bygh... ...styfall... Henr... ; Owned by the medieval community of Ely Cathedral Priory during the 15th century, and may have entered its collection as early as the late 12th or early 13th century (see above). The oldest significant provenance evidence for the precise location of the volume in the medieval period is the distinctive Ely pressmark (resembling a Roman majuscule numeral II, surmounted by a cross) in the outer margin of f. 1r. This confirms that the volume was part of the Ely Cathedral Priory collection by the 15th century, when these marks were added to some of its manuscripts (see CBMLC 4 for further information). Other Ely manuscripts with the mark include: Cambridge, University Library, MS Gg.1.21, f. 1r Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 44 Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.2.1, f. 1r CBMLC 4 (B27, esp. p. 127) ; Unidentified pressmark at the top of folio i recto, 'F. 6.' in ink at the top of the leaf above the medical recipe and next to the word 'Amularius'. The pressmark conforms to the Bury St Edmunds pressmark format (and that of several other religious houses), i.e., a majuscule letter followed by a Hindu-Arabic number), but the mark in CCCC MS 416 probably postdates the Bury St Edmunds pressmarking campaign by at least a century, nor is it a palaeographical match for any other Bury St Edmunds pressmarks. Further rejection of the 'F. 6.' as a Bury St Edmunds pressmark can be based on the use of an 'F' class at Bury St Edmunds being almost entirely unattested, and the Bury St Edmunds letter classes having a thematic link to the volume by either author or subject, and the letter 'F' not having an obvious relationship to the content of CCCC MS 416. ; Unidentified pressmark in the lower margin of f. 2r, '108' in ink.

binding: overview: Mid-17th century binding. Fully bound in leather over pulp-boards with matching decoration in blind to left and right covers. Covers are decorated with a triple-fillet frame with Oxford corners set at the perimeter of the boards. Head and tail bands visible, perhaps yarn over a cord core, but heavily stained with glue and red pigment. Four raised bands on spine, each with a single-fillet through their centre across the width of the spine. Spine compartments are decorated with a double fillet at their upper and lower perimeters and at the upper and lower openings of the spine. Four printed paper labels fixed to the spine with an adhesive, 'MSS.', '1', '3', '14', for a former shelfmark. Head, fore, and tail edges of the bookblock sprinkled with red. Pastedowns have been lifted and the inner faces of the boards are exposed. The inside of the right cover is blank. The inside of the left cover contains the following items: The number '70' in pencil set in a lozenge frame for the M. R. James Catalogue number of the volume The former shelfmark 'MSS 1. 3. 14' in ink and pencil An Emmanuel College armorial bookplate by Metcalfe of Cambridge: a lion rampant in the right paw a laurel wreath with the motto "ΕΜΜΑΝΟΥΗΛ" (the Greek form of 'Emmanuel') on the escutcheon and the words 'Collegii Emmanuelis Liber' below The endleaves ff. [i] and [vi] are former pastedowns, and both bear traces of adhesive on their outermost faces. The endleaf f. [iii] verso contains the following items: The number '54' in ink A description of the contents of the volume in ink in a humanist hand 'Provinciale Guilielmi Lynwood' Dimensions (L x W x D): 205 x 145 x 50 mm. Housed in a dark blue box with a label 'MS 66' stamped in gold and bearing a label on the inside of the box 'This box was made using a generous donation from Mark Drinkwater 2014'. Evidence of two metal clasps belonging to a former binding visible on f. [i] recto as small green metallic-oxide stains along the fore edge of the leaf.
