provenance: overview: An inscription on f. 175r indicates that the leaf was part of a volume owned by Lanercost Priory in Cumbria, England, by 1354 at the latest: Liber ffratris Nicholai de Morland ex dono Willelmi de Langedale cuius usum proprium idem Nicholaus concessit cessit Domino Iohanni de Buchaster (The book of Nicholas of Morland from the gift of William of Langdale, the use of which the same Nicholas had granted to master John of Bewcastle). The inscription names three men (Nicholas of Morland and John of Bewcastle who were granted the use of a book by William de Langdale), and of the three, only John of Bewcastle can be supplied with further biographic information as he was Prior of Lanercost (1338-1354). As Pam Robinson points out, Bewcastle, Morland and Langdale are all Cumbrian place names and so the three men mentioned in the inscription are probably all linked by geographic ties as well as social and religious connections.

provenance: overview: A note on f. i verso, badly rubbed: 'Caucio Walteri de Wasten exponitur ciste Batulfi ... concepionis beate Marie anno Domini Mo CCCo xxx', i.e., the book was pledged as surety for a loan and placed in Botolph's chest on 8 December 1330 by Walter de Wasten. Caucio inscriptions in manuscripts reflect a practice common (but not limited) to Oxford and Cambridge in the 14th and 15th centuries where borrowers could pledge books or other high-value items in exchange for a monetary loan supplied by a lender who would store the manuscript in a chest for the duration of the loan. The loan chests and their funds were often supplied by a single benefactor whose name became associated with the chest long after their death and became incorporated into the Caucio inscriptions usually in the form 'ciste [name]'; in this case, the 'ciste Batulfi' probably refers to a loan-chest in Cambridge known as 'Botoloph's Chest', which, if that identification is correct, places at least some parts of Peterhouse MS 251 in Cambridge in December 1330. 'Botolph's Chest' was supposedly endowed by a Thomas de St Botolph, chaplain to John Le Romeyn, archbishop of York, see Fuller and Billingfield, 'Section IV' in The History of the University of Cambridge, esp. p. 130. This Caucio note is briefly discussed in Thomson's Catalogue, p. 158; Thomson suggests that 'Walteri de Wasten' may be the Walter de Weston in Emden BRUC, p. 631, a cleric of Cambridge who complained about the violence from the mayor and townspeople of Cambridge in 1322 as recorded in Calendar of the Patent Rolls preserved in the Public Record Office 1216-1509, 54 vols (1891-1916). The Caucio note is also briefly discussed in CBMLC 10 UC48.291 where the note is transcribed as follows: 'Caucio Walter de Kasten exspositus ciste Botulph' Concepionis beate Marie anno Domini Mo ccco xxx' T. Fuller and R. Billingfield, ‘SECTION IV’, in M. Prickett and T. Wright (eds.), The History of the University of Cambridge: From the Conquest to the Year 1634, (Cambridge, rpr 2009), pp. 126–42 R. M. Thomson, A Descriptive Catalogue of the Medieval Manuscripts in the Library of Peterhouse, Cambridge (2016) BRUC: A. B. provenance: overview: Certainly a communal production by associated hands, and certainly members of the same religious group. Cf. the invocations at the openings of individual stints: f. 29 (scribe 2), 'Assit principio sancta Maria mea'; f. 71 (scribe 3), 'Maria thomas katerina'; f. 95 (i.e. real 97, scribe 1) 'Assit principio sancta Maria mea katerina'. ; A not especially legible inscription, 15th century (fol. 37, in the outer margin), ? 'Ihon de Ihorn'; no plausible candidate appears in either BRUO or BRUC. ; 'Thomas Wele', mid-15th century, (f. 19v and 20r, in the upper margins): probably to be associated with a man of the name, who was vicar of St Cyriac's, Swaffham Prior (Cambs.), 1458x1468 (Emden, BRUC 625). ; 'Edward Phelyps 1552' (variously, ff. 40v, 61v, 89v, 102v and 103). ; Hanna suggests that the manuscript is very likely from a Dominican house, and although there are a number of East Midland candidates, the most proximate at Thetford and Northampton, most probably from that in Cambridge.

provenance: overview: On the first flyleaf over an erasure a near 1500 hand has inscribed: ‘Liber Johannis Bullur alias Spyllesby Emptus london[iensis]’, then in a bold hand: ‘unde myen sc. Johannis husey yeffen to me be the sed sr John’. Other notes in the same hand as the first inscription appear on 50v: ‘Deo gracias. Bullur.’ and on 65r: ‘Memorare nouissima et in eternum non peccabis Ecc' 4o When thy hede quakyth Memento Then thy lyppys blakyth Confessio Whien thy noose sharpyth Contricio Then thy lymys starkyth Satisfaccio When thy Brest pantyth Nosce te ipsum Then thy wynde wantyth Miserere When thy nyen hollyth Libera me domine Then deth folowyth Veni ad Judicium.’ An inscription in script of the sixteenth century on the recto of the final flyleaf (65r), in the hand of John Hussey, 1st Baron Hussey of Sleaford John Hussey, 1st Baron Hussey of Sleaford (also spelt Huse) and chamberlain to Mary Tudor Mary I., Queen of England 1516-1558 , indicates that this book was possibly owned by King Henry VIII’s elder daughter: ‘Thys bok ys my ladey Maryes [?] the Kyenges dautter. jhs keppe and send the kyenge a pryenche. John huse the kyenges treu seruantt’. The second flyleaf bears the inscription of Edward Martin, President of Queens’ College (1631–44 and 1660–61) Martin, Edward, -1662 : ‘Fuit Viri admodum Reverendi D[omi]nis Martin Collegij hujus presidis dignissimi 1662’.

provenance: overview: Perhaps made at, and certainly owned from an early stage by the Durham Cathedral PrioryDurham Priory community. Sidney Sussex MS 51 is listed in the 'Spendement' Catalogue of 1391 and the updated catalogue of 1416where it is described as: 'P. Uersus Hildeberti de Exposicione Missae. Tractatus de corpore Christi. Regulae de Medicinale. Glosa in Psalterium. II fo. Neve superveniens' (see Botfield, Catalogi Veteres). The 'P' siglum is recorded in the manuscript in the upper outer corner on f. 1r. Shrader, in his survey of the survivng copies of Heriger's works on the Eucharist seems to suggest that this MS (or perhaps the first part thereof) is among the books listed in the late 12th century catalogue of Durham Cathedral Library preserved in  Durham, Cathedral Library, MS B.IV.24 ('The Durham Cantor's Book') ff. 1r-2v and printed in Botfield, Catalogi Veteres, pp. 1-10, as the entry 'Epistolæ Hildeberti, iv paria' in MS B.IV.24, f. 1va (Botfield, Catalogi Veteres, p. 4), but this idea is considered independently and rejected by Wallis and Gasper who did not believe Sidney Sussex MS 51 was a close match for any of the volumes recorded in MS B.IV.24. B. Botfield (ed.), Catalogi Veteres Librorum Ecclesiae Cathedralis Dunelm, Surtees Society vii (1838), pp. 4 24, 101 F. Wallis, and G. E. M. Gasper, ‘Salsamenta Pictavensium: Gastronomy and Medicine in Twelfth-Century England’, English Historical Review, 131.553 (2016), pp. 1353–85, esp. p. 1354 ; Owned by John Pilkington John Pilkington who added the inscription 'Sum Iohannis Pilkingtoni Dunelmensis 1591' to the volume twice on ff. 1r and 47r. John Pilkington was an Archdeacon of Durham from c. 1563-1602 and was the brother of James Pilkington James Pilkington (1520-1576), Bishop of Durham. In addition to his inscriptions in MS 51, Pilkington also added his name to Sidney Sussex MSS 30 and 55, and may have encountered MS 92. M. R. James, A Descriptive Catalogue of the Manuscripts in the Library of Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1895) F. Wallis, and G. E. M. Gasper, ‘Salsamenta Pictavensium: Gastronomy and Medicine in Twelfth-Century England’, English Historical Review, 131.553 (2016), pp. 1353–1385 ; Probably owned by former Master of Sidney Sussex (1572–1643, master 1610-1643), Samuel Ward Samuel Ward . It seems very likely that MS Sidney 51 was seen in the possession of Samuel Ward by Ward's friend, the author and Archbishop of Armagh, James Ussher James Ussher . In Ussher's An answer to a challenge made by a Iesuite in Ireland (1625), Ussher wrote (abbreviations expanded, typesetting modernised): '[i]n the libraries of my worthy friends, Sir Robert Cotton, (that noble Baronett, so renowmed for his great care in collecting and preserving all antiquities) and Dr Ward, the learned Master of Sidney Colledge in Cambridge; I met with an ancient Treatise of the Sacrament (beginning thus: Sicut ante nos quidam sapiens dixit, cujus sententiam probamus, licet nomen ignoremus.) which is the same with that in the Iesuites Colledge at Lovaine, blindely fathered upon Berengarius'. The quotation that Ussher gives, 'Sicut ante nos quidam sapiens dixit, cujus sententiam probamus, licet nomen ignoremus', matches the text of the treatise on the Eucharist in Sidney MS 51, ff. 17r-26v. The text that Ussher is referring to is the Dicta Herigeri abbatis de corpore et sanguine Domini now usually attributed to Heriger of Lobbes Heriger of Lobbes , but which was for a long time believed to be by Berengar of Tours. The Dicta Herigeri survives in very few manuscript copies and the likelihood is that the one Ussher saw in Ward's hands is the same manuscript that came into the possession of Ward's former college. J. Ussher, An answer to a challenge made by a Jesuite in Ireland (1625), pp. 17-18
acquisition: overview: It has not been established with absolute certainty when or by what means Sidney Sussex College acquired MS 51, although a plausible argument can be made that the volume was an unrecorded donation by former master Samuel Ward Samuel Ward . A list of Ward's donations is preserved in the college archives, but it does not appear to describe a manuscript identifiable as Sidney Sussex MS 51. It may be that Ward gave the manuscript as a separate donation, or that left Ward's possession and came to Sidney Sussex indirectly by some other route, as happened with many of Ward's personal papers (see Todd, 1985). The manuscript had certainly arrived at the College by c. 1697, when its presence was recorded in Bernard's Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (c. 1697), p. 104, no. 714. For an account of the early history of the library of Sidney Sussex College, see Rogers, 'Early History of Sidney Sussex College Library', esp. n. 53; Rogers points out that MS 51 is likely to have been given by Ward on the strength of MS 51's prior ownership by John Pilkington, who had also owned known Ward donation MS 55. N. Rogers, 'The Early History of Sidney Sussex College Library', in D. E. D. Beales and H. B. Nisbet (eds.), Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge: Historical Essays in Commemoration of the Quartercentenary (Woodbridge, 1996), pp. 75-88

Although the first quire presently indeed consists of ten leaves, it is clearly missing leaves at the beginning. That at least one leaf is missing is suggested by the fact that the quire opens with a paper leaf but that the quire ends with a parchment leaf. That, in fact, two leaves are missing is evident from the location of the (parchment) inner leaves at ff. 1:4-1:5, and the leaf numbers in the lower margins of the versos which appear to begin with '3' [cropped] and run until '12'. All of this makes clear that the first quire is a sexternion with two missing leaves before f. 1:1. Leaf signatures in Roman numerals written in the lower margins of the versos of pages throughout each quire (f. 1:17 is the exception, where the leaf signature '9' has been written on the recto side), but regularly cropped off. Catchwords in brown ink in the right-hand lower margins of the last versos of quires.

codicology: collation: Quire 712-2 (ff. 2:3r-2:12v: 1st-2nd leaves missing) Quire 818-4+1 or 20-5 (ff. 2:11-2:30: 1st, 2nd, and 16th leaves missing, and 13th leaf cancelled) Quire 912+2 (ff. 2:31-2:42: 2 (?) added leaves after 12) Quire 108 (ff. 2:99-2:107) Quire 118-4 (ff. 2:138-2:143: 5th-8th leaves missing; 1st leaf may be from another quire) The collation in this record deviates from James (1913) where quire 7 is defined as a quaternion (ff. 2:3-2:10) and quire 8 as a quire of 18 leaves with one leaf cancelled (ff. 11-30), and Claire Jones (2000) where quire 7 is defined as a quaternion (ff. 2:3-2:10) and quire 8 as a quire of 18 leaves with its 13th leaf cancelled (ff. 2:11-2:30): this catalogue record assumes that quire 7 is a sexternion with 2 missing leaves at its beginning (ff. 2:3-2:12), which explains why there are two paper stubs in front of the quire and the medieval foliation starts at '3'. The location of the thread tackets in the gutter between f. 2:6 and f. 2:7 would support either theory but the original medieval foliation sequence suggests that quire 7 runs until f. 2:12 instead of f. 2:10. James (1913) and Claire Jones (2000) think that quire 8 runs from f. 2:11 until f. 2:30. This quire would originally have consisted of 18 leaves but one leaf, leaf 13, was cancelled, now represented by a stub between f. 2:24 and f. 2:25. However, this collation disregards breaks in the original medieval foliation that suggest that three more leaves are no longer present: two leaves between f. 2:12 and f. 2:15 (i.e. there are no leaves with the folio numbers '13' and '14') and one leaf between f. 2:27 and f. 2:29 (i.e. there is no leaf with the folio number '28'). These jumps in the foliation coincide with breaks in the texts and with breaks in a medieval sequence of capital letters, organised in alphabetical order, that was added to the outer margins to indicate the beginnings of different sections of the recipes. Consequently, the absent numbers '13', '14', and '28' in the foliation cannot be the result of errors on the part of the foliator and must represent missing leaves. The observation that three leaves are missing from quire 8, in addition to the cancelled leaf, means that quire 8 would have had at least 21 leaves if it indeed started at f. 11. Placing the quire's start at the missing f. [13] also gives an uneven number: namely, a quire of 19 leaves. It is therefore possible that one leaf was cancelled from the first half of the quire (ff. [2:13]-2:21) or added to the second half of the quire (ff. 2:22-2:30). In other words, quire 8 is likely to have been a quire of 18 with an additional leaf in its second half or a quire of 20 from which one leaf was cancelled in it's first half. Further foliation breaks suggest that there might be other anomalies in the collation: In quire 10 the foliation jumps from '100' to '101' and in quire 11 it jumps from '138' to '140' but in neither case has it been possible to conclusively determine whether these jumps coincide with breaks in the text.

binding: overview: Late 13th or early 14th century binding, repaired in 1971. Fully bound in an underlayer of tawed skin and then an outer layer of ?parchment over wood boards. Three sewing stations, and three narrow slightly raised bands on spine. No head or tail tabs or bands visible. Two small printed paper labels affixed to spine, 'D' and '3' for the current shelfmark, and stuck over 'D' and '3' written in ink in an early modern hand. Traces of a former title in brown ink on the spine now almost entirely illegible. The binding may once have been fitted with two strap and pin fastenings: there are two raised 'bumps' in the fore edge of the front cover, probably where the strap ends were mounted, and there are two small puncture marks along the centre-vertical of the rear cover, which were probably caused by the pin plate fittings. Both the parchment cover and the tawed-skin underlayer sit over the remains of the fastenings, in some cases without holes or damage in the cover-surfaces, so the covers may have been repaired or repositioned after the fastenings were lost or removed. Paper pastedowns added in 1971 at the beginning and end of the volume. The front pastedown contains a St John's College bookplate, and William Crashaw's donation bookplate. The rear pastedown contains a note in pencil recording the repair of the volume: 'Repaired, endpapers lifted, by J. P. Gray & Son Ltd December 1971 for £5'. The former pastedowns are ff. [i] and 135. Folio [iii] appears to have been used to line the binding underneath the right pastedown. All of the medieval pastedowns and liners have been lifted and are now free and both sides of the leaves are visible. Dimensions (L x W x D): 260 x 180 x 40 mm Housed in a black archival box with custom-fitted padded inserts to stabilise the volume.

provenance: overview: Compiled in the late 15th or early 16th century by Thomas Betson (d. 1516) Betson, Thomas, d. 1516 , librarian of Syon Abbey (1481-1516), religious author, and compiler: his name inscribed on f. 2r: Orate pro anima Thome Betson de Syon. The list of books on f. 124v likely identifies titles that were in his private possession or in Syon Abbey's library. On Betson, see Doyle (1956), 115-118; and Becket (2015).; The manuscript may have been incorporated into the library of Syon Abbey after Betson's death: recorded in Ker (1964), p. 308; and as 'Collectanea T. Betson (Notebook)' in the MLGB3 (mlgb3.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/mlgb/book/5354/) [accessed 15 August 2023].; Owned or accessed in the 16th century by Starley, (fl. 16th century) Starley, fl. 16th century , their surname inscribed on f. [ii] recto: Starley [3x] and f. 15r [1x] and f. 19r [1x]. ; Owned or accessed in the 16th century by Thomas Blythman, (fl. 16th century) Blytman, Thomas, fl. 16th century , his name inscribed on f. 35r: Thomas Blythman. His hand has previously not been noticed or transcribed. Perhaps Thomas Blithman, commissioner for first fruits and tenths within the Diocese of Durham, the Archdeaconry of Richmond, and Northumberland, and Westmorland (appointed in 1535) who was acquainted with Thomas Cromwell, Visitor-General of the Monasteries. As Chief Steward of Syon Abbey, a position he held from 1524, Cromwell was closely involved in the dissolution of the monastery. Perhaps Blithman acquired the manuscript directly from Cromwell. On Blithman, see Wilmott and Bryson (2013), pp. 140-142. ; Purchased at an unknown time before 1624 by William Crashaw Crashaw, William, 1572-1626 , a lawyer, book collector, and former Johnian. Crashaw's collection numbered around 200 manuscripts and 1000 printed books. ; The manuscripts and printed books owned by William Crashaw were purchased by Henry Wriothesley, 3rd Earl of Southampton Southampton, Henry Wriothesley, Earl of, 1573-1624 , at an unknown time before Wriothesley's death in 1624. Wriothesley had been a student-contemporary of Crashaw at St John's College and he purchased Crashaw's collection with the intention to present the volumes as a gift to the Library of St John's College. The library was still partly under construction at the time of the purchase resulting in the Wriothesley family storing Crashaw's collection and delivering it piecemeal to the College over a number of years. ; After Henry Wriothesley's death in 1624 and William Crashaw's death in 1626, care of Crashaw's books and manuscripts passed to Wriothesley's son, Thomas Wriothesley, 4th Earl of Southampton Southampton, Thomas Wriothesley, Earl of, 1607-1667 . Although Crashaw's printed books seem to have been passed to the College without incident, Thomas Wriothesley seems to have taken a particular interest in the manuscripts, adding his name typically in the form 'Tho: C. S.' for Thomas comes southamptoniensis ('Thomas, Earl of Southampton') to most of them, and apparently exhibiting such reluctance to deliver the manuscripts that the College wrote to his mother, Elizabeth Vernon Southampton, Elizabeth Vernon Wriothesley, Countess of, 1573-1655? to ask her to encourage her son to hand over the volumes.
acquisition: overview: Given to St John’s College in 1635 by Thomas Wriothesley, 4th Earl of Southampton Southampton, Thomas Wriothesley, Earl of, 1607-1667 on behalf of William Crashaw Crashaw, William, 1572-1626 and Henry Wriothesley, 3rd Earl of Southampton Southampton, Henry Wriothesley, Earl of, 1573-1624 . The initials ‘Tho. C. S.’ in ink (for Thomas Comes Southamptoniensis) are present on the outside of the upper cover. William Crashaw's bookplate recording the donation is present on the inside of the lower cover. St John's College's bookplate pasted on the inside of the front cover.

The full-size leaves are pastedowns that have now become unstuck. Projecting wound endbands are present at the head and tail. They are sewn in a natural-coloured thread and extend approximately a quarter of the way onto the boards. Where the endbands extend onto each board they are tied down to three holes drilled through the thickness of the board. Evidence of an overall spine lining can be seen at the inner joints; how far the lining extends onto the boards cannot be determined. The board attachment is bridling. There are three attachment stations each consisting of a pair of drilled holes perpendicular to the spine, with a recess cut between each hole. The sewing thread is wound between each pair of holes (the sewing path on the outside of the board is obscured by the covering). The start/end of the sewing thread can be seen at the tail-most station on the left board and the head-most station of the right board, held under other winds of thread to secure. The boards are made from wood. The head-, tail- and fore-edge of both boards are grooved. The thickness of the boards is greater at the fore-edge (≈12mm including covering) gradually becoming lesser towards the spine (≈7mm including covering). The outer spine-edge is shaped to a gentle round to meet the spine of the textblock. Full covering in dark red-brown tanned skin. The turn-ins suggest the skin was originally a red colour. The turn-ins are rough-trimmed and the corners are mitred. Later brown tanned skin repairs are present at the head- and tail-caps. The repairs partially cover the endbands and extend onto the inner face of the boards. On the edge of the left board, at the centre, are the remnants of a hole likely to have held an edge pin. Remnants of the corresponding tanned skin straps can be found towards the fore-edge of the right board, cut flush with the outer face of the board but left long on the inner face. Four pieces of leather remain, evenly passing through a pair of holes. It is likely that the straps would have been braided and held a metal open pin-clasp. At the top of the right board, in the centre, is a title frame secured with six brass coloured metal pins. The label is ink on paper, the translucent horn has suffered some loss and the original metal frame has been lost. The label reads γραμματικὴ Grammatica graeca. There are three modern paper labels on the spine. The top and centre are printed and the one at the tail is handwritten, all are in black ink. The cover is decorated with blind tooling over the left and right boards. Both boards follow the same tooling pattern, which consists of a number of concentric frames created with two-line fillets. The central frame contains five round, double-headed eagle, intaglio tools aligned from head to tail. This frame is intersected with six small star tools at each long edge. The second frame is filled with lozenge-shaped, floral, intaglio tools rotated so the base faces the centre frame. The second frame intersects the third frame, which contains small star tools, six along the long side and three the short side. Additionally, four small star tools are used in each corner at the points which the second and third frame intersect. The fourth frame is filled with a small round tool containing a tree. The fourth frame intersects the boarder frame. The boarder frame contains small star tools, eight along the long side and five the short side. Additionally, four small star tools are used in each corner at the points which the fourth and boarder frame intersect. What appears to be the beginning of the author's name (Man) had been written inside the left board in pencil before being overlaid by the college bookplate. The number 641 has been written in pencil inside the right board. 227 154 51

provenance: overview: John Grant (1998, pp. 55-59) has shown that the two parts were not bound together before the 17th century.; According to Pierre D. Huet (cf. Koetschau (1899), p. lxxxiii-iv), when the Worms library was plundered during the Thirty Years' War, a certain Rumf, physcian to Elizabeth, Queen of Bohemia, managed to buy the manuscript from a soldier. The physician then sold it at The Hague to Isaac Vossius (1618-1689) Vossius, Isaac, 1618-1689 in the mid 1640s. In 1648 Vossius took it with him to Stockholm and entered the Royal Library. After the abdication of Queen Christina (1654), Vossius regained possession of the manuscript and later gave it to Herbert Thorndike.

They survive on Quires 14-15 (ιδʹ-ιεʹ). The signature on Quire 15 (f. 105r) has been partially lost to cropping, and it may be supposed that the same cause led to the loss of the other signatures of this sequence. There are later quire signatures in Greek numerals, in brown ink, on the first folio of each quire, recto, lower left, and the last folio of each quire, verso, lower right. They survive on Quires 1-12 (αʹ-ιαʹ). These date from a time later than the removal of the lower margin of f. 41 (since a signature of this sequence has been marked in the upper margin of f. 41r), and probably later than the insertion of the replacement quires, since signatures apparently of this sequence appear on the replacement Quire 9 (θʹ) (ff. 58r, 65v). It may be supposed that they were added to replace signatures of the earlier sequence where these had been lost, but were not required where they had survived, since the sequence of quire numbers remained the same. The signature on f. 73v, the last folio of Quire 10 (ιʹ) is accompanied by what appears to be a zero, converting it into the Arabic number 10. This was perhaps added by a binder familiar with Arabic numerals to avoid the Greek numeral from being mistaken for an Arabic 1.

provenance: overview: The manuscript was owned by John Christopherson (d. 1558) Christopherson, John, -1558 , Master of Trinity College (1553–1558). On f. [a] recto there is an ownership note, stating also that Christopherson had lent the manuscript to the Basel printers Froben and Episcopius: Est D. Ioannis Christofersoni Angli, Frobenio et Episcopio ab ipso crediti. The edition of Froben and Episcopius, printed in 1556 in Basel, is a Latin translation of Athanasius' works by Petrus Nannius (Pieter Nanninck, 1500-1557); the loan of a manuscript from Christopherson is acknowledged in the prefatory dedication ( Athanasii Magni Alexandrini episcopi, graviss. scriptoris, et sanctiss. martyris, Opera, in quatuor Tomos distributa: quorum tres sunt a Petro Nannio Alcmariano, ad Graecorum exemplarium fidem iam primum conversi, exceptis paucis antehac imperfectis ab eo denuo plenius et Latinius redditis: Quartus, Latina multorum interpretatione fere totus seorsum emissus, nunc in unum digestus et concinnatus [...], Basel 1556.).
acquisition: overview: It is not known when precisely the manuscript entered the collection of Trinity College Library. In his will of 1556 John Christopherson bequeathed his books to the library; he died in 1558, but his will was not proved until 1563 (see Gaskell (1980), p. 47). The manuscript arrived in the Library after that date and before 1601, when the edition of Athanasius' works by Commelinus was printed (Heidelberg, 1601), in which the manuscript was used and cited as a codex collegii S. Trinitatis Cantabrigiensi, olim D. Joannis Christophorsoni (the introduction to Commelin's edition can be read also in PG 25, XLIII D l. 7-11). On f. I recto, p. 874, f. 892v and f. 893r there are stamps of Trinity College Library.

provenance: overview: The Haldenby familyHaldenby family of Isham, Northamptonshire: compiled and owned the manuscript: Ownership inscription on f. 2:118v: Iste liber constat Haldynby. References to Haldenby in colophons on f. 2:16v: Wodeman ad Haldenby; f. 2:95r: quod Haldenby; and f. 2:101r: Explicit tractatus quod Haldenby [erased]. The Calendar contains the obits of John Haldenby and William Haldenby (brothers) (f. 2:2r), Robert Haldenby and Domina Matild' (f. 2:3v), probably Maud de la Carville of Isham. The Calendar also records the births of William Haldenby in 1420 (f. 2:1v) and Robert Haldenby in 1433 (f. 2:4r). Obits for members of the Mortemer family are found on f. 1:4r and genealogical notes on f. 2:129r. William Haldenby, son of Robert Haldenby and Maud de la Carville of Isham, and John, his nephew, married, respectively, Eleanor and Joan Mortemer, daughters of John Mortermer of Grendon. ; One of the manuscripts of George Carew (1555-1629) Carew, George, 1555-1629, Baron Carew of Clopton and Earl of Totnes: his signature (G: Carew) inscribed in dark ink at the top of f. 1:3v. Carew is principally known for the collection of books on Irish history that he amassed as an administrator in Ireland between 1574 and 1592. He bequeathed this collection to Sir Thomas Stafford (d. 1655), from whom they passed to William Laud (1573–1645), Archbishop of Canterbury. The latter placed forty-two volumes at Lambeth Library while four reached the Bodleian Library as part of the Laudian collection (see M.R. James, 'The Carew Manuscripts', The English Historical Review, 42 (1927), 261-267; James H. Todd, 'Account of an Ancient Irish Manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, Oxford', Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy, 2 (1936-1869), 336-346; and Ute Lotz-Heumann, 'Carew, George, earl of Totnes (1555–1629)', Oxford Dictionary of National Biography (2004) [accessed 23 February 2024]). About Carew's possession of medieval manuscripts from England much less is known, but these appear to have travelled different routes after they left his collection. His signature (G: Carew) can be found in at least six such medieval manuscripts (besides the present volume): Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.2.22 (f. 1v) (James, III, p. 115) Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.7.23 (f. 1:1r) (James, III, pp. 361-62) Edinburgh, University Library, MS 107 (f. 1r) [identified in the online record: 'MS 107: Composite manuscript including twenty-four texts, 13th-14th century'] London, British Library, Harley MS 204 (f. 1r) London, British library, Harley MS 223 (f. 7r) London, British Library, Harley MS 234 (f. 1r) (see Andrew G. Watson, The Library of Sir Simonds D'Ewes (London: British Museum, 1966), pp. 210-211 (no. 926); Cyril Ernest Wright, Fontes Harleiani: A Study of the Sources of the Harleian Collection of Manuscripts Preserved in the Department of Manuscripts in the British Museum (London: British Museum, 1972), p. 96) It is possible that Carew received all these manuscripts from John Dee. Five of the seven aforementioned manuscripts have ownership marks associated with John Dee: while Harley MSS 204, 223, 234, and Trinity College MS O.2.21 all contain his Jupiter-marks, Trinity College MS O.7.23 – which may have featured the Jupiter-mark in the torn off upper margin of f. 1r – has been identified with an item ('M35') in the 1583 catalogue of Dee's library (see Roberts and Watson, John Dee's Library Catalogue (1990), p. 115). ; One of the manuscripts of Thomas Gale (1635/6-1702) Gale, Thomas, 1672-1744, dean of York, antiquary and fellow of Trinity College Cambridge. The manuscript is listed in the list of Gale's manuscripts in Bernard, Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (1697). ; One of the manuscripts of Roger Gale (1672-1744) Gale, Roger, 1672-1744, antiquary and scholar, son of Thomas Gale. Inherited from his father.

provenance: overview: Perhaps owned by John Dee Dee, John, 1527-1608 (b. 1527, d. 1608), English mathematician and court astronomer at the court of Queen Elizabeth I. Dee was a prolific collector of manuscripts and printed books and amassed a substantial personal library in his lifetime. A mark in ink on f. [i] recto (above and to the left of 'L. 3') strongly resembles a mark identified by M.R. James in Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.8.5, front flyleaf 5r as a 'monogram, seemingly JD'. Roberts and Watson reject James' identification of the monogram, but suggest that the occasional marginal annotations (found particularly in the latter half of the volume) may be in Dee's hand. The mark warrants further investigation. This volume does not appear to be one of the unidentified volumes listed in Dee's Library Catalogue (Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.4.20 and printed as an annotated facsimile by Roberts and Watson, but Roberts and Watson identify more than 160 manuscripts owned by Dee and not included in the MS O.4.20 catalogue, so absence from that catalogue cannot be relied upon to (dis)prove ownership. M.R. James, The Western Manuscripts in the Library of Trinity College Cambridge - A Descriptive Catalogue: Volume III: Containing An Account of the Manuscripts Standing in Class O (Cambridge, 1902), p. 391, no. 1380 J. R. Roberts, and A. G. Watson, John Dee’s Library Catalogue (London: Bibliographical Society, 1990) ; Owned by Gale, Roger, 1672-1744 Roger Gale (1672-1744) , who acquired the volume from an unknown source.

codicology: collation: A small, tightly bound volume arranged as described below. The volume has been conserved, and all quires have been taken down and remounted on guardstrips at an unknown time; these guard strips are visible at the boundaries between the quires. Folios [i] and [ii] are parchment, and [iii] is paper. Quires 1-25 are paper, and Quire 26 is parchment. A quire has almost certainly been lost between the present Quires 13 and 14 (i.e., between the present ff. 105v and f. 106r) as the medieval alphanumeric leaf sequences are disrupted at the boundary between these quires; there are two medieval alphanumeric leaf sequences in this volume, the first (cancelled) sequence jumps from 'S' (Quire 13) to 'V' (Quire 14) omitting 'T', and the second sequence jumps from 'n' (Quire 13) to 'p' (Quire 14) omitting 'o'. binding: overview: Quarter-bound in ?tawed skin with paper sides over paste- or mill-boards. No raised bands on spine. Spine capped at head and tail by back-material, no headbands visible. Paper pastedowns at each end of the volume. The inside front cover contains the present shelfmark 'O.7.37' written in pencil and a Trinity College armorial bookplate. Two post-medieval paper endleaves, ff. [a]-[b] at the front of the volume and two postmedieval paper endleaves at the rear of the volume, f. [c]-[d] at the rear of the volume; all post-medieval paper endleaves probably contemporary with the binding and all blank. Dimensions (L x W x H): 110 x 75 x 45 mm Traces of a former binding (probably the original 15th-century binding) present in oxidation stains on ff. [i] and ff. 201-202. The original binding of MS O.1.77 probably included a strap-and-pin closure, which was not a particularly fashionable style of book-fastening in 15th-century England, but may have been necessary for this volume due to its unusual proportions. There is a small round hole in the centre of both ff. 201-202, and the edge of the hole is stained green - this is indicative of a brass pin plate having been mounted at the centre of the rear board of the former binding. There is a small abrasion stained green and a slightly rectanglar impresion in the parchment directly under the '77' on f. [i] recto indicative of a strap with a metal enclosure mounted in the centre of the fore edge of the former front board. The traces of the strap and the pin plate are aligned across the volume.

provenance: overview: Owned by Sir John More (c. 1453-1530) More, John c. 1453-1530 , lawyer and father of Sir Thomas More, Lord Chancellor to King Henry VIII. Notes relating to the birth of John More's children, written presumably by his hand, on ff. 139v-140r. John More's will survives, but does not give specific instructions for the dispersal of his books. The National Archives, PROB 11/23/381 ; Owned by John Dee (1527-1608) Dee, John, 1527-1608 , English mathematician and court astronomer at the court of Queen Elizabeth I. Dee's characteristic three 'Jupiter marks' ♃ ♃ ♃ are present on f. 1r and a further two ♃ ♃ are written in the upper margin of f. 2r. The manuscript is recorded in Roberts and Watson 'Additions and Corrections' (2009) where it has the siglum DM3a. Roberts and Watson include the information that Professor W.H. Sherman identified the title inscription in the upper margin of f. 5r 'Galfredus monumetensis' as being in Dee's hand. J. Roberts and A.G. Watson, 'John Dee’s Library Catalogue: Additions and Corrections', The Bibliographical Society (Special Publication) (2009), no. DM3a ; Owned by George Carew Totnes, George Carew, earl of, 1555-1629 (b. 1555, d. 1629), Baron Clopton and 1st earl of Totnes. Carew signed his name as 'G: Carew' in a blank space in the right-hand column of f. 1v. Carew is principally known for the collection of manuscripts and printed books on Irish history that he amassed as an administrator in Ireland between 1574 and 1592. He bequeathed this collection to Sir Thomas Stafford Stafford, Thomas, Sir, (b. c. 1574, d. 1655) (b. c. 1574, d. 1655), antiquary (and probably Carew's illegitimate son), who passed it to William Laud (1573-1645) Laud, William (1573-1645) (b. 1573, d. 1645), Archbishop of Canterbury 1633-1645 who dispersed the collection. The largest single holding of Carew's collection (42 items) now belongs to Lambeth Palace Library, but Carew volumes are also among the Laudian collection at the Bodleian Library, at University College in Oxford, and at the British Library. The fate of the Carew collection was discussed by M. R. James (1927), but James seems to have been unaware of the following medieval manuscripts of English origin and signed by Carew (including this one) now at Trinity College Cambridge, Edinburgh University Library, and the British Library: Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.1.57 (f. 1:3v) [previously unidentified as a Carew manuscript] (James, Catalogue III, pp. 54-58) Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.2.21 (f. 1v) (James, Catalogue III, pp. 113-114)  Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.7.23 (f. 1r) (James, Catalogue III, pp. 361-362) Edinburgh, University Library, MS 107 (f. 1r) (identified in the online record: 'MS 107: Composite manuscript including twenty-four texts, 13th-14th century') London, British Library, Harley MS 204, (f. 1r) London, British library, Harley MS 223 (f. 7r) London, British Library, Harley MS 234 (f. 1r) (see A.G. Watson, The Library of Sir Simonds D'Ewes (London: British Museum, 1966), pp. 210-211 (no. 926); Cyril Ernest Wright, Fontes Harleiani: A Study of the Sources of the Harleian Collection of Manuscripts Preserved in the Department of Manuscripts in the British Museum (London: British Museum, 1972), p. 96) Four of the above manuscripts contain John Dee's 'Jupiter marks' (British Library, Harley MSS 204, 223, 234, and Trinity College MS O.2.21) and two more were owned by him (Cambridge, Trinity College, MSs O.1.57 and O.7.23) Carew may have received the volumes directly from Dee as the two men seem to have been friends, and according to one biography of Dee, Carew was godfather to one of Dee's children (see C. F. Smith (1909), p. 220). It may be that Trinity MS O.2.21 followed a similar path to other parts of Carew's collection and having initially passed from Dee to Carew, it then passed on to Stafford and then to Laud before appearing among the possessions of the next known owner, Levin Fludd. J. H. Todd, 'Account of an Ancient Irish Manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, Oxford', Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy (1836-1869), Volume 2 (1840-1844), pp. 336-346 C. F. Smith, John Dee: 1527-1608 (London, 1909) M. R. James, 'The Carew Manuscripts', The English Historical Review, 42 (1927), 261-267 J. Roberts and A.G. Watson, John Dee's Library Catalogue (1990) U. Lotz-Heumann 'Carew, George, earl of Totnes' ODNB (2004) (Oxford Dictionary of National Biography) J. Roberts, and A. G. Watson, 'John Dee’s Library Catalogue: Additions and Corrections', The Bibliographical Society (Special Publication) (2009), [DM3a] ; However, there is other evidence of provenance that might indicate that Trinity MS O.2.21 followed a different route after Carew's possession of the volume. Instead MS O.2.21 may have passed from Carew to Sir Thomas Fludd (c. 1530-1607) Fludd, Thomas, Sir, c. 1530-1607 , MP for Maidstone, collector of books and manuscripts and acquaintance of several prominent antiquarians - or to his son, Robert Fludd (1574-1637) Fludd, Robert, 1574-1637 , a physician and author with scientific and spiritualist interests. Robert Fludd's nephew, Levin Fludd (?1611-?1709) Fludd, Levin, ?1611-?1709 , signed MS O.2.21 on f. 1r as 'LE Fludd': some accounts claim that Levin Fludd inherited part of Robert Fludd's library, although the source for these claims is not easily discovered. Another manuscript, partly in Robert Fludd's hand, also came to Trinity College via the Gale donation (Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.2.46: Robert Fludd, A philosophicall key), though this was not signed by Levin Fludd. Levin Fludd was probably the son of Robert Fludd's brother Thomas Fludd, and Thomas' wife, Catherine Bufkin (married c. 1600/1601), daughter of Levin Bufkin (c. 1533-1617), MP for Maidstone, Kent. A Levin Fludd matriculated as a pensioner at Trinity College in 1629, was a scholar there in 1631, and was awarded a B.A. there c. 1631/2. Venn suggests that this Levin Fludd may be the same person as the Levinus Fluvius who was a student in Leiden in July 1634. Fludd signed his name as 'LE Fludd' in this manuscript and also in Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.2.56, front flyleaf 4r and Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.5.6, f. 1r , both of which were also part of the Gale donation (see below). binding: overview: Quarter-bound in ?tawed skin with paper sides over paste- or mill-boards. No raised bands on spine. Spine capped at head and tail by back-material, no headbands visible. Painted head, fore, and tail edges of the bookblock in red, ochre and black; design seems to have been geometric in nature but has been significantly disrupted due to rubbing and subsequent rebinding of the leaves. The alpha-numeric elements of the manuscript's current classmark ('O.2.21') are printed separately on three paper labels fixed to the spine with an adhesive. Paper pastedowns at each end of the volume. The inside front cover contains the present shelfmark 'O.2.21' written in red-brown crayon. Three paper endleaves, ff. i-iii at the front of the volume and three paper endleaves at the rear of the volume, ff. iv-vi at the rear of the volume; all paper endleaves probably contemporary with the binding. Folio i recto contains: The present shelfmark of the volume, 'O.2.21' in pencil A note in pencil - 'Two last fol. on More family, notes by Judge Sir John More, father of Sir Thomas More'. Folio [vi] recto contains the present shelfmark 'O.2.21' written in pencil. All other paper leaves blank. Dimensions (L x W x D): 230 x 150 x 50 mm

codicology: collation: The manuscript consists of 19 quires, all quaternia. Quires 1-198 ff. 1-152 There are early leaf signatures in Greek numerals, in brown ink, on the first folio of each bifolio, recto, lower right, probably original to the production of the manusript. On the first leaf of each quire only the quire number appears, on the rest both quire and leaf numbers on some quires, on others only leaf numbers. They survive on all quires (αʹ-ιθʹ), but a few have been partially lost to cropping or damage. There is also a later sequence of leaf signatures in Latin letters and Arabic numerals, in brown ink, on the first folio of each bifolio, recto, lower right. Some have been wholly or partially lost to cropping or damage. These have been identified as the work of the Scales Binder (Barker, 'Scales Binder', p. 373). A third sequence of leaf signatures appears, in Latin letters and Roman numerals, in red crayon, on the first folio of each bifolio, recto, lower right or lower centre. They survive on all quires, but some are severely faded. There are also quire signatures in Arabic numerals, in brown ink, on the first folio of each quire, recto, lower centre. Some have been wholly or partially lost to cropping. There are catchwords on the last folio of each quire, verso, lower right, by the original copyist.

The number 92 also appears to have been placed by this hand on f. 82r and later altered to 93. ff. 72r-106v have subsequently been paginated by another hand with the numbers 73-92, 93[a]-[93b], 94[a]-[94b], 95-140 in brown ink, in Arabic numerals, usually recto only, upper right. This numbering was evidently added to supply the lack of original foliation on ff. 71r-93v, misunderstanding that foliation as pagination. When the original foliation resumed, this was apparently considered erroneous and therefore struck through and replaced or overwritten. The overwriting of the earlier folio numbers on ff. 82r and ff. 83r, present in the middle of a stretch where these numbers are usually absent, perhaps caused some confusion, leading to the error whereby the number 94 has been placed where one would expect 95 and 95 where one would expect 97, leaving the page numbers thereafter too small by two. ff. i, 104r-106v are foliated with the numbers I, 104-106 in pencil, in Arabic and Roman numerals, recto, upper right. The numbers 93A-93B and 94A-94B have also been added to the pagination on ff. 82r-83v, compensating for the error in that sequence.

codicology: collation: The collation below is based on what can be gleaned from the manuscript's current physical structure. This collation, however, does not represent the the manuscript's orginal and intended structure, since the leaves in this part, as M.R. James put it, are much disordered (James (1902), p. 360). Although James has catalogued ff. 1:1-1:36 as a single part, this treatment can be questioned. While the materials in Quire 2 probably always belonged together, Quire 1 may consist of materials from two distinct parts. Whereas the text on the innermost bifolium of Quire 1 (ff. 1:7-1:8) partly concern scientific materials and was copied by a hand that also features in Quire 2, the remaining folios of Quire 1 (ff. 1:2-1:6 and ff. 1:9-1:12) contain texts on ars dictaminis, history, and biblical interpretation, in hands that differ significantly from those found in Quire 2. Consequently, the innermost bifolium of Quire 1 - together with f. 1:1 which contains an astronomical diagram - and Quire 2 may constitute one separate part, and the remaining leaves of Quire 1 (ff. 1:2-1:6 and ff. 1:9-1:12) another part. However, the materials in Quire 1 and Quire 2 could also originate from the same manuscript: in that case, ff. 1:1, 1:7-1:8, and Quire 2 represent the original core of a scientific manuscript, and the materials on ff. 1:2-1:6 and ff. 1:9-1:12 additions that were made either on blank leaves or an added quire. For this reason and practical considerations - presenting the materials in Quire 1 and 2 as two separate parts would result in a complicated overview of the manuscript's present structure - it has been decided to retain M.R. James's treatment of the manuscript's first part in this catalogue record. James, 'The Carew Manuscripts', The English Historical Review, 42:166 (1927), 261-267; James H. Todd, 'Account of an Ancient Irish Manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, Oxford', Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy, 2 (1936-1869), 336-346; and Ute Lotz-Heumann, 'Carew, George, earl of Totnes (1555–1629)', Oxford Dictionary of National Biography (2004)[accessed 23 February 2024]]. About Carew's possession of medieval manuscripts from England much less is known, but these appear to have travelled different routes after they left his collection. His signature (G: Carew) can be found in at least six such medieval manuscripts (besides the present volume): Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.1.57 (f. 1:3v) [previously unidentified as a Carew manuscript] (James, III, pp. 54-58) Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.2.22 (f. 1v) (James, III, p. 115) Edinburgh, University Library, MS 107 (f. 1r) (identified in the online record: 'MS 107: Composite manuscript including twenty-four texts, 13th-14th century') London, British Library, Harley MS 204 (f. 1r) London, British library, Harley MS 223 (f. 7r) London, British Library, Harley MS 234 (f. 1r) (see Andrew G. Watson, The Library of Sir Simonds D'Ewes (London: British Museum, 1966), pp. 210-211 (no. 926); Cyril Ernest Wright, Fontes Harleiani: A Study of the Sources of the Harleian Collection of Manuscripts Preserved in the Department of Manuscripts in the British Museum (London: British Museum, 1972), p. 96) It is possible that Carew received all these manuscripts from John Dee. Five of the seven aforementioned manuscripts have ownership marks associated with John Dee: while Harley MSS 204, 223, 234, and Trinity College MS O.2.21 all contain his Jupiter-marks, Trinity College MS O.7.23 – which may have featured the Jupiter-mark in the torn off upper margin of f. 1r – has been identified with an item ('M35') in the 1583 catalogue of Dee's library (see Roberts and Watson, John Dee's Library Catalogue (1990), p. 115)]. ; One of the manuscripts of Thomas Gale (1635/6-1702) Gale, Thomas, 1672-1744, dean of York, antiquary and fellow of Trinity College Cambridge. It is likely that he also added the fragmentary leaves at the beginning of the manuscript, since the mark in the top left-hand corner of f. 3v (which M.R. James took as a possible classmark, reading it as TT) is in fact Tenet's own initials TR, which are also seen in a colophon written in a textura display script on f. 15v. As Jones (2024) notes, Tenet also copied part of a copy of John Baconthorpe (c. 1290-1346)'s commentary on the of Peter Lombard's Sententiarum libri IV in London, British Library, Royal MS 11 C VI. Although the commentary on the Sententiarum libri IV on ff. 1r-3v does not appear to be Baconthorpe's, the fragmentary leaves may still testify to Tenet's interest in Lombard's work. On Tenet, see R. codicology: foliation: Current foliation: 16th century foliation sequence of core leaves with additional later designations for endleaves. Folios [a]-[b] + i-iii | 1-112 | 113-126 | 127-162 | 162a, 163-175 | 176-196 | iv-v + [c] The core leaves (ff. 1-196) are foliated in ink in Hindu-Arabic numerals in the upper outer corner of each recto in an early modern hand. The early-modern foliation sequence is correct apart from a duplicate designation of folio '162'; a later foliator has supplied the designation '162a' to the second of those two leaves. The early modern foliator's numbering is clear except for a tendency to write the character '1' in a form that resembles a narrow modern '4'. M. R. James misread some of this foliator's 1s as 4s and thereby introduced minor foliation inconsistencies into his catalogue record for this item. The parchment endleaves are foliated in pencil in Roman numerals in the upper outer corner of each recto; the parchment endleaves at the beginning of the volume have the designations ff. i-iii and those at the rear of the volume have the designations iv-v. The paper endleaves at each end of the volume were assigned designations in 2024 when the manuscript was catalogued as part of the Curious Cures project in order to produce a functional TEI-XML record for this manuscript. The paper endleaves were assigned the designations ff. [a]-[b] for the leaves at the beginning of the volume and f. [c] for the paper leaf at the rear of the volume; these unofficial designations are enclosed in [square brackets] throughout this record.
binding: overview: Quarter-bound in parchment with paper sides over paste- or mill-boards. No raised bands on spine. Spine capped at head and tail by back-material, no headbands visible. Paper pastedowns at each end of the volume. The inside front cover contains the alphanumeric components of the present shelfmark 'O.7.37' written in ink. Two paper endleaves, ff. [a]-[b] at the front of the volume and two paper endleaves, f. [c]-[d] at the rear of the volume; all paper endleaves probably contemporary with the volume and all blank. Dimensions (L x W x H): 220 x 150 x 55 mm Folios i-iii | 1-112 | 113-126 | 127-162 | 162a 163-175 | 176-196 | iv-v have almost certainly been bound together since the volume was used by Roger Marchall (c. 1417-1477) Rogerus Marshall (c. 1417-1477) . Marchall seems to have been interested in curating the manuscripts in his possession, and seems to have made (or comissioned) a number of codicological interventions in the volumes he owned; many of the surviving Marchall manuscripts (such as this one) are highly composite, and show signs of having been deliberately arranged for Marchall into their current codicological format. Trinity MS O.8.31 contains narrow parchment sewing guards along the spinefold around the back and at the centre of each quire. They were probably added when the composite volume was bound in its current arrangement, most likely for Roger Marchall (see Introduction for further discussion). The guards are narrow (less than 10mm wide, prior to folding) and were cut vertically from their source, so only a couple of letters of a minute textualis bookhand can be read on each. Furthermore, the fragility of the binding has limited the degree to which the manuscript may be opened safely in order to inspect the guards. Nevertheless, the presence on several of brief sequences of medieval Hindu-Arabic numerals, and the style of handwriting, suggest that their source was a late 13th- or early 14th-century book of scientific texts.

After his death in 1509, the manuscript could have returned briefly to the hands of Erasmus ( Garrod 1950, p. 9). It was later owned by the cartographer Abraham Ortelius (1527-1598) Ortelius, Abraham, 1527-1598. , see his note on f. 1r, Constat hoc mihi Ab. Ortelis. Ortelius collected autographs by Erasmus ( Garrod 1950, p. 10). The codex, after his death in 1598, passed to his nephew Colius, Jacobus, 1563-1628 Jacobus Colius (Jacob/James Cool/Cole) , see note on f. 1r, Jacobi Colii Orteliani 1598. After Cole's death in 1628, the manuscript was given to his nephew, Abraham Bush ( Garrod 1950, p. 10).

codicology: collation: 18+1 (1st leaf added) 2-48 5two 6-158 168-2 | 176-1 | 1810+2 (10th and 11th leaves inserted) | 19-228 234 24-268 | 2712+1 (13th leaf added) The collation in this catalogue record deviates from the collation provided by James (1901) and a modern librarian who has added quire numbers the lower outer corners of the first rectos of quires. Whereas James identifies Quire 1 as a quinternion with 10 missing, this catalogue record notes the presence of a catchword on f. 9v and identifies it as a quaternion with one added leaf at the beginning (also suggested by the fact that f. 1 appears to be made of a thicker parchment). Whereas James identifies Quire 17 as consisting of 6 leaves, this catalogue record notes the presence of a stub after 5, indicating that there is a missing leaf. Consequently, it identifies the start of Quire 18 at f. 127 and not f. 128 as James does. While James states that Quire 18 is a quaternion, this catalogue record, noting the presence of thread tackets between f. 131 and f. 132 and f. 136 and f. 137, identifies it as a quinternion with an added bifolium between f. 135 and f. 138. Consequently, the quire numbers in this catalogue record are always one behind those provided by James and the modern librarian. Finally, this catalogue record also does not recognise the absence of a quire between the second to last and last quires: where James jumps from Quire 27 to Quire 29, the collation in this catalogue record progresses from Quire 26 to Quire 27. Like James, this catalogue record identifies five distinct parts in the manuscript but it disagrees with the ranges provided for the codicological units: whereas James places the end of Part 2 at f. 131, this catalogue record places it at f. 126.

binding: overview: Armorial binding of George Willmer (1582-1626) George Willmer, 1582-1626 of Stratford-le-Bow, Middlesex. Rebacked. Full bound in leather over pasteboards with matching decoration in blind to front and rear covers. Covers are each decorated with a quintuple-fillet in blind set at the perimeter of the boards and a gilt single fillet superimposed over the central fillet in the blind quintuple-fillet roll. Blind single fillet on the cover material over the head, fore, and tail edges of the boards. A large gilt armorial stamp in the centre of the cover blazoned as follows: Crest: mural coronet, eagle displayed Helmet: esquire Mantle: acanthus, terminal tassles Escutcheon: a chevron between three eagles displayed Motto: 'expertus credo' Rebacked in leather with a defined grain. Four raised bands on spine. Spine is decorated with a blind single fillet along the upper and lower perimeter of each compartment and at the head and tail openings of the back. Spine is capped at head and tail, no head or tail bands visible. Three small printed paper labels fixed to spine with an adhesive 'R', '1' and '3', the middle label probably originally '10' for a former shelfmark 'R.10.3'. No pastedowns. A former shelfmark 'R.10.3' written in ink on the inside of the front cover and struck out. Two paper endleaves at either end of the volume, ff. [b]-[c] and [d]-[e], the outermost of these (ff. [b] and [e]) probably once pastedowns in the volume as both have traces of adhesive stains on their outermost faces. Two parchment stubs (ff. [a] and [f]), one at either end of the volume between the inner face of the cover and the outermost paper endleaves. These stubs were probably once fixed to the inner covers to reinforce the hinges but both are now free and are described separately as they contain medieval text. Two paper endleaves at each end of the volume, ff. [b]-[c] and [d]-[e]; all of the paper endleaves are blank. A small portion of a watermark is visible on f. [b] at the gutter, but not enough of the mark is visible to identify the design. British Armorial Bindings: Willmer, George (WIL013)

provenance: overview: Symon Newell (fl. 1526-1541) Newell, Symon, fl. 1526-1541 of Shipdham, Norfolk: owned the manuscript as indicated by a previously unrecorded 16th-century ownership inscription on f. 2:89r: Symon Newell me possidet - Symon Newell de Shypdham in Com. Norffolk. He may be the same Symon Newell/Nevell who in Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.8.17 is stated to have translated it into English and copied an astrological-medical work that fills the entire manuscript (ff. 1r-119v). The prologue to this unidentified work (f. 1v) reads: [crossed out: Translated and] vryten by me Symon newell in the yere of oure lorde .1535. begon þe 28 daye of marche. A comparison of the scripts in MS O.8.17 and the ownership inscription in MS R.14.39 suggests that they may have been copied by one and the same person. He may also be the very same Symon Newell who is recorded in the for a 'debt of grace' to practice medicine in the early 16th-century accounts of the University of Cambridge (see Grace Book B: Containing the Accounts of the Proctors of the University of Cambridge, 1511-1533, Part 2, ed. by Mary Bateson (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1905), p. 218 and Venn:NVL526 S).

provenance: overview: John Frost (fl. c. 1460) Frost, John, fl. c. 1460, mercer of Saint Mary Aldermanbury, City of London: possibly copied and/or owned part of this manuscript. As Gross (1996), p. 117 fn. 74 points out, the accounts on pp. 185-186 contain an entry for Sir Thomas Cooke (c. 1410-1478), draper, knight, and Lord Mayor of London, who appears to have had a family connection with Frost although their exact relationship is unclear. In Frost's will of 1463-4 (see Kew, The National Archives, PROB 11/5/211; ? proved on 9 April 1466), he bequeathed twenty shillings to a certain Thomas Cooke my cousyn in Cambrigge if he þat tyme continue at scole to augmentacioun of lernyng. The latter may be the son and namesake of Sir Thomas Cooke, who was born in 1452. The will suggests that Frost knew Sir Thomas Cooke through his sister, to whom he refers as Isabell Cooke my suster. However, no further information appears to be available on her marriage. The final entry on p. 186 concerns a reference to William Dunthorn as the executor of John Frost's will, which is indeed confirmed by the aforementioned will.

provenance: overview: John Vale (fl. c. 1460-1480) Vale, John, fl. c. 1460-1480, steward and secretary to Sir Thomas Cook, draper and Mayor of London in 1462-3: a monogram with his initials QJV for Quod John Multon at the top of f. 2:1r may indicate his ownership of this manuscript. There is some doubt since, as Mooney (2006) points out, quod usually indicates an author, translator, or scribe. John Vale's monogram also occurs in London, British Library, Harley MS 2251 (f. 175r) and Worcester, Cathedral Library, MS F.172 (f. 169v). He identifies himself in signatures as the scribe of London, British Library, Add MS 48031A. ; John Brampton [Bampton] (fl. 1450-1550) Brampton [Bampton], John, fl. 1450-1550: his (erased) ownership inscription in a heraldic coat of arms with a merchant's mark and motto on f. 2:272v: Iste liber constat Johannis B[r]ampton. Gross (1996), pp. 110-111 fn. 68 proposes that he must have been related to the family of fishmongers and wool merchants descended from the alderman William Brampton. A John Brampton held a tenement near Bishopsgate from the Hospital of St Bartholomew and was auditor of the accounts of the Wardens of London Bridget in arrear in 1467. The latter was MP for London in 1472-5, collector of the Petty Custom until 1483, and royal pensioner in 1485-6. Evidence for this identification can be found in Cambridge, Trinity College, O.3.11, another manuscript copied by the Hammond Scribe, which features a copy of a legal document with reference to a John Brampton at ff. 101r-101v. ; Janet Forster (fl. late 15th century) Forster, Janet, fl. late 15th century: her name written a late 15th-century hand in the outer margin of f. 2:140v: Jenet fforster. As Pahta (2006) notes, this may refer to the daughter of Sir Thomas Cook, Joan, who married John Forster. ; Thomas Sandy [Sandye] (fl. 16th century) Sandy [Sandye], Thomas, fl. 16th century: his name occurs in the lower margin of f. 2:135r: Thomas Sandye; and below two recipes in his hand on f. 2:270v and f. 2:272r. The name Thomas Sandy also occurs in Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Rawlinson B. 173 (ff. 144r, 200r). ; Henry Dyngley (1515-1589) Dyngley, Henry, 1515-1589, of Cropthorne, Worcestershire, collector of medieval manuscripts: owned and annotated the manuscript. He added his initials: HD 1573 on f. 2:28r; his name Henry Dyneley on f. 2:269r; the date of easter in the year 1573 to f. 2:269r. For his other notes see Pahta (2006), p. 12. acquisition: overview: Bequeathed to Trinity College by John Fortho [Furthoe] (d. 1633), M.A., M.D., Fellow and Senior Bursar of Trinity CollegeFortho [Furthoe], John, d. 1633. In his will of 22 January 1633 (proved on 5 March of that year), Fortho stipulates that the Master and Fellows of Trinity College can select 'twenty of my best books whereof I shalbe possessed of at my death being such as then have not already in their Colledge Library to be delivered to them at their choyce within sixe moneths after my decease. And if they shall make choyce of Fryer Bacons manuscript for one of them, then my will and minde is that if at any time hereafter the trew owner of the same that can make true and lawfull challenge therevnto and proove it his owne, will not be contented or intreated to give the originall manuscript to the said Colledge Library then I desire the said Master and ffellowes at their owne charge to cause the same to be fayrely copied out and the same copy to be and remaine in the said Colledge library' [see Kew, The National Archives, PROB 11/163/269; cited in Pahta (1998), p. 141]. The manuscript is listed as no. 539 in the list of manuscripts in Bernard, Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (1697), I, part 3. The alpha-numerical elements of its current classmark are printed on three labels pasted onto the spine (R.14.52), inscribed in pencil on the inside of the front cover. Its printed ex libris featuring its armorial coat of arms and name (Collegium S.S. et Individuae Trinitatis in Academia Cantabrigiensi) pasted on f. [i] verso. Its modern library stamp on ff. 1:1r, 2:270v, [ii] verso.

provenance: overview: The manuscript belonged to the Venetian scholar Barbaro, Ermolao, 1454-1493 Ermolao Barbaro il Giovane (1454-1493) , and it later entered the possession of Lucius Victor Falchonius (Lucio Vittorio Falconio), identified with Fausto, Vittore, active 16th century Fausto Vittore (1490-1546) , pupil and collaborator of Aulus Janus Parrhasius in Venice (1508-1511) and public lecturer on Greek eloquence in Venice. Fausto Vittore quotes the Exegesis of Tzetzes in his De comoedia libellus (1511), and this manuscript R.16.33 has been identified among a list of manuscripts in a letter of Falchonius/Fausto to Jacopo Sannazaro (1458-1530; Vind. lat. 9737e, ff. 11r-v): according to this letter, the manuscript seems to have been taken from Falchonius by Parrhasius. After the death of Aulus Janus Parrhasius (1470-1522) Parrasio, Aulo Giano, 1470-1522 the manuscript was inherited by the Neapolitan humanist Antonio Seripando (1476-1531) Seripando, Antonio, 1476-1531 , as stated in the note on f. [v] verso: Antonij Seripandi ex Jani Parrhasii testamento. At Seripando’s death, his books passed on to his brother, Cardinal Girolamo Seripando (1493-1563) Seripando, Girolamo, 1493-1563 , who in turn bequeathed his library to the Augustinian convent of San Giovanni a Carbonara in Naples. Before being declared a 'Royal Library' by King Ferdinand IV of Naples in 1792, the convent library was raided on several occasions and in some instances manuscripts and books were sold by the monks themselves. The manuscript eventually entered the possession of Richard Bentley Bentley, Richard, 1662-1742 , Master of Trinity College.

provenance: overview: [?]Antony: a man of this name may have owned or accessed the manuscript: the word Atone that was aded to the upper margin of f. 12r in a late 15th- or early 16th-century hand may be a name inscription. ; [?]Margery: a woman of this name may have owned or accessed the manuscript: the word Margere that was aded to the outer margin of f. 28r in a late 15th- or early 16th-century hand may be a name inscription. This previously unnoticed inscription may be of particular interest for the unique copy of a female-voiced version of Chaucer's Against Women Unconstant on f. 77r: as Mooney (2000) argues, the revision was probably made by a woman author. Although the hands of the (possible) name inscription and the poem seem to be different, it may indicate a particular circulation of this incunable among a female audience.

binding: overview: Medieval Greek binding. Parchment textblock cut to the size of the boards. Four sewing stations prepared with v-notches. Sewing is an unsupported loop-stitch with an S-twist sewing thread. Only the tailband remains complete; only remnants over the boards are visible on the headband. Classic Greek endbands with wound cream threads around two cord cores. The thread is passed diagonally around the lower core and wraps vertically around the upper core. One transverse continuous textile lining with two transverse patches of lining at head and tail. There are no endleaves. Board attachment is sewn, passing from the outside face of the board to the inner face and then back out. Wooden boards. The boards have grooved edges and are shaped at the spine edge both inside and outside of the board. The inside of the board creates a gentle curve to the spine; the outside edge of the board is rounded. Full covering of red tanned skin, decorated with blind tooling, with the use of intaglio tools for some of the tooling. Triple fillet border with triple fillets intersecting creating a diamond shape. Intaglio and floral tools are used between the fillets. On the right board, there is blind tooling at the head and tail turn-ins. Designs include double-headed eagles, dragons and pairs of quadrupeds. There are five holes located on the right board (corners and centre) that held metal furniture. Fragments of two pins remain. Evidence of fastening remnants from several attachments: two sets of three holes through the right board; a pair of holes at each board edge on both board; two extra larger holes on the left board fore-edge (these seem to correspond with the two set of three holes). Two modern paper labels designating the classmark are stuck at head and tail on the spine. Remains of red cloth tabs marking the beginning of Gospels are attached to ff. 81 and 223. 152 119 90

binding: overview: Alla Graeca binding from the second half of the 16th century. Five sewing stations prepared with v-notches. Sewing is an unsupported loop-stitch with an S-twist sewing thread. Greek-style endbands: wound cream threads around two cord cores (Greek-style simple endband) with a decorative woven secondary endband creating chevron patterns with pink and green silk threads. Blue transverse continuous textile lining. There is a separate cream-coloured textile panel between the lowermost sewing station and the tail. This may also be the case at the head but cannot be confirmed. Laid paper endleaves made of one pastedown and a flyleaf. The left endleaves are separate sewn through a stub, the right endleaves are separate tipped. Couched laminate boards with no squares and attached with bridling. Full covering of brown-red tanned skin with lapped turn-ins with foredge over. Blind tooling decoration on both boards. Quintuple fillet border with a quintuple fillet inner frame, and quintuple diagonal fillets intersecting the borders at the corners. The lower diagonal fillets meet towards the centre and the upper diagonal fillets do the same, however the pairs do not meet. Use of floral tools, the same tool being repeated at each corner, the centre of each frame edge, and where the diagonals meet. Central almond shaped medallion with a smaller floral tool on its centre. Two modern paper labels with the classmark are stuck at head and tail on the spine. 326 231 67

Various hand tools have been used between the fillets and at intersections, these include roundels, small and large diamond shaped florals, a square shaped floral at intersections, round tool of a double-headed eagle and a smaller round zoomorphic tool. contents: title(s): Wooden board
binding: overview: A single board of a medieval or early modern binding from the eastern Mediterranean. The grain of the wood runs parallel from head to tail. The edges of the board are square with the exception of the spine edge, which has a peripheral cushion. Sewing thread once used as a board attachment remains. The sewing thread passes between eight sewing attachment holes in four pairs. From the head edge these pairs are measured at 46mm, 89mm, 175mm, 211mm. The sewing thread passes between the holes in an S-pattern on the inside of the board from head to tail. Recesses are cut for the thread to pass between each pair but not for the diagonal thread. One end of the sewing thread can be seen at the uppermost pair of sewing attachment holes. There is one hole just below the uppermost pair of sewing attachment holes which contains thread remnants, though its use is unclear. A pair of anchor holes at head and tail exist to accommodate the endband sewing tie downs. They are no further than 25mm from the spine edge of the board and no further than 20mm from the head- or tail-edge. Three endband threads remain, very similar to the sewing thread, passing through the endbanding holes closest to the spine edge and three through the next, at both head and tail. Recesses are cut for the endband threads to pass on the outside face of the board only. Two groups of three holes, in a triangular pattern, exist towards the fore-edge of the board, these holes possibly indicate the presence of straps at one point. It is unclear whether the three holes are a set or a pair and a single. Remnants of a textile spine lining exist, passing over the spine edge of the board and extending onto the outer face. Patches of parchment, and possibly tawed skin (seen on the outer face of the board but obscured by a later parchment sheet on the inner face) have been used to repair a split in the board, which can be detected at the head edge. A sheet of parchment, almost the size of the board, is adhered to the inner face of the board, probably once again to stabilise splits in the board. Remnants of previous leather coverings exist, at the outer face towards the spine edge of the board and as turn-ins at the head and tail on the inner face of the board.

codicology: collation: Quire 18-3 ff. 1-5, [i] This quire of five surviving folios followed by a stub was probably originally a quaternion, in which the cancelled stub was the seventh original folio, while the outermost bifolio, forming the original first and eighth folios, has been lost. In this case the eighth folio was probably cancelled prior to the whole bifolio being lost, as the text appears to have continued from this point without loss. It may also have been a ternion of which the last folio has been cancelled, without loss of text, although the construction of the quire with hair side outermost which this would require would be unusual. However, the foliation of the Sinai fragment ends with 161, and there is a gap between the end of the text in that fragment and the beginning of this one, of a length corresponding to the content of a single folio, indicating that one intervening folio has been lost. This would tend in favour of the hypothesis that one folio was lost from the beginning of this quire.
codicology: foliation: The fragment is foliated with the numbers 1-5, [i] in Arabic numerals, in pencil, recto, upper right. The fragment also retains foliation from the source manuscript, not original to its production: the numbers 163-167 in Greek numerals, in black ink, recto, upper right.

binding: overview: Early 16th-century binding, style reminiscent of late-15th century work; stamped leather covers over bevelled oak boards. Rebacked and repaired by the Wilson bindery in 1889. The left cover is decorated with two concentric double-fillet frames with Oxford corners, the inner panel within the central frame divided in half horizontally with a double fillet, and each half-panel divided per saltire with a double fillet. A circular 'ihs' stamp impressed in each quarter-compartment and at the corners of the centre panel. Right cover is decorated with two concentric double-fillet frames with Oxford corners, the centre panel divided per saltire with a triple fillet. A square-matrix stamp of a stag lodged (seated with legs tucked under body) in each quarter-compartment of the central panel, each stamp decorated with a small dotted cross [⁜] tool in a round matrix at each corner. The stag tool is similar to but not the same as the two lodged stag tools used by the so-called 'Demon binder' on Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 3022, as the MS Add. 2994 stag stamp presents the head in a different attitude and includes a small piece of foliage underneath the stag. Remains of two hook-and-bar fastenings on each cover. The left cover retains two strap ends, the lower one tangible as a stub between the leather and the boards, the upper one visible and (?unusually) made of tawed skin stained red. The right cover retains a metal bar-fastening plate in the upper position, the lower one is gone. It should be noted that the strap ends and the fastening plates are not perfectly aligned. Spine rebacked in a light brown polished leather decorated with geometric blind tooling. Three raised bands on spine. Spine capped at head and tail with no head or tail tabs or bands visible. Label of green leather tooled in gold affixed to spine: 'LYTTLETON'S TENURES | NATURA BREVIUM | M.S.S'. Two small printed paper labels affixed to spine: 'ADD' and '2994' for the present shelfmark. Paper pastedowns pasted over the turn ins. The left pastedown contains: A stamp 'BOUND BY WILSON' and underneath a price and date '6£9. 1989' i.e., bound for 6 pounds and 9 shillings in 1889. A 'D' in pencil reflecting a CUL size-classification in use in the Department of Manuscripts at CUL. A brief handwritten record of the purchase of the volume by CUL: 'J. E. Cornish 1889 £2.2.0'. The right pastedown contains a textual and codicological summary of the contents of the volume in pencil, perhaps in the hand of Francis Jenkinson Francis Jenkinson, Cambridge University Librarian (1853-1923) , Cambridge University Librarian from 1889-1923. The volume is stored in a green slipcase with 'LYTTLETON' and 'Add 2994' tooled in gold on the face opposite the opening. Dimensions (L x W x D) not including slipcase: 294 x 208 x 45 It should be noted that Dr David Pearson kindly offered a brief assessment of this binding during the preparation of this record, but any mistakes or inaccuracies herein remain the responsibility of the author.
