codicology: foliation: The manuscript is foliated with the numbers 1-48, 51-54, 57-72, 75-78, 89-96, 98-103, 105-120, 129-143, 145-190, 192-219, 222-303, 305-307, in pencil, in Arabic numerals, recto, upper right. Folio numbers 49-50, 55-56, 73-74, 79-88, 97, 104, 121-128, 144, 191, 220-221, 304 have been assigned to leaves no longer present in the volume (as per historic foliation practices at Cambridge University Library). From f. 17r onwards there is another foliation in pencil, in Arabic numerals, recto, upper right, which has been struck through. This sequence numbers f. 17r as 25, and was evidently the original Cambridge University Library foliation, following the practice of counting absent folios and based on the loss of a single original quire preceding this; there is a note to this effect on this folio. Since the classmark is also marked here, this was presumably the first folio of the manuscript at the time, the replacement paper quires preceding it perhaps having become detached. They must then have been identified as belonging to this manuscript and the foliation amended to reflect the fact that the replacement quires used sixteen folios in place of the original eight.
binding: overview: Medieval Greek binding. The textblock is cut level to the bookboards. There are three sewing stations prepared as v-notches. The sewing is an unsupported loop stitch. Greek-style endbands with a cream coloured thread wound around a single core. The endbands extend approximately one quarter of the way onto the board. Where the endbands extend onto each board they are tied down to three holes that extend through the board - from the inner face to the outer face. The transverse continuous spine lining is made of a textile with a printed pattern. The spine lining extends to one third of the way onto the left board and half of the way onto the right board. The board attachment is bridling. The sewing thread enters at the spine edge of the boards, emerges on the inner face and then travels to the outer face, where the path would presumably change stations (the sewing path on the outer face of the boards is obscured by the spine lining). There is a single knot present on the inner face of both boards, next to the uppermost sewing station. This is likely to be the start of the sewing and therefore suggests that the textblock was sewn in two halves. The boards are made from wood. The edges are square on both boards, except the outer spine edge where they have been shaped to form a round that meets with the shoulder of the textblock. Full covering of dark brown leather. Two of the turn-ins do not meet, one on each board; two of them are overlapping. A single metallic pin is set into the centre of the foredge of the left board. Corresponding to the pin there are three holes through the right board that contain remnants of a leather strap. These holes are located close to the foredge approximately half way up the board. There are annotations in Greek inside the left and right boards, and traces of an annotation in Syriac inside the right board. 208 171 107

On the left cover, the oval contains a half-length figure bearing a scroll (an Evangelist?); on the right cover it contains an arabesque motif. Two metal catch plates on the left board; one leather strap in the upper part of the right board, with metal hook; only the attachment of a second, in the lower part, is preserved. Blind tooling on the boards' edges, which are bevelled towards the inner face. Gauffered edges (a four-leaf clover and leaves design) with traces of color. Gold tooling on spine with shelfmark, only partially extant, Add. 30 220 160 70

binding: overview: Conservation binding by Cambridge University Library 2021, with card cover. 222 167 75 The former binding, of Greek origin and probably original to the production of the manuscript, has been retained and is housed with the manuscript. There are four sewing stations prepared with v-notches. The sewing is an unsupported loop-stitch with an S-twist sewing thread. Greek-style endbands around two cord cores. The primary endbands are made of wound cream threads around one core. The secondary decorative endband creates a chevron pattern on top of the primary and over a thinner upper core. Yellow and red threads have been used to create the decorative chevron. A yellow and blue loop is visible on the headband towards the left board. This loop probably marks the previous location of a page marker now lost. One transverse continuous plain textile lining covering up to one third of the boards. Board attachment is bridling, each station including three holes. The three holes create a v-shape configuration. The thread passes from the spine edge to the inner side of the board. The cover obstructs the study of the outer face of the board; however it can be assumed that the thread travels from the inner side of the board to the outer side and then back inside. Hardwood wooden boards with horizontal grain. The boards have no grooved edges but are shaped at the spine edge both inside and outside of the board. The inside of the board creates a gentle curve to the spine; the outside edge of the board is rounded. Full covering of dark brown tanned skin with butt-mitred turn-ins. Both boards have the text of prayers written on the inside, in a late 16th or 17-century hand. There are four holes on the corners of both boards suggesting previous use of furniture. There is a peg on the foredge of the left board towards the bottom corner, and a hole in the upper foredge suggesting the presence of another peg now lost. There are two pairs of holes through the right board near the foredge, matching the peg location. There are remnants of a braided leather strap on the inner face of the right board on the bottom pair of holes. Blind tooling decoration, with a similar pattern for both boards. Outer single-fillet border with two double-fillet frames enclosed. Three circles at each corner of the two inner frames. A single tool forming two hearts facing is repeated between the second and the third frame, creating a decorative roll. A single floral tool is used at the corners of the inner frame. The classmark is printed on two modern paper labels stuck at the head and tail of the spine. 228 181 79

Some have been wholly or partially lost to damage or cropping. They survive in whole or in part on Quires 27-32 (βʹ-ζʹ). A fourth sequence of quire signatures in Greek numerals, in black ink, on the first folio of each quire, recto, upper right, beginning again from the number 1, runs from Quire 34 onward (from f. 261 until at least f. 308). They survive in whole or in part on Quires 34-39 (αʹ-ϛʹ). It is unclear whether Quires 40-41 ever had quires in this sequence. They could have been lost to cropping, but the crosses that usually appear on the first folio of each quire are also absent from these two. The cross on Quire 26 appears on the second folio, which is the first of this quire to bear any writing (f. 198r).

codicology: signatures: There are original quire signatures in Greek numerals, in brown ink, on the last folio of each quire, verso, lower right. They survive on quires 1-6 and 9 (ιζʹ-κβʹ, κϛʹ).
codicology: foliation: The manuscript is foliated with the numbers 49, 51-103, 106-111, 121-126, 128, in pencil, in Arabic numerals, recto, upper right. Folio numbers 1-48, 50, 104-105, 112-120, 127 have been assigned to leaves no longer present in the volume (as per historic foliation practices at Cambridge University Library). The conjectures of the foliation are clearly erroneous. It supposes the loss of five quires at the beginning of the manuscript, whereas the signatures indicate the loss of sixteen. The loss of a quire following f. 96, indicated by the extent of the lacuna in the text at this point, has not been noted, while the loss of nine folios (a single folio followed by a full quire) has been wrongly supposed after f. 111, where the extent of the lacuna indicates only the loss of a single folio.

binding: overview: Textblock cut to the size of the boards. Four sewing stations prepared with v-notches. Sewing is on double-cords with a Z-twist sewing thread. Both endbands have broken threads. Greek-style compound endbands. Primary wound endband around a cord core, with secondary chevron in blue and yellow with a third thin crowning cord. There are two cloth spine linings, one extending up to one third of the board and one up to two thirds of the board. The endband tiedowns pass through these patches of cloth. Laid paper integral endleaves made of one pastedown only. Board attachment is the cord sewing supports laced into the board. Small channels are visible on the outside face of the boards in which the supports lay. Wooden boards. The boards have grooved edges and the outer spine edges are shaped to form a round that meets the textblock at the shoulder. Full covering of dark brown tanned skin. Decoration uses blind tooling with intaglio hand-tools and fillets. Quintuple fillet border with two diagonals made of triple fillets. Floral hand-tool on the four corners of the outer border and in the middle, as well as in the diagonal intersection. Intaglio tooling of a double-headed eagle in the centre of the four panels created by the two intersecting diagonals. Fleur-de-lys tools surround the double-headed eagles (ten flowers in total). Both boards have the same decoration pattern. There are two metal alloy foredge catch pins and the remains of three plaited straps on the right inner board. 168 121 130

These cancellations were apparently made before the quire was ruled, as the ruling system accords with the present rather than the original structure of the quire. Quires 14-208 ff. [117]-172 Quire 213+2 ff. 173-189 This quire has been assembled out of physically disparate folios, formerly grouped as two separate quires, made up of the first-third and fourth-fifth folios of the present quire. The text proceeds continuously. The first folio (f. 173) is a single leaf, copied by Hand B, and bears the quire signature 23 (κγʹ). The second and third folios are single leaves copied by Hand C (ff. 174-175). The fourth and fifth folios (ff. 182 and f. 189) were copied by Hand A. The fourth and fifth are attached to one another by means of a parchment strip wrapped around them and pasted to them. The original text on ff. 182r and 189v has been written across this strip, indicating that it was added during the production of the manuscript. The fourth folio bears the quire signature 24 (κδʹ), written on this strip. A further strip, one side of which protrudes between f. 173 and f. 174, was wrapped around the second-fifth folios of the present composite quire and these stitched together along with the first. The text proceeds continuously. The first and second folios (ff. 243-244) are single leaves joined to each other only by stitching. The first folio bears the quire signature 32 (λβʹ). The third and fourth folios (ff. 245-246) are attached to one another by means of a parchment strip wrapped around them and pasted to them. The third folio bears the quire signature 33 (λγʹ), written on this strip. The text proceeds continuously. The first and second folios (ff. 255-256) are attached to one another by means of a parchment strip wrapped around them and pasted to them, further secured to the first folio by stitching. The first folio bears the quire signature 36 (λϛʹ), written on this strip. In places the strip overlays the text, indicating that it was attached after this was copied. Part of a letter protrudes from beneath it near the quire signature, perhaps part of a signature marked on the quire before the strip was attached. The third-eighth folios form a quaternion. The third folio bears the quire signature 37 (λζʹ). The two parts of the the quire are joined by stitching. binding: overview: Textblock cut to the size of the boards. There are four sewing stations. Preparation cannot be determined. Sewing is of loop stitch using an s-twist thread of medium thickness. Classical Greek endbands extending approximately ¼ of the way onto the boards – sewn around two cord cores, the lower is diagonal and the upper is wound vertically. The tailband is largely complete but the headband only exists over the left board. Transverse continuous textile spine lining, extending approximately 1/3 of the way onto the board. There are no endleaves. The board attachment is bridling. Wooden boards with square edges apart from rounding at the spine edge which meets the textblock at the shoulder. On the foredge of the left board, there is a hole that probably would have contained a metal fastening. On the inner side of the right board are remnants of covering leather and two braided leather straps. A deformed remnant of dark brown tanned skin covering remains attached to the right board, and a separate piece is housed alongside the manuscript, which is decorated with blind tooling. The tooling consists of a triple fillet at the edge of the board, then a vegetative roll, then a triple fillet border. Within this border triple fillets extend from the corners and centres to create an intersecting pattern. At the intersections of the triple fillets round intaglio tools have been used. 268 191 50

codicology: collation: The codex is formed mostly of quaternions. The first quire is a ternion from which the first two leaves have been excised, without loss of text. 1 parchment endleaf f. [i] Quire 16-2 ff. 3-6 ( 1st, 2nd leaf missing) Quires 2-218 ff. 7-166 Quire 226 ff. 167-172 Quire 238 ff. 173-180 Quire 242 ff. 181-182 1 parchment endleaf f. [ii] Throughout the manuscript, the first leaf of the second part of each quire is signalled by a cross traced in black ink or in pencil in the lower margin, right, recto, see the first on f. 11r (the one on f. 4r seems different from the others, could it be a later addition?), the last on f. 177r. There are moreover two series of signatures. The first is in Greek numerals (the number ζ΄, 7, is not present, but no quire is missing), written in brown ink or in pencil (these could be later additions), in the lower margin of the first leaf, recto, of the quires; in ink are written β 1, β 2, β 3 ( ff. 15r-17r) δ΄ ( f. 31r) ε΄, ε 2 (ff. f. 39r and 41r) ϛ΄ ( f. 47r). The remaining signatures, from η΄ ( f. 55r) to ο΄ ( f. 119r) are written in pencil. Moreover, there is a series of signatures, written in brown ink by the scribe, in Arabic numerals, from 1 ( f. 127r) to 6 ( f. 167r), in the lower margin, right, of the first leaf recto of the quires. Horizontal catchwords by the scribe, in brown ink, in the lower margin, right, directly under the text, on the verso of each leaf, passim also on the recto.

provenance: overview: Owned by the Augustinian Priory of St Giles and St AndrewBarnwell Priory (Cambridge, England) in Barnwell, Cambridge. The name 'Bernewell' is written in ink on f. i verso in a medieval hand. The book seems to have been in the possession of a member of the Barnwell community in 1451: on f. 13r, there is an erased inscription printed by J.S. Ringrose in her Summary Catalogue of the Additional Manuscripts: Hic liber pertinet domui canonicorum de Bernwell [...] domino Willelmo Teb[...] canonico eiusdem domus [...] die Octobris Anno Domini 1451. As Ringrose points out, this is probably William Tebbald Tebbald, William, who was Prior of Barnwell from 26 Nov 1474 until his death on 6 August 1489. ; The name Anthony Shupton Shupton, Anthony appears on ff. 14r, 134v, and iii recto. This appears to be the same Anthony Shupton who added his name in several places to London, British Library, Sloane MS 4. Evidence in the Sloane manuscript suggests that Shupton was alive in 1510, but the dates of his birth and death are unknown. ; Owned by James Cobbes (b. ?1602, d. 1685) Cobb(e)s, James (b. ?1602 d. 1685) of Bury St Edmunds, who owned several manuscripts that had once belonged to the Abbey in Bury St Edmunds. Cobbes foliated the manuscript and added running titles to the centre of the upper margin of each leaf, as well as a table of contents on f. ii recto. For further information about Cobbes as a collector see Beadle (2004). R. Beadle, 'The manuscripts of James Cobbes of Bury St Edmunds (c. 1602-1685)' in T. Matsuda, R. A. Linethal, J. Scahill (eds.), The medieval book and a modern collector: essays in honour of Toshiyuki Takamiya (Cambridge, 2004), pp. 427-442 ; In his will, James Cobbes (b. ?1602, d. 1685) Cobb(e)s, James (b. ?1602 d. 1685) left his Bookes and papers concerning Literature to his grandchild, James Harvy Harv(e)y, James. Several items that passed from James Cobbes to James Harvy eventually became part of the collection of Rev. Dr Cox Macro (b. 1683, d. 2 Feb 1767) Macro, Cox, b. 1683, d. 2 Feb 1767. For further information about Cobbes as a collector see Beadle (2004). ; Owned by Rev. Dr Cox Macro (b. 1683, d. 2 Feb 1767) Macro, Cox, b. 1683, d. 2 Feb 1767 of Bury St Edmunds. Macro probably purchased the volume from James Cobbes' grandson James Harvy as several Cobbes manuscripts became part of Macro's collection. Cambridge, University Library, Add. MS 6865 was manuscript was no. 29 in Cox Macro's library and a label with that designation is still present on the spine, as is his former title label, now mostly torn away. The manuscript was seen among the items in Macro's library by Thomas Tanner (1674-1735) Tanner, Thomas, 1674-1735 and appears among Macro's possessions in Tanner's Bibliotheca Britannico-Hibernica published in 1748. For further information about Macro's collection see Beadle (2004) and (2016). R. Beadle, 'Macro MS 5: A Historical Reconstruction', Transactions of the Cambridge Bibliographical Society 16.1 (2016), pp. 35-77 ; After Dr Cox Macro's death, his library passed to his daughter, Mary Macro Macro, Mary . Mary Macro married William Stainforth Stainforth, William in 1767. After their deaths, the manuscripts passed to William Stainforth's niece Elizabeth Stainforth (b. 1760) Stainforth, Elizabeth (b. 1760) . She married John Patteson (b. 1755, d. 1833) Patteson, John, 1755-1833 who owned the manuscripts until 1820. For further information about Macro's collection see Beadle (2016). ; John Patteson Patteson, John, 1755-1833 encountered financial difficulties in the second decade of the 19th century, and in 1820 he sold the Macro manuscripts to London bookseller James Christie (b. 1773, d. 1831) Christie, James, 1773-1831 . For further information about Macro's collection see Beadle (2016). ; The Macro manuscripts were purchased as a group from James Christie the Younger (b. 1773, d. 1831) Christie, James, 1773-1831 by Dawson Turner (b. 1775, d. 1858) Turner, Dawson, 1775-1858 on the understanding that fellow collector Hudson Gurney would later purchase a portion of the collection. For further information about Macro's collection see Beadle (2016). ; Purchased from Dawson Turner Turner, Dawson, 1775-1858 by Hudson Gurney (b. 1775, d. 1864) Gurney, Hudson, 1775-1864 of Bawdeswell Hall, Bawdeswell, Norfolk. The manuscript remained with the Gurney family until it was sold by Major Quintin Edward Gurney (b. 1883, d. 1968) Gurney, Q. E. (Quintin Edward), 1883-1968 in a sale of the Gurney family manuscripts at Sotheby's in 1936. For further information about Macro's collection see Beadle (2016).

This comprises a mix of 17th- and 20th/21st-century foliation, as follows. 17th-century foliation. 2-12 | 13-134 Foliated in the upper outer corner of each recto in ink in Hindu-Arabic numerals. Foliated ff. 2-134 by James Cobbes (d. June 1685), a former owner of the manuscript who also added running headings to the upper margins, and a list of the contents on a pasted in piece of paper (f. ii recto at the beginning of the volume. The foliation sequence added by Cobbes is not disrupted by leaves lost at the boundary of Quires 5 and 6, which indicates that those leaves were lost before Cobbes added his foliation sequence. 20th- and 21st-century foliation. i, ii, 1 ... | ... 42a ... iii Additional foliation supplied in several phases by Cambridge University Library staff after the purchase of the volume in March 1936, discussed in the order in which they appear in the manuscript: The left pastedown foliated as f. i in pencil in the upper left corner of the leaf The pasted-in paper leaf with Cobbes' list of the contents of the volume foliated as f. ii by Dr James Freeman, Medieval Manuscripts Specialist, Cambridge University Library in 2022. The first leaf, which lacked an explicit designation by Cobbes, foliated as f. 1 in pencil. The second of the two leaves designated f. 42 by Cobbes has been refoliated as f. 42a by Dr James Freeman, Medieval Manuscripts Specialist, Cambridge University Library in 2022. The final leaf, the former right pastedown, has been designated f. iii by Dr James Freeman, Medieval Manuscripts Specialist, Cambridge University Library in 2022.
binding: overview: Medieval binding. Full bound in tawed skin over bevelled-edge wood boards cut flush with the book-block. Five sewing supports of split tawed skin laced into the boards horizontally and secured in place with wood pegs. Covers have an impressed repeating pattern as if wrapped by a thin cord for a significant period of time. Head and tail bands sewn in a neutral cream yarn and anchored through the tawed skin cover at the spine openings. Hook-and-bar fastening in the centre of the fore edge: tawed skin strap embedded in the fore edge of the left board, the free end terminating in a decorative metal hook; metal bar fastening embedded in the fore edge of the right board. Faint traces of spotted design painted onto head, fore, and tail edges of the bookblock. Two paper labels fixed to the spine with text handwritten in ink: upper label almost entirely gone; lower label '29'. Spine labels added while the manuscript was in the possession of Dr Cox Macro and reflect his library designations. Left pastedown f. i is parchment and conjoint with the last leaf of the first quire (now cancelled). Left pastedown contains: - Current shelfmark in ink 'Add. 6865' - The letter 'E' - a size classification used by Cambridge University Library - Medieval ownership inscription: 'Bernewell' - A note in ink recording the purchase of the manuscript by Cambridge University Library by the hand of Alwyn Faber Scholfield (b. 1884, d. 1969) Scholfield, A. F. (Alwyn Faber), 1884-1969, University Librarian 1923-1949 - A paper leaf pasted onto the pastedown along the paper leaf's left edge containing a list of the contents of the volume by James Cobbes. The paper leaf has the separate designation ii. Former right pastedown is parchment and has been lifted and is now foliated as f. iii. What is now the recto, f. iii recto, contains the name 'Anthony Shupton' twice in ink, and some pen trials, also in ink. Medieval sewn repairs to the turn ins on the right board. Head and fore edge of book-block decorated with red (and blue?) dot pattern.

provenance: overview: Fillongley/Fylongley, Henry (fl. c. 1440-1460)Henry Fillongley/Fylongley (fl. c. 1440-1450): courtier, sheriff and between 1453 and 1457 Keeper of the Great Wardrobe of Henry VI. At some point during the 1440s, Fillongley was in possession of the Dunmows manor house, which stood on a rectangular moated site at Hall Orchard, on the outskirts of Fulbourn, near Cambridge. The earthworks for the moat survive, but the house was demolished in the 18th century. See A.F. Wareham and A.P.M. Wright, A history of the County of Cambridge and the Isle of Ely, Victoria County History (2022), vol. 10: Cheveley, Flendish, Staine and Staploe Hundreds (North-Eastern Cambridgeshire) and Aileen Connor, 'Investigations on a Medieval Moated Site at Hall Orchard, Fulbourn: An Archaeological Training Dig' (Fulbourn: Archaeological Field Unit, Cambridgeshire County Council, 2006), p. 6.

It has since been reattached in its correct location after f. 165 and the former folio number struck through and replaced. ff. 169 bis and 189 bis are stubs with a small amount of surviving text, which were originally omitted from the foliation sequence but have since been numbered (a similar stub survives following f. 217v, here designated f. binding: overview: 14th or 15th-century Greek binding. Sewn on five stations prepared with v-notches. Sewing is an unsupported loop-stitch with an S-twist sewing thread. Classic Greek endbands with wound cream threads around two cord cores, extending to approximately 1/5 of the board. The thread is passed diagonally around the lower core and wraps vertically around the upper core. A few tailband threads are broken. One transverse continuous textile lining extending to approximately 1/5 of the board. The endband tiedowns pass through the cloth. Laid-paper endleaves. The left endleaves are made of one pastedown sewn through a stub. A separate small piece of paper is visible and also sewn, which might suggest the previous presence of another bifolio now lost. The right endleaves consist of one pastedown with a small stub hooked around the last gathering and tipped to the penultimate gathering. Board attachment is bridling passing from the outside face of the board to the inner face and then back out. Wooden boards. The boards are shaped at the spine edge both inside and outside of the board. The inside of the board creates a gentle curve to the spine; the outside edge of the board is rounded. Channels have been cut outside and inside the boards to accommodate the sewing threads. Full covering of dark brown tanned skin. There is a metallic pin in the centre of the left board foredge, and remnants of straps (peg, cord and red thread) are visible in the inner side of the right board. Blind tooling with the use of intaglio tools. Both boards seem to have had the same tooled design. Quadruple fillets intersect creating a diamond shape, with intaglio floral tools on the fillets. Lozenges containing fleurs-de-lys and roundels containing floral and zoomorphic designs are tooled on the intersecting points. A yellow modern round sticker is stuck on the spine tail. The leather tab of a page-marker survives on f. 135. 334 252 83

provenance: overview: Sir Edmund Jenney (d. 1522) Jenney, Edmund, 1522 : some of the notes are in his hand and may have obtained other items from his father, William Jenney (d. 1483), who was administered to Lincoln's Inn in 1430, and was Justice of the King's Bench 1481-1483. Jenny's role of compiler is supported by the second item (ff. 10r-75v), which was made for Thomas Banyard of Lincoln's Inn, who was administered in 1459, with William Jenney as his sponsor. Folio 287v also contains the name 'Tymperley', which probably refers to John Tymperley (d. 1491) of Hintlesham, Suffolk, who was administered to Lincoln's Inn in 1463. The name 'Andrewys' is written on the manuscript's old cover in a 15th-century script; this may be the 'Andrew' who was adminstered to Lincoln's Inn in 1433, possibly John Andrews of Baylham, Suffolk, Justice of the Peace of Suffolk between 1445 and 1460. The issues of William Jenney, the eldest son of Edmund, and Francis Jenney (b. 1510) , son of William, on ff. 8r-9v suggest that the manuscript passed down to his son and grandson. provenance: overview: Possibly owned by Clare College, Cambridge (then known as Clare Hall): an ownership inscription by a hand of the fourteenth century on f. iv verso reads: 'Liber colegii de [...]'. The removal of the following word makes a conclusive identification impossible, however this may be one of the four books donated to Clare Hall by William de Acton/Aketon (d. by Feb. 1391) de Aketon, William (b. ?1293, d. ?1391) (the others were copies of John of Gaddesden, Rosa medicinae, Avicenna, Canon medicinae, tr. Gerard of Cremona, and Bartholomeus Anglicus, De proprietatibus rerum). R.W. Hunt, 'Medieval Inventories of Clare College Library', TCBS 1.2 (1950), pp. 105-125 CBMLC 10, pp. 138-39, 655 MLGB3 Venn:ACAD (no reference ID - search 'Aketon') ; Owned by the Tollemache family of Helmingham Hall, Helmingham, Suffolk, England: Helmingham MS 15, pressmark L.J.IV (paper label, inside of the left board). A loose leaf of paper kept with the manuscript bears a brief description written in ink in a ?20th century hand, with the pressmark reference L.J.IV.2 (with the '2' struck out). It is not known when the Tollemache family acquired MS Add. 9213; according to Edwards and Griffiths the Tollemache family seems to have began assembling a private library by the mid-16th century, and subsequent generations continued to acquire manuscripts and rare books. The 1993 Sotheby catalogue description suggests that the the manuscript was 'probably bound for Sir Lionel Tollemache Tollemache, Lionel, Earl of Dysart (British noble, politician, 1649-1727) , 1648-1726, third earl of Dysart', which would place the family's acquisition of the volume before 1727. Probably the manuscript described as 'Liber Medicines Abubecri' in the 1762 Catalogue of the Library at Helmingham Hall in Suffolk (Suffolk Record Office, Ipswich HD 1538/253/167, printed in Edwards and Griffiths, pp. 362-364). Edwards and Griffiths tentatively suggested that the 'Liber Medicines Abubecri' might be their 'MS 64', now  Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania, Library, Lawrence J. Schoenberg Collection, MS 24 , a copy of the medical works of Isaac Israeli ben Solomon, but since the opening words of MS Add. 9213 are 'Abubecri arazi filij zacarie liber incipit' (1r) it seems much more likely that that the 'Liber Medicines Abubecri' entry in the in the 1762 Catalogue refers to CUL MS Add. 9213. Peter Kidd, 'The Helmingham Hall Manuscripts', Medieval Manuscripts Provenance: Notes and Observations (18 March 2015) A.S.G. Edwards and J. Griffiths, 'The Tollemache Collection of Medieval Manuscripts', The Book Collector 49.3 (2000), pp. 349-364. binding: overview: 17th century (?second half) binding, 'probably bound for Sir Lionel Tollemache, 1648-1726, third Earl of Dysart' (Sotheby's Sale Catalogue for 6 December 1993, Lot 52). Full bound in sprinkled calf over millboard with matching decoration to left and right covers. Covers are decorated with a blind double fillet frame with Oxford corners inset from the perimeter of the board by c. 10mm. The cover material over the head, fore, and tail edges of the boards is decorated with a thick single fillet tooled in gold. Five raised bands on spine, each decorated with a blind double fillet through their centre (i.e., across the width of the spine). Spine compartments are decorated with a blind single fillet along their upper and lower perimeters. Head and tail bands are a beige fibre wrapped around a core of what appears to be straw or reed; head band is exposed as the upper opening of the spine has been torn away down to the first raised band. Two paper labels fixed to spine with an adhesive: - Upper label: 'Medical Tracts MSS XIII' in ink - Lower label: 'Add. 9213' in ink (the present Cambridge University Library shelfmark) No pastedowns; turn ins and inner faces of boards are exposed. The number '15' circled and struck through on the inner face of the left board. Head, fore, and tail edges of the bookblock are stained red. Paper bifolia forming two endleaves at each end of the bookblock (ff. ii-iii and ff. v-vi). Each paper bifolium has a watermark at the centrefold of a crown over a scroll-eared escutchon with two bendlets. This watermark is a close visual match for a watermark found in Oxford, Christ Church College, MS Mus. 1018-1020, a collection of partbooks of music composed by Thomas Talbot, probably copied in the 1630s. The watermark is printed in Ashbee, Thompson, and Wainwright (eds.), The Viola Da Gamba Society Index of Manuscripts Containing Consort Music, 2 vols (2014), II.302. Parchment endleaves at the opening of the volume (ff. i and iv) are contemporary with the main text and have probably always travelled with the main quire stack as the opening endleaves. A parchment stub at the end of the volume (f. vii) of a document dated to the 33rd and 34th regnal years of Queen Elizabeth I (c. November 1590 - November 1592).

provenance: overview: 'Thys ys thomas hullis boke of stebbyng' (f. i recto; repeated in part on f. iv recto): Stebbing is a village in Essex and numerous Thomas Hulls are attested in manorial and other records relating to it. binding: overview: A Byzantine binding using five sewing stations prepared with v-notches. The sewing is unsupported loop-stitch with a Z-twist sewing thread. There are classic Greek endbands extending approximately ¼ of the way onto the boards. They are sewn around two cord cores. The lower is diagonal and the upper is wound vertically. Both endbands have broken threads. The headband is complete, the tailband is partially missing. The cloth spine lining extends up to one third of the board. The endband tiedowns pass through the cloth. Board attachment is bridling passing from the outside face of the board to the inner face and then back out. Channels are visible on the outside and inner faces of the boards to accommodate the threads. The boards are wooden, with slightly grooved edges, and the inner spine edges are shaped to form a round that nestles in the textblock shoulders. There is a full covering of dark red tanned skin. The skin has been patched on both boards; one piece has been added, which extends from the upper left part of the left board to the upper part of the right board. This piece has been stitched in place with a natural coloured thread. An additional triangular piece is visible on the upper turn-in of the right board foredge. The turn-ins are now all open-mitred. On the left board there are two metal bosses in the middle of the board, one towards the spinedge and one towards the foredge. There are remnants of two other bosses on the left board, and remnants of four bosses at the corners of the right board. On the left board, marks of four larger round pieces are visible on the four corners; those areas might have been covered by round metallic plates, held in place by pins. One pin is visible on one of those holes on the bottom right corner. Several smaller holes are also spread across both boards, suggesting the presence of smaller metallic furniture pieces. There is a metallic pin on the left board foredge. Another hole is visible next to this pin on the left hand side; and two other holes are visible on the lower part of the foredge. Those holes suggest the previous presence of metallic pins. There are remnants of cord ties on the inside of the right board, going through two holes on the lower part of the right board; and through two out of three holes on the upper part of the right board. Decoration uses blind tooling with intaglio hand-tools and fillets. On the left board, two vegetative rolls framed with double fillet borders extend from to the outer edges towards the centre. A central cross fills the central panel, the cross being framed by a single fillet with floral tool on the corners. Small holes on the cross suggest the previous presence of metallic furniture or gems. Double fillets are visible starting from the upper right corner of the frame, and disappearing where the cross motif starts. Smaller hand tools are visible on the frame corners. On the right board, there are two vegetative rolls framed with double fillet borders extending from to the outer edges towards the centre. Four triangular shaped tools with floral decoration are impressed on the central area within the inner frames, alongside two rounded tools inclosing fleurs-de-lys motifs. Smaller hand tools are also visible on the frame corners. 295 191 108

binding: overview: Medieval Greek binding. Sewn in unsupported loop stitch, with three sewing stations prepared as v-notches. Primary endbands are in the classic Greek style, wound with a cream thread and extending approximately one-fifth of the way onto the boards. The lower core is wound diagonally and the upper vertically. Remnants of yellow and blue threads that would have created a decorative secondary endband remain. Textile transverse continuous spine lining can be seen, which extends at least a quarter of the way onto the boards. There are pastedowns of plain paper. The left pastedown is integral, with sewing passing through a fold suggesting that the pastedown is a bifolio where both elements (at least one a full leaf) have been pasted down. The right pastedown may have had the same construction but in its present condition it cannot be determined whether the sewing passed through a fold or if there is a second leaf which can therefore be described as a separate pastedown. The board attachment is bridling, the thread first passes through the outer face of the board, from which point a lacing path cannot be confirmed. The boards are wooden, with grooved edges. The outer spine edge is rounded to meet the shoulder of the textblock. There is full covering in dark brown leather with remnants of a red velvet secondary covering over the top. Over the boards there is faint blind tooling which is partially obscured by the secondary velvet covering. The edges of the boards are tooled with a double fillet boarder. Repetition of a diamond-shaped tool containing a double-headed eagle creates a border inside the double fillet. Inside this is a border of decorative lacing. Within the lacing there is a final double fillet border within which double fillets are used to create an undetermined intersecting pattern. At the intersections small roundels are used. Within the panels created by the pattern the double-headed eagle and decorative lacing are used again. There is no tooling on the spine. Two metal pins are located at the foredge of the left board. Remains of braided leather straps can be found on the inside of the right board, two sets each passing through three holes in the board. Various holes can be seen on both boards, some containing remnants of metal furniture. A particular pattern cannot be determined. The edges of the folios have been painted red. 296 243 130

codicology: collation: This manuscript is a composite volume comprised of 16 quires from three originally separate sources. Quires 11 and 13 are both irregular. Annotations by H.L. Pink on ff. 92r and 106r show that it was previously thought that each of these quires lacked a leaf. However, comparison of the text in this volume with that found in Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Digby 79 confirms that no text is missing, which would ordinarily point to these leaves having been cancelled. The typical arrangement in this volume is 'HFFH', meaning the hair side faces outwards on each quire, and the sides match across openings: hair sides facing hair sides, and flesh sides facing flesh sides. However, irregularities in the disposition of hair and flesh sides in the leaves of parchment in these quires point to more complicated changes having taken place. In Quire 11, the hair/flesh sequence continues normally until f. 88v (=flesh) and f. 89r (=hair). Folios 89-90 are a bifolium, after which may be seen a stub that is conjoint with f. 88. However, there is no irregularity in the hair/flesh sequence at this juncture: f. 90v (=hair) and f. 92r (=hair). It appears, therefore, that at the time of production the scribe replaced or inverted the 6th and 7th leaves of the quire, arranging them with the flesh side facing inwards (rather than outwards, as would have been the usual arrangement), as well as cancelling the 8th leaf. The intention may perhaps have been to disguise the cancellation by arranging the leaves in such a way that an interruption to the disposition of the leaves was disguised. In Quire 13, a similar pattern of behaviour is detectable. Although the 2nd leaf has been cancelled (after f. 104), there is no interruption to the disposition there: f. 104v (=flesh) and f. 106r (=flesh). The stub that is visible between these leaves is conjoint with f. 112. At that location, however, there is an interruption to the disposition: f. 112v (=hair) and f. 113 (=flesh). Again, after having made a cancellation, the scribe appears to have rearranged the disposition of the remaining bifolia, disguising the removal of the leaf at this place where the cancellation was made. Quire 15 is more difficult to construe correctly, it comprises six single leaves, now stitched behind Quire 14 and of an uncertain original structure; the disposition of hair and flesh sides suggests that they may have once been part of a quire, or else have been arranged to reflect the typical arrangement of the leaves in a quire. The collation of the volume can be described as follows: Quire 110-5 (ff. 1-5: 6th-10th leaves cancelled) | Quires 2-38 (ff. 6-21) Quire 412 (ff. 22-33) Quire 58 (ff. 34-41) Quire 610 (ff. 42-51) Quires 7-98 (ff. 52-75) Quire 108-2 (ff. 76-81: 7th and 8th leaves, ff. 82-83 excised, probably blank) Quire 1112-1 (ff. 84-95: one leaf cancelled; see above for further details)) Quire 128 (ff. 96-103) Quire 1310-1 (ff. 104, 106-113: one leaf cancelled; see above for further details) Quire 144-1 (ff. 114-116: 1st leaf cancelled) | Quire 15six (ff. 117-122: six single leaves stitched behind Quire 14) Quire 168 (ff. 123-130) 110-5 (6th-10th leaves excised) | 2-38 412 58 610 7-98 108-2(7-8th leaves excised) 1112-1 (one leaf cancelled) 128 1310-1 (one leaf cancelled) 144-1 (1st leaf cancelled) | 15six 168 No leaf signatures pertaining to the entire volume. Beginning at Quire 2, quires are numbered 1-14 in pencil in Hindu-Arabic numerals in the lower outer corner of the first recto of each quire; readers should be aware that all of the quire designations in pencil in the volume are '1' lower than described in this record. No catchwords pertaining to the entire volume.

provenance: overview: The two parts now bound together in MS Dd.3.86.10.11 were owned by John Moore (1646-1714) Moore, John, 1646-1714 , bishop of Ely: they appear together as number 87 in the list of Moore's manuscripts published in E. Bernard, Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (Oxoniae 1697), II, p. 363 (Fragmentum Γεωπονικῶν, Gr. Fragmentum computi Maximi Monachi.). Apparently these two parts were already kept together at that time (and perhaps the present part II, containing the fragment from the Geoponica preceded the present part I with the Computus by Maximus the Confessor); the next mention of them is found in the Cambridge University Library catalogue of manuscripts of 1856, where they are parts 10 and 11 of a larger volume coprising 11 parts, Dd.3.86. The number of the manuscript in Bernard's list is written on f. 2:[1]r. That the fragment from the Geoponica was in Moore's possession is also testified by its mention in Needham's edition of the text of 1704 as Fragmentum Manuscriptum penes Episcopum Norvicensem (see Summary).

provenance: overview: Owned by the Venitian scholar Niccolò Leonico Tomeo (1456?-1531?) Tomeo, Niccolò Leonico, 1456?-1531? who left some notes (ff. 241r, 260r, 263v) and some leafed twigs as page markers (e.g. f. 112v and f. 327v). It later entered into the collection of John Moore (1646-1714), bishop of Ely Moore, John, 1646-1714 . The manuscript is neither listed in Bernard, Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (1697) nor in the handwritten supplementary list of Moore's manuscripts, now CUL MS Oo.7.50.2, compiled by Thomas Tanner after the publication of Bernard's catalogue, but a note on f. 1r states Late Bp of Elys MSS. lent to Mr. Dechaire for Mr. Pearse of Edmund Hall. The manuscript is also listed in the old catalogue of Parris-Whisson CUL MS Oo.7.53, f. 20r. The manuscript was probably previously owned by Jean-Baptiste Hautin (1580?-1640) Haultin, Jean-Baptiste, approximately 1580-1640 , whose collection partially passed to Moore. On f. 1v remains a short title in French: Receuil.

provenance: overview: Preliminary note: Much of the medieval and early modern provenance of MS Dd.4.24 remains uncertain. The manuscript contains numerous annotations and inscriptions, often of names - all, some or none of which may be connected with its ownership. Many of the connections between these names and specific individuals were first put forward by John Manly and Edith Rickert (1940), but the evidence is often tenuous and the connections speculative, and they remain the subject of some debate. See Seymour (1997), Mosser (2011) and Da Rold (2013) for further discussion. Rather than reproduce what was proposed by Manly and Rickert, this description will instead list the locations and approximate dates of the names written into MS Dd.4.24, providing convenient links to these instances and the basis for future research. ; 8r: 'HungerfordHungerford' (15th century). 'Hungerford' has not been identified. (A 'Margery Hungerford' signed her name in Cambridge, University Library, MS Ff.1.6, f. 14v, however the style of handwriting is different to that used here). ; 38r: 'Rychard MervynRychard Mervyn' (16th century). Rychard/Richard Mervyn has not been identified. ; 146r: 'Thys ys Wyllyam Langstuns Boke' (16th century). William Langston/Langdon (16th century) Langston/Langdon, William (16th century) has not been identified.; 180r: 'Said william rokes' (16th/17th century). Another inscription on f. 120v might repeat the surname 'rokes'. William Rokes/Rookes (16th/17th century) Rokes/Rookes, William (16th/17th century) has not been identified, though the same name may also be found in Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 6864. ; 150r: 'Wyllyam pully ys my name and he' (16th/17th century). William Pully Pully, William (16th/17th century) has not been identified. (A William Pulley was at Trinity College, Cambridge, 1584-91, vicar at various parishes in Kent 1596-1608 onwards. Will proven 1645. See: Venn:PLY584W.; 'S W' (16th/17th century). Initials blind-tooled on the covers of an earlier, 16th/17th-century binding, preserved on the front and rear pastedowns of the 19th-century binding (which itself has been replaced and is retained with the manuscript). 'S. W.S. W.' has not been identified. Seymour suggests that the initials could indicate the manuscript's ownership by Samuel Ward (d. 1605)Ward, Samuel (d. 1605) of Ipswich, though on what basis is not made clear, and this connection remains speculative.
acquisition: overview: The date and circumstances of the manuscript's acquisition by Cambridge University Library remain unclear. It has not been identified among the manuscripts listed as belonging to John Moore (1646-1714), bishop of Ely Moore, John, 1646-1714 in Bernard, Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (c. 1697) or the handwritten supplementary list of Moore's manuscripts (now Cambridge, University Library, MS Oo.7.50(2)) compiled by Thomas Tanner (1674-1735). However, it must have arrived by c. 1753, since it was recorded in the handwritten catalogue compiled at that time by Francis Sawyer Parris, Protobibliothecarius (now Cambridge, University Library, MS Oo.7.53-55). It is marked there as 'R', as were other books known or thought to have been among Moore's library. This collection was purchased en bloc and presented to the University Library in 1715 by George I George I, King of Great Britain, 1660-1727 , and known thereafter as the 'Royal Library' (hence, 'R'). If Moore did indeed own this manuscript, Manly and Rickert suggested that he may have obtained it from Samuel Hoadly/HodleyHoadly/Hodley, Samuel, of the grammar school at Hackney, who was noted as having in his possession a copy of 'Chaucer's Works' - though this description does not match the contents of this manuscript and the connection seems doubtful.

binding: overview: Modern conservation binding, Cambridge University Library 2021, with red full leather covering over wooden boards. 223 166 141 The pieces of the former binding, of early modern western European origin, have been retained, and are housed with the manuscript. The manuscript has been rebound a number of times. There is evidence of a number of stages of sewing, with eight sewing stations visible along the spine, including four early v-notches and later piercing. There is also evidence of cord sewing supports on the boards. There are no visible endband remnants and no evidence of spine lining. Laid paper endleaves, separate from the textblock; however due to the condition of the binding it is difficult to ascertain whether they were sewn or tipped. Both endleaves consist of a bifolio, one folio acting as a pastedown. A loose paper folio is also present at the right endleaves; this folio is made of a similar paper. Couched-laminate boards with back cornering, completely detached when examined. Previous board attachment with three laced-in cords. Board dimensions are larger than the textblock, suggesting there might have been small squares of approximately 5mm on three edges. Full covering of light brown reverse leather with lapped turn-ins with the fore-edge over. The spine was completely missing. Blind tooling decoration on both boards. Double fillet border with a double fillet inner frame, which include an inner decorative roll. Four decorative fleurons are blind tooled at the corners of the frame. 231 170 117

NB: The collation in this catalogue record deviates from the modern collation supplied in the manuscript in that it identifies ff. 2-9 as Quire 1 (instead of a1). Consequently, the subsequent quire numbers used in this catalogue record are incremented by one from the designations visible in the manuscript (e.g. Quire 1 in the manuscript is 2 in this record). The collation in this catalogue record also deviates from existing descriptions in that it divides the manuscript into two codicological units. Although there are many similarities between the handwriting, decoration, layout, and watermarks in both parts that suggest that they may have been produced in a single copying endeavour, they are treated separately in this catalogue record in order to give a detailed account of their particular aspects.

provenance: overview: Jackson 1998, p. 95, finds Parts II and V in two entries in a list of texts that Janus Lascaris (c. 1445-1535) Lascaris, Janus, 1445?-1535 brought to Florence in 1492. This list is now preserved in Hannover, Niedersächsische Landesbibliothek, MS XLII 1845 , ff. 107r-111r. The scholia to Sophocles are listed on f. 107v line 3 as Antiquae Glosulae in quasdam tragaedias Sophoclis. Lascaris had been sent by Lorenzo de' Medici to the East to acquire Greek manuscripts for the Laurentian Library, and also printed the metrical scholia to Sophocles in 1518 (see Proietti 2018, pp. 226-227). Jackson 2006, p. 32, further speculates that Part I was also brought to Florence in the same year.

On ff. 1-41 the folio numbers appear recto in the upper right-hand corner. The text on ff. 42-87 proceeds inwards from the right-hand end of the book, and is therefore inverted. Although it carries the Royal Library bookplate usually (but not invariably) indicating that a book belonged to the Moore collection, this manuscript is not recorded as part of that collection in Bernard, Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (1697), nor in the handwritten supplementary list of Moore’s manuscripts, now MS Oo.7.50(2), compiled by Tanner, Thomas, 1674-1735. codicology: foliation: Current foliation: 1-2 + 3-20, i-v, v a, vi-cvii, cvii a-cvii f, cviii-cxxiii, cxxiii a-cxxiii d, cxxiv-cxlvii, cxlvii a, cxlviii-clxvi, clxvi a, clxvii-clxviii, cxlviii a, clxix-ccx, ccx a, ccxi-ccxlix, cclx-cccxviii + 21-22 The foliation sequence stated above is the one currently in use for this volume (as of December 2022). It comprises a mixture of 15th-, 20th- and 21st-century numbering (see below for further, detailed description of each). Folios 1-2 are the front pastedown (now lifted) and endleaf; 21-22 are the rear endleaf and pastedown (still stuck down). The main portion of the manuscript had originally been foliated using Roman numerals in the 15th century, with various errors or inconsistencies - the same number used twice (ff. cxlvii, clxvi, ccx) gaps left (after ff. cvii, clxviii) blank leaves left unfoliated (after ff. v, cxxiii) a jump in numbering (from f. ccxlix to cclx) leaves that were not numbered but after which the foliation sequence continued as if they had been (after ff. ccxxvii and ccxlvi) - and leaving the latter part of the manuscript (after f. cclxiii) and accompanying matter at both ends of the volume unnumbered. In the 20th century, an attempt was made by Basil Atkinson to fill some of these gaps. Atkinson numbered the leaves after ff. cvii using lower case letters: so ff. cvii, cvii a-cvii f. He also continued the sequence of Roman numerals for the remaining leaves in the main section of the manuscript, and used Arabic numerals for the accompanying matter at each end. However, a mistake was made in the sequence of Roman numerals: starting with 'cclxiv', Atkinson continued the sequence up to 'cclxxiii' but on the next leaf accidentally slipped back ten digits to 'cclxiv', which error persisted for the rest of the main section of the volume. In 2022, in preparation for the manuscript's digitisation, the decision was taken to correct this recent mistake and ensure that all other leaves in the volume were assigned a folio number, as follows: Where the same number was used twice in the 15th-century sequence, the second leaf was marked 'a': so, f. cxlvii is followed now by f. cxlvii a; f. clxvi by f. clxvi a; f. ccx by f. ccx a. Where gaps had been left and the numbering continued incorrectly, the omitted leaf was marked 'a': so, ff. clxviii, clxviii a. Where blank leaves had been left unfoliated, the omitted leaves were marked using lower case letters: so, f. cxxii is now followed by ff. cxxiii a-cxxiii d. Where there was a jump in the 15th-century foliation, this has been left as it: so, f. ccxlix is followed by cclx. Where leaves were not numbered but the foliation sequence continues as if they had been, numbers have been written onto these leaves accordingly: so, f. ccxxvii is followed by ff. ccxxviii and ccxxix, and f. ccxlvi is followed by ccxlvii. Atkinson's foliation has been cancelled from the point of his mistake onwards (so, after f. cclxxiii) and the numbering continued correctly: so f. cclxxiii is followed by ff. cclxxiv through to cccxviii. The following imperfect leaves were also foliated: f. 12: this had been counted in Atkinson's sequence but not physically numbered. f. v a As per standard practice at the University Library, stubs have not been numbered. These changes were made in pencil in the upper right-hand corner of the rectos, on 17 November 2022, by James FreemanFreeman, James, Medieval Manuscripts Specialist, Cambridge University Library. 15th-century foliation: i-cclxiii Numbering in Roman numerals, written in brown ink in the upper right-hand corner of the rectos, perhaps by Simon Elryngton. 20th-century foliation: 1-20, cvii a-cvii f, cclxiv-cclxxiii, cclxiv-cccviii, 21-22 Numbering in pencil in the upper right-hand corner of the rectos, by the hand of B.F.C. The first of the duplicated folio 172s retains the designation f. 172 and the second has been redesignated as f. [172a]. The gaps in the foliation sequence due to omitted designations for folios 155, 202, and 233 have been retained - these designations do not exist in the current foliation sequence. The unfoliated leaf after f. 157 has been assigned the desigation f. [157a]. The unfoliated leaf after f. 174 has been assigned the desigation f. [174a]. provenance: overview: The manuscript was bought in 1596, in Messina, by a certain hieromonk Neophytos of Sinai for the price of 15 tarì, as it is written in an annotation on the left pastedown: ͵αφϙϛ΄ ἀγόρασα τὸ παρὸν ταρία ιε΄ Νεόφυτος ἱερομόναχος Σιναίτης ἐν Μεσσήνῃ τῆς Σικελίας. ; The hieromonk Neophytos probably acquired the manuscript for Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai. The codex indeed was there in 1618/1619: this date is mentioned in an official note by Ioasaph written on f. 257v, below the last text: Ἡ παροῦσα βίβλος τῇ ἱερᾷ μονῇ τοῦ Σιναίου ἁγίου ὄρους κεκλήρωται· συνοχῇ ἀρᾶς, καὶ δεσμοῦ, τὸν σφετερησόμενον ἀπείργουσα, διὰ τοῦ παρόντος τῆς ἐμεῖς ταπεινότητος, διωρισθικοῦ γράμματος. ͵ζρκζ΄ ἐκ τοῦ (?) Σινᾶ ὄρους Ἰωάσαφ. (The last five words in monocondyle). The same note signed by Ioasaph in monocondyle is present in a manuscript which has remained until now in Saint Catherine's Monastery, MS Sinai, Saint Catherine's Monastery, gr. 74, f. 246r (a transcription of the note is found in Δ. Στρατηγοπουλος, Τὸ χειρόγραφο Θεοτοκάριο τοῦ Ἱδρύματος Παπανικολάου (Κομοτηνή) καὶ ὁ κωδικογράφος Ἱερεμίας Μαγγαφούρης ο Σιναϊτης, in Byzantina Symmeikta 27 (2017), pp. 315-346: 337). ; The codex was in the hands of the English merchant Edward Abbott, consul at Cairo in the 1650s (concerning him see Oates 1986, pp. 292-294 with bibliography), who donated it to Hobart, Nicholas, approximately 1605-1657 Nicholas Hobart (ca. 1605-1657) , Fellow of King's College in Cambridge from 1625 to 1650. This is stated in a message from Abbott to Hobart written on f. i verso, dated 16th July 1650 in Cairo: nº 1. Sir, this manuscript I obteyned by favor of a friend out of the publique library of the Bishopp of Mount Sinai resident heere in Grand Cayro, wharein though the Synopsis on Gallens' book of Terapephtike and his problems on the humours bee common, yet I suppose that the Physicall Treatises of Simeon Protomestraki of Antioch, of the most learned Psellius, and the problems of Alexander Aphrodisius, are more rare and usefull. You will finde it iust 100 yeares from this 16th of July 1650 since the finishing of this book by George of Constantinople. Wich accept from your most affectionate servant Edw. Abbott. Grand Cayro, this 16th July 1650.

provenance: overview: The manuscript was owned by the Neapolitan humanist Antonio Seripando (1476-1531) Seripando, Antonio, 1476-1531 , as stated in the note on f. 108v: Antonij Seripandi ex Jani Parrhasii testamento. Seripando inherited the library of the humanist Aulus Janus Parrhasius (1470-1522) Parrasio, Aulo Giano, 1470-1522 . At Seripando’s death, his books passed on to his brother, Cardinal Girolamo Seripando (1493-1563) Seripando, Girolamo, 1493-1563 , who in turn bequeathed his library to the Augustinian convent of San Giovanni a Carbonara in Naples. Before being declared a 'Royal Library' by King Ferdinand IV of Naples in 1792, the convent library was predated on several occasions and in some instances manuscripts and books were sold by the monks themselves.

acquisition: overview: The precise date of acquisition by Cambridge University Library is not known. It contains a donation bookplate engraved by John Pine in 1736 (front cover, inner), suggesting that it was presented to the University Library in 1715 by George I, and had previously been owned by John Moore (b. 1646, d. 1714), bishop of Ely. However, the manuscript is not identified among those listed in Bernard, Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ (c. 1697), or in the handwritten supplementary list of Moore's manuscripts, now CUL Oo.7.50(2), compiled by Thomas Tanner (1674-1735). The presence of a donation bookplate in manuscripts known to have not been part of Moore's collection means that this instance cannot be taken as definitive proof of his ownership.

binding: overview: Rebound in March 1967 by Douglas Cockerell and SonDouglas Cockerell and Son in Grantchester, Cambridgeshire. Quarter bound in Morocco leather with marbled paper sides and parchment-tipped corners over millboard. Marbled paper sides are in tones of cream, ochre, brown, and grey in the typical Cockerell style of a dense comb-marbled pattern in geometric forms. Three raised bands on spine. Head and tail bands sewn in a neutral cream yarn. Spine is mid-brown Morocco leather, with blind-tooled single fillets at the upper and lower perimeters of the compartments and horizontally through the centre of the raised bands (i.e., across the width of the spine). Title label in black Morocco leather applied to spine, with title 'MACROBIUS | PLATEARIUS' tooled in gold. Shelfmark label in black Morocco leather applied at the lower opening of the spine with 'Gg.1.10' tooled in gold. Paper pastedowns pasted over the turn ins. All quires taken down and remounted between paper guards during the 1967 rebinding and some quires resewn - paper stubs visible between quire boundaries throughout the volume. The left pastedown contains: a note by H.L. Pink recording the 1967 rebinding; another by Pink of the shelfmark 'Gg.1.10', in pencil; a bookplate commemorating the donation of the 'Royal Library'; and an 'F' in pencil, which refers to the size of the book according to a Cambridge University Library classification scheme. The right pastedown contains a collation statement, written in pencil by the hand of H.L. PinkPink, H. L.. Leaves ff. [a] and [b] are paper, blank, and are cojoint with the pastedowns.

Bradshaw introduced the practice of assigning folio numbers to leaves that he judged to be missing on the basis of the manuscript's collation. Unfortunately, in the case of MS Gg.4.27(1), Bradshaw's interpretation of the structure of the manuscript's leaves in Quire 25 changed: having previously thought that one leaf was missing after f. 302v, he later decided that two leaves were missing. As a consequence, his first foliation sequence was thereafter cancelled and a second sequence added that differed from the first by 1. Some this second sequence has since been over-written by a later hand. Although replacement leaves were added throughout the manuscript during its conservation, and although these technically carry a folio number (in accordance with Bradshaw's foliation practice), the foliation statement given above counts only medieval leaves and omits replacement leaves and stubs (see also Collation). The leaves of parchment that have been inserted for missing leaves are: ff. 1-4, 12-13, 28-29, 54, 80-81, 102, 127-131, 142-144, 185, 193, 195, 211, 228, 233-234, 242-243, 260, 276, 285-286, 298-301, 303-304, 313, 318-320, 325-326, 350, 363-364, 372, 374, 383, 399-400, 405, 412, 418, 425, 428-429, 444, 469, 513, 517. The leaves of parchment that have been inserted for cancelled leaves are: ff. [109a], [118a], [123a], [123b], [430a], [430b], [493a], [508a], [515a]. As Parkes and Beadle (1979-80) explain (see vol. 3, p. 10), f. '444' is a questionable case. Bradshaw thought that a leaf was missing here, and thus assigned it a folio number: 'the recto could have contained the 'Retractions', and the verso would have been blank. However, the display at the foot of f. 443v could have been regarded as a colophon (the script is larger than that of other displayed headings and colophons in the Canterbury Tales...), in which case the leaf would have been blank'. Blank, modern endleaves [ii]-[iv] and [v]-[vii] have not been digitised. 17th-century foliation: 5-482 (with gaps where leaves are missing) Written in black ink in the upper right-hand corner of the recto side of each leaf, after the insertion of replacement leaves of text (which are now bound separately as Cambridge, University Library, MS Gg.4.27, additional leaves), probably by Holland, Joseph, active 1585 Joseph Holland (d. 1605).

James has provided in his unpublished notes on this manuscript: James suggests that Quire 9 is missing one leaf but the quire, however, is a complete sexternion. While James tentatively identifies Quires 20-24 as sexternions, this collation proposes different structures at this point. While James suggests that his final quire, Quire 34, consist of 16 leaves, the different quality and thickness of ff. 370-371 and the clearly visible thread thackets between f. 378 and f. 379, make it likely that there are two different quires: a quire that consists of 2 bifolia only and has one missing leaf (Quire 35) followed by a regular sexternion (Quire 36). Due to the fact that the manuscript is tightly bound, it is not possible to establish a fully verifiable collation. While James adds that his collation is not practicable, the collation in this record is partially also a suggestion in lieu of codicological evidence. While James considers this manuscript a compsoite that consists of four separate codicologial units (ff. 1r-270v [Part 1]; ff. 271r-304v [Part 2]; ff. 305r-357v [Part 3]; ff. 358r-385v [Part 4]), this collation considers the manuscript a single unit that was probably produced over a longer period of time (years if not decades) but probably within the same university context. codicology: collation: The manuscript consists of 23 quires, of which one is a binion, three are ternia, two consist of twelve folios and the rest are quaternia. Quire 18+1 ff. 2-9 There is a small leaf inserted after the sixth folio. Quire 28 ff. 10-17 Quire 34 ff. 18-21 Quire 46 ff. 22-27 Quires 5-612 ff. 28-50 Quires 7-178 ff. 51-137 Quires 18-218 ff. 138-169 Quire 226 ff. 170-175 Quire 238+1 ff. 176-184 An extra folio has been added to the end of the quire. There are quire signatures in Greek numerals, in brown ink, on the first folio of each quire, recto, lower right, on Quires 2-3 (βʹ-γʹ). The same hand has placed signatures on the last folio of each quire, verso, lower right, on Quires 3-6, but these numbers are incorrect (δʹ-εʹ, ζʹ-ηʹ). The sequence in Greek numerals on the first folio of each quire has been continued in pencil by a different hand, placing the signature for Quire 4 (δʹ) on Quire 5 and misplacing the numbers 5 and 7 (εʹ, ζʹ) on ff. 38r and 57r. This sequence has been continued on Quire 8 with the number 8 (ηʹ), but this has been struck through. A fresh sequence has been begun beside this with the number 1 (αʹ), but continued no further. A sequence of signatures in lower-case Latin letters, in red ink, appears on the first folio of each quire, recto, lower right, on Quires 1-7 (a-g). A new sequence of quire signatures in Greek numerals, in red ink, on the first folio of each quire, recto, lower right, beginning again from 1, appears on Quires 8-11 (αʹ-δʹ) (ff. 59-90, containing the Gospel of Mark). Another new sequence of quire signatures in Greek numerals, in pencil, on the first folio of each quire, recto, lower right beginning again from 1, appears on Quires 12-17 (αʹ-ϛʹ) (ff. 91-137, containing the Gospel of Luke). The number 6 (ϛʹ) in this sequence is erroneously placed one folio too late (on f. 131r rather than f. 130r). This suggests that these signatures were placed on the basis of the foliation rather than physical examination or directly counting folios, and that the person responsible was misled by the error in the foliation resulting from the omission of a folio number from f. [121a]. Another new sequence of quire signatures in Greek numerals, in brown ink, on the first folio of each quire, recto, lower right, beginning again from 1, appears during Quires 18-22 (ff. 138-175, containing the Gospel of John). Some of these have been wholly or partially lost to cropping. They survive in whole or in part on Quires 18, 20-22 (αʹ, γʹ-εʹ). Losses and partial losses to this sequence have been filled by a later sequence of signatures in Latin letters, in pencil, on the first folio of each quire, recto, lower right. These appear on Quires 19-21, 23 (b-d, f).

Covers are decorated with a narrow double-fillet at the perimeter of the boards and a dotted single-fillet inset from the perimeter of the boards by c. 20mm. Small fleurons at each corner of the dotted-fillet frame, positioned between the dotted-fillet frame and the double-fillet frame. Head, fore and tail edges of the covers decorated with a double-fillet. Spine is green-brown leather. Five raised bands with double-fillet decoration at the upper and lower perimeter of each compartment and at the upper and lower openings of the spine. Spine is capped at head and tail: head and tail bands are not visible. A title 'ALCHEMICA' tooled in gold on the spine in one compartment and 'Ii.3.17' for the current shelfmark tooled in gold in another. Paper pastedowns pasted over the turn ins. The right pastedown is blank. [i]-[iv] and [v]-[viii] probably contemporary with this binding. Binding height: 295 mm, width: 200 mm, depth: 45 mm. This damage is typically caused by brass (or other copper-alloy) book furniture such as a staple, boss, or fastening plate. codicology: extent: Codex: ii + 6 + 1, i, 148, ii, 147, ii, 1, i, 1, ii + i + xvi + i + ii leaves. The manuscript opens with eight endleaves, two added to the volume when it was most recently bound and six added when it was bound in the 16th century (see Binding for further details). From that point onwards, the medieval portion of the manuscript begins, however leaves were added in various places during the 16th century in order to supply space for a table of contents, a printed accompaniment to part of the text, or text missing through the loss of leaves. These different leaves have been enumerated above and distinguished from the medieval leaves by commas. The plus sign separates this medieval section from the various endleaves or added leaves that precede or follow it. (See Part 2's Additions for further details of the contents of some of these). Two unfoliated paper stubs are present after f. 21, in place of two excised leaves, and were added in order to secure the binding of the two leaves (ff. 16-17) that were originally conjoint with them. Being stubs rather than partial leaves, they are not included in this statement of extent. However, since one of them does contain a 19th/20th-century annotation in pencil, they have been assigned numbers for the purpose of this digital record (see Foliation).

provenance: overview: Owned by King Henry VII of England Henry VII, King of England, 1457-1509 and Elizabeth of York Elizabeth, Queen, consort of Henry VII, King of England, 1465-1503 . There is an added bifolium in the volume (ff. 5r–6v) one leaf of which (f. 6v) is painted with the arms of Henry VII impaled with those of his wife, Elizabeth of York. Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in 1486, and so the joint demonstration of their ownership of the volume presumably postdates the date of their marriage. ; The name 'Will(?elmus) Walter(?us)' on f. 86r next to a Latin couplet (see Contents for further information) and the word 'llinpenff'(?), all in what appears to be the same 16th-century hand. A William Walter (d. 1523) was known to Henry VII, whom he briefly served as an envoy at the papal curia in the late 1490s. This Walter had studied at Bologna earlier in that decade and was subsequently recorded as doctor of canon and civil law there; he spent the last two decades of his life as archdeacon of Brecon. The word 'llinpenff' bears the hallmarks of an as yet unidentified Welsh placename that began 'Llyn...' (meaning 'lake'), which is also suggestive of a possible connection between this manuscript and this Walter. Another William Walter (fl. c. 1525-1533), poet and translator, was alive around this time. He may have been the owner of London, British Library, MS Sloane 1686, f. 1r , a copy of the Canterbury Tales, which bears an ownership inscription matching his name, written in a later, different style of handwriting to the inscription found in MS Ii.5.11. Little is known about this second Walter's life, and Ralph Griffiths has put forward suggestive evidence that the two Walters are one and the same. R. Griffiths, 'From Bologna to Brecon: The Cosmopolitan World of a Pre-Reformation Archdeacon', Medieval Prosopography 33 (2018), pp. 153-166 A.S.G. Edwards, 'Walter, William (fl. c. 1525-1533), Oxford Dictionary of National Biography (2004) [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/28641] ; The manuscript may have left the royal library by c. 1535-1542. MS Ii.5.11 is not listed among the 123 French manuscripts and printed books recorded by an anonymous French visitor to Richmond Palace in 1535. The list is printed in H. Omont, 'Les manuscrits français des rois d'Angleterre au château de Richmond', in Etudes romanes dédiés à Gaston Paris (Paris: É. Bouillon, 1891), pp. 1-13 and in CBMLC 7, pp. 3-29 as list 'H1' with minor variations from Omont's list. Nor is MS Ii.5.11 in the list of the books in the Upper Library at Westminster made in 1542 shortly after the death of Henry VIII, which includes four copies of the Régime du corps identified in CBMLC 7 as Lisbon, Biblioteca de Ajuda MS 52-XIII-2, London, British Library, MS Royal 20.B.ix, London, British Library, MS Royal 16.F.8, and London, British Library, MS Royal 20.B.x; the 1542 Westminster list is printed in CBMLC 7 as list 'H2', see esp., H2 nos 1291, 1294, 1299(1-2). codicology: collation: The manuscript is a composite item and consists of several parts: one 2-leaf fragment, and three parts consisting of one or more quires. The majority of the extant quires are gatherings of 8 leaves, with variation in quire size typically found at the beginning and the end of the parts. The 9th leaf of Quire 10 is an inserted singleton. The 5th leaf of Quire 13 is absent and may have been blank and later excised: following historic foliation practice at Cambridge University Library, this leaf has been assigned a folio number (f. 102), though it is not certain that text is missing as a consequence of its removal. There are traces of at least two lost quires within the manuscript. The current Quire 14 contains the first half of al-Khwarazmi's Arithmetic in Latin, and catchwords on the last verso of that quire f. 111v suggest that the text once continued onto a subsequent quire, now lost. The current Quire 15 ends part of the way through Chapter 10 of Hermannus Contractus' De utilitatibus astrolabii, and the opening of Quire 16 begins part of the way through Chapter 19 of that text, which suggests that there was once an intervening quire with the remainder of Chapter 10, through to the beginning of Chapter 19 of that text. Both quires have been missing since at least the late Medieval period as a medieval collator has added leaf signatures and catchwords to the volume that treat Quires 14-16 as a sequence without any gaps. There are two paper endleaves at each end of the volume, ff. [a]-[b] at the beginning, and ff. [c]-[d] at the end. The rest of the leaves are arranged as follows: Fragment: 2 parchment leaves (ff. i-ii) | Parchment endleaves: (ff. 1-2) + Quires 1-68 (ff. 3-50) Quire 74 (ff. 51-54) Quires 8-98 (ff. 55-70 Quire 1010+1 (ff. 71-81; 9th leaf, f. 81, inserted) Quires 11-128 (ff. 82-97) Quire 136-1 (ff. 98-103; 5th leaf cancelled, but counted in foliation as f. 102) | Quire 148 (ff. 104-111) | Quires 15-168 (ff. 112-127) i-ii | ff. 1-2 + Quires 1-68 74 8-98 1010+1 (9th inserted) 11-128 136-1 (5th missing) | 148 | 15-168 A late-medieval collator has added alphanumeric leaf signatures to several quires across the composite parts of the manuscript; these signatures demonstrate that the manuscript has been in its current composite arrangement since the later middle ages. Where the quires have late-medieval alphanumeric leaf signatures, the signatures are in red ink and appear on the rectos of the first half of each quire in the format 'letter + Roman numeral' where the Roman numeral expresses the position of the leaf within the quire, e.g., 'b iii' indicates the third leaf of quire 'b'. Quires 10 and 11 are designated 'a' and 'b' and Quires 14-16 are designated as 'x', 'y', 'z' respectively. Quires 7, 9, 12, and 13 all have Roman numerals in red ink on the leaves in the first half of each quire, but no letter designations. Quire signatures in the lower outer corner of the first recto of each quire in pencil in Hindu-Arabic numerals, added in the 19th century. Small + signs added to the lower outer corner of the first recto in the second half of each quire (i.e., on the 5th recto of a typical quire of 8 leaves). A late-medieval collator has added catchwords to several quires acrss the composite parts of the manuscript; these catchwords demonstrate that the manuscript has been in its current composite arrangement since the late middle ages. At f. 111v there are both the catchwords for a lost quire in the hand of the main scribe of that text 'Sicque constitues .viii.', and catchwords by the later-medieval collator 'est quidem' which reproduces the text on the following recto which belongs to a separate composite part.

provenance: overview: The name of Arthur Hopton Hopton, Arthur is inscribed in the upper margin of f. 242v ('Arturus Hopton'): he was a member of the Hopton family of Westwood in Blythburgh in North-East Suffolk, as a 16th-century or early 17th-century note suggests: 'P[our] my humfre owen de suffolke amen / Selled and delyvered in the presens of master thomas hoopton' (f. 100v, upper margin). The same hand has written a note with the date 'Anno Domini 1571' (f. 97r, outer margin); a note on a payment to master Harvey of Darsham in Suffolk: 'Item payd to master harve of darsam / Item the county of Suffolke knave Amen' (f. 131v, upper margin); and 'Suffolk and Norffolk / amen dico vobis' (f. 245r, outer margin). Darsham is situated a few miles to the south-east of Blythburgh. If these notes were written by Arthur Hopton (which is unclear because he writes his name in a different stylised script), then he almost certainly was Arthur Hopton (c. 1540-1607), High Sheriff of Suffolk.; The name of Arthur Melle Melle, Arthur: 'Arthur melle ded wryt thys' (f. 2r, lower margin). Perhaps Arthur Melle, son of Henry Melle and his wife Frances, born in 1548 at Bramfield, five miles south-west from Blythburgh.

codicology: collation: The manuscript comprises almost entirely quires of ten leaves. It is formed of five codicological units, which bear some evidence of different methods of preparation and production but which appear to have been planned and produced contemporaneously, with the intention that they be bound together from the outset. The sequence of medieval leaf signatures also runs continuously across the entire manuscript. Except for the fourth unit, where leaves are missing and the text ends imperfectly, each section ends with a blank space or page and the excision of the remaining leaves of the final quire, which were themselves probably blank. These units are: 1: Quires 1-15 (ff. 2-147) 2: Quires 16-19 (ff. 148-179) 3: Quires 20-21 (ff. 180-193) 4: Quires 22-24 (ff. 194-215) 5: Quires 25-27 (ff. 216-245) Prior to Quire 1, there is a single ruled leaf surviving (f. 1r), bearing text, and a further blank but similarly ruled stub. It is not clear whether these once formed a quire or were intended as endleaves; the stub bears some evidence on its recto side of having been used as a pastedown. It is not included in the collation, therefore.
